posts.title: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) injection
posts.summary: V Immunosuppressants · Pyrimidine analogue antimetabolite (antineoplastic)
posts.body:
_Injectables · V Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Pyrimidine analogue antimetabolite (antineoplastic)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted to fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate, which inhibits thymidylate synthase → no thymidine → no DNA synthesis
- Also incorporated into RNA
- In keloids: inhibits fibroblast proliferation and TGF-β-driven collagen production

## Pharmacokinetics
- IL use gives minimal systemic levels; systemic drug is metabolised by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Intralesional: keloids and hypertrophic scars (alone or mixed with triamcinolone), warts, keratoacanthoma, small BCC (selected)
- Vitiligo (with microneedling/dermabrasion, off-label)
- Topical 5% cream for actinic keratosis, Bowen disease, superficial BCC (topicals slot)

## Dose & formulations
- Supplied as 50 mg/mL injection
- Keloids: 50 mg/mL alone, or mixed with triamcinolone (e.g. 0.9 mL 5-FU + 0.1 mL triamcinolone 40 mg/mL); 0.2–0.5 mL per cm² of lesion; total usually under 2–3 mL per session; every 1–4 weeks
- Keratoacanthoma: 50 mg/mL, 0.1–1 mL weekly

## Adverse effects
- IL: pain, burning, ulceration, purpura, hyperpigmentation
- Systemic (rare with IL): myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhoea; severe toxicity in DPD deficiency
- Systemic 5-FU skin effects: hand–foot syndrome, serpentine supravenous hyperpigmentation, photosensitivity

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding
- Known DPD deficiency; bone marrow suppression; infection at site

## Drug interactions
- Warfarin effect increases
- Sorivudine/brivudine (antivirals): fatal DPD inhibition

## Monitoring
- CBC if large or frequent doses are used

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category D/X depending on form).

## Viva points
- Thymidylate synthase inhibitor
- 5-FU + TAC combination for keloids reduces atrophy and recurrence
- DPD deficiency → severe toxicity
- Supravenous serpentine hyperpigmentation with IV use

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.47 (Topical and intralesional chemotherapeutic agents); Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Abacavir + Lamivudine
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · Fixed-dose combination of two NRTIs (nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors)
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** Fixed-dose combination of two NRTIs (nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors)

## Mechanism of action
- Both are nucleoside analogues, phosphorylated inside cells to active triphosphates
- They compete with natural nucleotides for HIV reverse transcriptase and cause chain termination of viral DNA
- Abacavir is a guanosine analogue (active form carbovir triphosphate); lamivudine is a cytidine analogue that is also active against hepatitis B

## Pharmacokinetics
- Both are well absorbed with or without food
- Abacavir: metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase and glucuronidation (no CYP); lamivudine: excreted by the kidneys
- Long intracellular half-lives allow once-daily dosing

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Backbone of first-line ART in children (with dolutegravir) under the national (NACO) programme
- Adults when tenofovir cannot be used (e.g. renal disease, osteoporosis)

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: abacavir 600 mg + lamivudine 300 mg once daily
- Children: weight-band dosing with dispersible tablets (abacavir 120 mg + lamivudine 60 mg) as per NACO tables

## Adverse effects
- Abacavir hypersensitivity syndrome (about 5–8%, usually in the first 6 weeks): fever, rash, GI symptoms, malaise, cough or breathlessness
- It is strongly linked to HLA-B*57:01. Rechallenge after a reaction can be fatal, so never restart
- Abacavir: possible increase in myocardial infarction risk
- Lamivudine: very well tolerated; pancreatitis in children; flare of hepatitis B when stopped
- NRTI class: lactic acidosis and hepatic steatosis (rare with these two)

## Contraindications
- HLA-B*57:01 positive (test before use where available)
- Previous abacavir hypersensitivity (lifelong contraindication)
- Moderate–severe liver impairment (abacavir)

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol raises abacavir levels
- Lamivudine: co-trimoxazole raises levels slightly; do not combine with emtricitabine (same drug class and target)

## Monitoring
- CD4 count and viral load as per programme schedule
- Hepatitis B status before starting (lamivudine stopping can cause a flare)
- LFT; lipids; cardiovascular risk

## Pregnancy & lactation
Both can be used in pregnancy; the national programme prefers TLD (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir) for pregnant women.

## Viva points
- Abacavir hypersensitivity = HLA-B*57:01 — never rechallenge
- Lamivudine also treats hepatitis B; stopping it can cause a hepatitis flare
- Current NACO preferred first-line for adults is TLD; ABC + 3TC + DTG is used in children

## Note on sources
Wolverton covers ART only briefly (HLA associations and a list of drugs), so Khopkar and NACO were the main guides here. Regimens change often — please confirm with the latest NACO guidelines.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4 (Antiretroviral drugs); Wolverton 4e ch.3 (HLA-B*57:01 pharmacogenetics) and ch.11; check against current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Acitretin
posts.summary: I Retinoids · Second-generation (mono-aromatic) retinoid; active metabolite of etretinate
posts.body:
_Oral · I Retinoids_

**Class:** Second-generation (mono-aromatic) retinoid; active metabolite of etretinate

## Mechanism of action
- Binds nuclear RAR and RXR receptors and changes gene transcription
- Normalises epidermal proliferation and differentiation
- Anti-inflammatory: reduces neutrophil migration (hence its good effect in pustular psoriasis)
- Not immunosuppressive — useful in HIV-associated psoriasis and in transplant recipients

## Pharmacokinetics
- Bioavailability about 60%, better with food; 95% albumin bound; half-life about 50 h
- With alcohol it is re-esterified to etretinate, which is stored in fat and has a half-life of 80–160 days
- This is why contraception must continue for years after stopping

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Psoriasis: pustular (generalised and palmoplantar) and erythrodermic respond best to monotherapy
- Plaque psoriasis: modest alone; much better combined with phototherapy (Re-PUVA, Re-NB-UVB), which also lowers UV dose
- Disorders of keratinisation: ichthyoses (lamellar, epidermolytic), Darier disease, PRP, palmoplantar keratoderma
- Hypertrophic and palmoplantar lichen planus; hypertrophic lupus erythematosus
- Chemoprevention of squamous cell carcinoma in organ-transplant recipients

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 25–50 mg once daily with the main meal (start at 25 mg; avoid high starting doses)
- Lower doses (10–25 mg) are often enough when combined with phototherapy
- Children (keratinisation disorders): about 0.5–1 mg/kg/day, using the lowest dose that works
- Capsules 10, 25 mg; full response in psoriasis may take 3–6 months

## Adverse effects
- Mucocutaneous: cheilitis, xerosis, 'sticky' skin, peeling of palms and soles, retinoid dermatitis, paronychia, pyogenic granuloma
- Hair loss (telogen effluvium, dose-related) is commoner than with isotretinoin
- Raised triglycerides and cholesterol; raised transaminases (rarely toxic hepatitis)
- Bone: DISH-like hyperostosis, extraspinal calcification, premature epiphyseal closure in children on long courses
- Pseudotumor cerebri, night blindness, myalgia
- Teratogenic (long-lasting because of etretinate formation)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy, and women who may become pregnant within 3 years of stopping
- Breastfeeding; severe liver or kidney disease; chronic alcohol use; marked hyperlipidaemia
- Concurrent methotrexate (risk of hepatitis) or tetracyclines (pseudotumor cerebri)

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol → conversion to etretinate (long-lasting teratogenicity)
- Methotrexate: severe hepatotoxicity — avoid
- Tetracyclines: pseudotumor cerebri
- Progestin-only pill becomes unreliable
- Vitamin A: additive toxicity; phenytoin displaced from protein binding

## Monitoring
- Pregnancy tests: before, monthly during treatment, and periodically for 3 years after stopping
- Lipids and LFTs at baseline, then every 1–2 weeks for the first 1–2 months, then every 3 months
- Children on long courses: watch growth; X-ray only if bone symptoms appear

## Pregnancy & lactation
Absolute contraindication (old FDA category X). Contraception from 1 month before, throughout, and for 3 years after stopping. No alcohol during treatment and for 2 months after. No blood donation for 3 years.

## Viva points
- Best indications are pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis; for plaques, combine with UV (Re-PUVA)
- Alcohol turns acitretin into etretinate — hence 3 years of contraception
- It is not immunosuppressive, so it is safe in HIV and in transplant recipients
- Never combine with methotrexate

## Note on sources
Some Indian and European texts give 2 years of contraception after acitretin; Wolverton (US label) gives 3 years, which we follow.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.22; Khopkar (Oral retinoids). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Acyclovir
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Anti-herpes · Synthetic acyclic guanosine (nucleoside) analogue
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Anti-herpes_

**Class:** Synthetic acyclic guanosine (nucleoside) analogue

## Mechanism of action
- Phosphorylated first by viral thymidine kinase (so it is activated only in infected cells), then by host kinases to acyclovir triphosphate
- Acyclovir triphosphate competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and is incorporated into viral DNA → chain termination
- Active against HSV-1 and HSV-2 (most), VZV (needs higher doses); weak against EBV and CMV

## Pharmacokinetics
- Oral bioavailability only 15–30% → frequent dosing
- Half-life about 2.5–3 h; excreted unchanged by the kidneys (glomerular filtration and tubular secretion)
- Reduce dose in renal impairment

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Genital herpes: first episode, recurrences, suppression
- Herpes labialis (severe or frequent), eczema herpeticum, herpetic whitlow
- Herpes zoster (start within 72 h) and varicella in adolescents/adults or complicated cases
- HSV-associated recurrent erythema multiforme (suppression)
- Severe or disseminated infection, encephalitis, neonatal herpes (IV)

## Dose & formulations
- First-episode genital herpes: 400 mg three times daily (or 200 mg five times daily) × 7–10 days
- Recurrent genital herpes: 400 mg three times daily × 5 days, or 800 mg twice daily × 5 days, or 800 mg three times daily × 2 days
- Suppression: 400 mg twice daily
- Herpes zoster: 800 mg five times daily × 7 days
- Varicella: 20 mg/kg (max 800 mg) four times daily × 5 days
- Severe/disseminated HSV or VZV: 10 mg/kg IV every 8 h (neonatal herpes 20 mg/kg every 8 h)

## Adverse effects
- Oral: nausea, diarrhoea, headache (generally very safe)
- IV: crystalline nephropathy (keep well hydrated, infuse slowly), phlebitis at the drip site
- Neurotoxicity (confusion, tremor, hallucinations) in elderly or renally impaired patients

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to acyclovir or valacyclovir
- Dose reduction (not contraindication) in renal impairment

## Drug interactions
- Probenecid and cimetidine reduce renal clearance
- Mycophenolate: both drugs' levels rise
- Other nephrotoxic drugs (with IV acyclovir)

## Monitoring
- Renal function with IV use or in the elderly

## Pregnancy & lactation
Considered safe (old FDA category B); used for first-episode and late-pregnancy suppression of genital herpes. Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Needs viral thymidine kinase for activation → selective for infected cells
- Resistance (TK-deficient mutants) occurs in the immunocompromised → foscarnet or cidofovir
- Zoster needs about 4 times the HSV dose
- Hydrate patients on IV acyclovir

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.11 (Systemic antiviral agents); Khopkar ch.3. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Adrenaline (epinephrine) injection
posts.summary: VI Emergency drugs · Endogenous catecholamine; α and β adrenergic agonist
posts.body:
_Injectables · VI Emergency drugs_

**Class:** Endogenous catecholamine; α and β adrenergic agonist

## Mechanism of action
- α1: vasoconstriction → raises BP, reduces mucosal oedema
- β1: increases heart rate and contractility
- β2: bronchodilation; also stabilises mast cells (less mediator release)

## Pharmacokinetics
- IM into the anterolateral thigh gives faster, higher peak levels than SC
- Onset within minutes; short action (5–10 min) — repeat dosing may be needed
- Concentrations: 1 mg/mL (1:1000) for IM; 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000) for IV in cardiac arrest

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Anaphylaxis — the first-line, life-saving drug
- Cardiac arrest (IV/IO)
- Severe angioedema with airway involvement
- With local anaesthetics (1:100,000–1:200,000) to prolong action and reduce bleeding

## Dose & formulations
- Anaphylaxis: 0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL (1:1000) IM in the anterolateral thigh — adult and child over 12 years 0.5 mg (0.5 mL); 6–12 years 0.3 mg; under 6 years 0.15 mg
- Repeat every 5 min if no improvement
- Refractory anaphylaxis: IV infusion by experienced staff only (never give 1:1000 IV bolus)
- Cardiac arrest: 1 mg IV (1:10,000) every 3–5 min
- Autoinjectors: 0.3 mg (adult), 0.15 mg (child) — prescribe for patients with previous anaphylaxis

## Adverse effects
- Tremor, palpitations, anxiety, pallor, headache
- Tachyarrhythmias, hypertension, myocardial ischaemia (mainly with IV use or overdose)
- Tissue necrosis with accidental injection into digits (rare) or extravasation

## Contraindications
- None in anaphylaxis — always give
- Caution with local anaesthetic use: uncontrolled hypertension, severe heart disease, hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma

## Drug interactions
- β-blockers: anaphylaxis resistant to adrenaline → give glucagon 1–5 mg IV; non-selective β-blockers may cause severe hypertension
- Tricyclic antidepressants, MAO inhibitors, cocaine: exaggerated pressor effect
- Halothane: arrhythmias

## Monitoring
- BP, pulse, SpO₂, ECG; observe for at least 6–12 h after anaphylaxis (biphasic reaction)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Use without hesitation in anaphylaxis in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Anaphylaxis: 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) IM in the thigh — repeat after 5 min
- Antihistamines and steroids are only add-ons
- Glucagon for patients on β-blockers
- Every dermatology procedure room should have adrenaline ready

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.58 (local anaesthetics) and anaphylaxis sections; Resuscitation Council / WAO anaphylaxis guidance. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Apremilast
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor (small molecule)
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitor (small molecule)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits PDE4 → raises intracellular cAMP in immune cells
- Higher cAMP lowers pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23, IFN-γ) and raises anti-inflammatory IL-10
- Immunomodulatory rather than immunosuppressive — no lab monitoring needed

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; metabolised by CYP3A4; half-life about 6–9 h

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Approved: moderate–severe plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, oral ulcers of Behçet disease
- Scalp, nail, palmoplantar and genital psoriasis
- Off-label: atopic dermatitis, lichen planus, hidradenitis suppurativa, alopecia areata (limited)

## Dose & formulations
- Titration pack over 5 days (10 mg → 20 mg → 30 mg) to reduce GI side effects, then 30 mg twice daily
- Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance under 30 mL/min): 30 mg once daily

## Adverse effects
- GI: diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting (mostly in the first 2 weeks)
- Headache, upper respiratory infection
- Weight loss (about 5–10% of body weight in some patients)
- Depression and suicidal thoughts (rare) — ask about mood

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity
- Caution in depression or suicidal ideation, low body weight, severe renal impairment

## Drug interactions
- Strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin) lower levels — avoid

## Monitoring
- No routine blood tests
- Weight and mood at follow-up visits

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited human data; animal studies showed pregnancy loss at high doses — avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- PDE4 → ↑cAMP → ↓TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23, ↑IL-10
- No lab monitoring; no TB screening required
- Start with a titration pack to limit GI side effects
- Watch weight and depression

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.18; Khopkar edition predates apremilast. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Atropine sulphate injection
posts.summary: VI Emergency drugs · Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) belladonna alkaloid
posts.body:
_Injectables · VI Emergency drugs_

**Class:** Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) belladonna alkaloid

## Mechanism of action
- Competitively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors
- Heart: blocks vagal tone → raises heart rate and AV conduction
- Also reduces secretions, relaxes smooth muscle, dilates pupils

## Pharmacokinetics
- IV onset within 1 min; IM within 15 min; half-life about 2–4 h

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Symptomatic bradycardia — including severe vasovagal reaction during dermatological procedures
- Organophosphate/carbamate insecticide poisoning (large repeated doses)
- Pre-anaesthetic to dry secretions; reversal of neuromuscular block (with neostigmine)

## Dose & formulations
- Bradycardia: 0.5–0.6 mg IV every 3–5 min, up to a total of 3 mg
- Organophosphate poisoning: 1.2–2.4 mg IV, doubled every 5 min until the chest is clear and the heart rate is over 80/min
- Children: 0.02 mg/kg (minimum 0.1 mg)
- Ampoule 0.6 mg/mL

## Adverse effects
- Dry mouth, flushing, hot dry skin, fever (especially children)
- Tachycardia, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation
- Confusion, delirium in the elderly ('mad as a hatter, red as a beet, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, hot as a hare')
- Doses under 0.5 mg in adults can cause paradoxical bradycardia

## Contraindications
- Angle-closure glaucoma, obstructive uropathy, paralytic ileus, myasthenia gravis (relative), tachyarrhythmias
- No absolute contraindication in life-threatening bradycardia or poisoning

## Drug interactions
- Other anticholinergics (TCAs, first-generation antihistamines, phenothiazines): additive effects

## Monitoring
- Heart rate, BP, ECG

## Pregnancy & lactation
Crosses the placenta; use when needed in emergencies.

## Viva points
- Vasovagal attack during a procedure: lie flat, legs up; atropine if bradycardia persists
- Minimum dose 0.5 mg in adults to avoid paradoxical bradycardia
- Signs of atropine toxicity (anticholinergic toxidrome)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.58 (vasovagal reactions); ACLS/resuscitation guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Azathioprine
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Purine analogue (antimetabolite); prodrug of 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP)
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Purine analogue (antimetabolite); prodrug of 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted non-enzymatically to 6-MP, then to 6-thioguanine nucleotides (6-TGN)
- 6-TGN are incorporated into DNA and inhibit purine synthesis → T and B lymphocytes (which rely on de novo purine synthesis) are suppressed

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; 6-MP is broken down by three enzymes: TPMT (thiopurine methyltransferase), xanthine oxidase and HGPRT (which makes active 6-TGN)
- Low TPMT activity → more 6-TGN → severe myelosuppression
- Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) greatly increases toxicity

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Immunobullous diseases: pemphigus (steroid-sparing; paired with steroids as first line in the Derma Desk ladder), bullous pemphigoid
- Chronic actinic dermatitis, airborne contact dermatitis (Parthenium — weekly pulse), atopic dermatitis
- Dermatomyositis, cutaneous lupus, vasculitis, Behçet disease, pyoderma gangrenosum

## Dose & formulations
- Dose by TPMT activity (Wolverton): under 6.3 U/mL → do not use; 6.3–15 U/mL → 1 mg/kg/day; 15.1–26.4 U/mL (normal) → up to 2–2.5 mg/kg/day
- Without TPMT testing: start 50 mg/day and increase slowly with close CBC checks
- Usual 1–3 mg/kg/day; takes 6–8 weeks for full effect
- Parthenium dermatitis (Indian practice): weekly pulse of 300 mg once a week (as in the Derma Desk ladder)
- Tablets 50 mg

## Adverse effects
- Myelosuppression (leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, macrocytosis) — acute (low TPMT) or chronic
- GI: nausea, vomiting (commonest reason to stop); take with food or in divided doses
- Hypersensitivity syndrome (fever, rash, shock) in the first weeks
- Hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis
- Infections; non-melanoma skin cancer (especially SCC) and lymphoma with long-term use

## Contraindications
- TPMT activity absent/very low
- Pregnancy (relative — see below), active serious infection, malignancy
- Previous treatment with alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil) — higher malignancy risk

## Drug interactions
- Allopurinol/febuxostat: block xanthine oxidase → severe toxicity — avoid, or reduce azathioprine to 25% of dose
- ACE inhibitors, co-trimoxazole: added myelosuppression
- Warfarin effect reduced
- Sulfasalazine and mesalazine inhibit TPMT

## Monitoring
- Baseline: TPMT, CBC, LFT, renal function, hepatitis B/C, HIV, pregnancy test
- CBC every 2 weeks for 2 months, then every 1–3 months; LFT every 1–3 months
- Annual skin examination for skin cancer; sun protection

## Pregnancy & lactation
Old FDA category D, but widely used in pregnancy in transplant and inflammatory bowel disease patients with acceptable outcomes; decide case by case. Low levels in breast milk.

## Viva points
- TPMT testing before starting — key exam point
- Allopurinol interaction (xanthine oxidase)
- Slow onset (6–8 weeks), so start steroids alongside
- Long-term risk of SCC and lymphoma

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.15 (Azathioprine), Box 15.4; Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Azithromycin
posts.summary: II Antibiotics — b) Macrolide · Azalide (15-membered macrolide)
posts.body:
_Oral · II Antibiotics — b) Macrolide_

**Class:** Azalide (15-membered macrolide)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit (23S rRNA) and blocks translocation → stops protein synthesis
- Bacteriostatic; can be bactericidal at high concentrations
- Also anti-inflammatory (reduces neutrophil activity and cytokines)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Acid-stable; very high tissue and intracellular levels (concentrated in phagocytes, which carry it to infected sites)
- Very long tissue half-life (about 68 h) → single-dose or short-course regimens
- Mostly excreted unchanged in bile; little CYP3A4 inhibition (fewer interactions than erythromycin)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- STIs: chlamydia/NGU, chancroid, donovanosis, gonorrhoea (with ceftriaxone in some guidelines), early syphilis in special situations
- Skin and soft tissue infections; pyodermas in penicillin allergy
- Acne (pulse regimens) — used in India, but no better than doxycycline and promotes resistance
- Rosacea; trachoma; scrub typhus

## Dose & formulations
- Chlamydia/NGU: 1 g single dose
- Chancroid: 1 g single dose
- Donovanosis: 1 g once weekly, or 500 mg daily, for at least 3 weeks and until healed
- Early syphilis: 2 g single dose (resistance is common — penicillin remains first choice)
- Skin infection: 500 mg on day 1, then 250 mg daily on days 2–5
- Children: 10 mg/kg/day

## Adverse effects
- GI upset (less than erythromycin), diarrhoea
- QT prolongation and arrhythmia (caution in heart disease or with other QT drugs)
- Cholestatic hepatitis (rare), hearing loss with long high-dose courses
- Rash, rarely SJS/TEN; C. difficile colitis

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to macrolides
- History of cholestatic jaundice with azithromycin
- Caution: long QT, hypokalaemia, severe liver disease

## Drug interactions
- Other QT-prolonging drugs (fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, hydroxychloroquine)
- Antacids reduce peak levels
- Warfarin and digoxin levels may rise (less than with erythromycin or clarithromycin)

## Monitoring
- None routinely; ECG if cardiac risk factors

## Pregnancy & lactation
Considered safe in pregnancy (old FDA category B); used for chlamydia in pregnancy. Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Long tissue half-life makes single-dose STI treatment possible
- Least CYP3A4 inhibition among macrolides
- Part of the NACO STI kits (e.g. kit 1 with cefixime) — check the slot-2 STI kits post
- Azithromycin-resistant Treponema pallidum is widespread, so it is not first-line for syphilis

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9; Khopkar ch.1 (Macrolides). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: BCG vaccine
posts.summary: VII Vaccines · Live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis (Bacille Calmette–Guérin) vaccine
posts.body:
_Injectables · VII Vaccines_

**Class:** Live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis (Bacille Calmette–Guérin) vaccine

## Mechanism of action
- Induces cell-mediated (Th1) immunity to mycobacteria
- Protects children against severe TB (miliary TB, TB meningitis); variable protection against pulmonary TB and some protection against leprosy
- Non-specific immune stimulation (trained immunity) — basis for use in warts and bladder cancer

## Pharmacokinetics
- 0.1 mL intradermal (0.05 mL in infants under 1 month) over the left deltoid insertion
- Papule → pustule → ulcer → scar over 6–12 weeks

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Routine at birth in India (national schedule; up to 1 year of age)
- Dermatology: immunotherapy for warts (intralesional or intradermal), leprosy contacts (some programmes)
- Intravesical BCG for superficial bladder cancer

## Dose & formulations
- 0.1 mL intradermal (0.05 mL under 1 month)
- Warts (off-label protocols): 0.1 mL intradermal/IL every 2–4 weeks for a few sessions

## Adverse effects
- Normal: local papule, ulcer, scar
- Complications: large ulcer, abscess, suppurative lymphadenitis (BCG adenitis), keloid
- Cutaneous TB at the site: lupus vulgaris, scrofuloderma; tuberculids (lichen scrofulosorum, papulonecrotic)
- Disseminated BCG infection (BCGosis) in immunodeficient children (SCID, chronic granulomatous disease, IFN-γ pathway defects, HIV)
- Flare (redness) of an old BCG scar in Kawasaki disease (a diagnostic clue)

## Contraindications
- Immunosuppression (primary immunodeficiency, symptomatic HIV, steroids, biologics, chemotherapy)
- Pregnancy; generalised skin disease or infection at the site; active TB

## Drug interactions
- Antituberculous drugs inactivate the vaccine
- Immunosuppressants increase the risk of disseminated infection

## Monitoring
- Check the site at follow-up; investigate persistent ulcer or adenitis

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (live vaccine).

## Viva points
- Live vaccine — intradermal, left deltoid
- Cutaneous complications include lupus vulgaris and scrofuloderma at the site
- BCGosis signals immunodeficiency
- BCG scar reactivation in Kawasaki disease

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.43 (IL immunotherapy for warts — brief); national immunisation schedule; Khopkar (Immunobiologicals). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Benzathine penicillin G
posts.summary: III Antibiotics · Long-acting depot form of penicillin G (natural β-lactam)
posts.body:
_Injectables · III Antibiotics_

**Class:** Long-acting depot form of penicillin G (natural β-lactam)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits transpeptidation of the bacterial cell wall → bactericidal (needs actively dividing bacteria)
- Treponema pallidum divides slowly (every 30–33 h), so long, steady penicillin levels are needed — the benzathine salt gives low levels for 2–4 weeks

## Pharmacokinetics
- IM depot slowly releases penicillin G over 3–4 weeks
- Does not reach treponemicidal levels in CSF — not suitable for neurosyphilis
- Excreted by the kidneys

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Syphilis: primary, secondary, early latent (first choice); late latent and tertiary (non-neuro)
- Syphilis in pregnancy (the only adequate treatment; desensitise if allergic)
- Contacts of early syphilis; NACO white kit (kit 3, genital ulcer disease)
- Rheumatic fever prophylaxis; streptococcal pharyngitis; yaws, pinta, bejel

## Dose & formulations
- Early syphilis: 2.4 million units (MU) deep IM single dose (1.2 MU into each buttock)
- Late latent/unknown duration, tertiary (non-neuro): 2.4 MU IM once weekly × 3 weeks
- Congenital syphilis (asymptomatic infant, selected cases): 50,000 U/kg IM single dose
- Rheumatic fever prophylaxis: 1.2 MU every 3–4 weeks
- Reconstitute as per vial, inject deep IM with a wide-bore needle; observe for 30 min

## Adverse effects
- Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction (fever, chills, myalgia, worsening rash) within 2–24 h — from release of treponemal lipoproteins; commonest in secondary syphilis; manage with antipyretics; in pregnancy may cause preterm labour
- Anaphylaxis (rare; have adrenaline ready); urticaria, serum sickness
- Injection-site pain; accidental intravascular injection → Hoigné syndrome (with procaine penicillin) or Nicolau syndrome (embolia cutis medicamentosa — painful livedoid necrosis)

## Contraindications
- Penicillin allergy (in pregnancy or neurosyphilis → desensitise, do not substitute)
- Not for IV use; not for neurosyphilis

## Drug interactions
- Probenecid raises penicillin levels
- Tetracyclines (bacteriostatic) may antagonise

## Monitoring
- Non-treponemal titre (VDRL/RPR) at 3, 6, 12 (and 24) months; a four-fold fall (two dilutions) by 6–12 months shows adequate response
- Test for HIV and other STIs; trace and treat partners

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe and essential in pregnancy (old FDA category B). Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for all stages of syphilis except neurosyphilis (needs aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV)
- Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction vs drug allergy
- Nicolau syndrome — inadvertent intra-arterial injection
- Pregnant women with penicillin allergy must be desensitised
- Skin sensitivity testing is still commonly done in India before injection (keep adrenaline ready)

## Note on sources
Skin testing before benzathine penicillin is routine in many Indian hospitals; international guidelines (WHO/CDC) do not require it but stress readiness for anaphylaxis.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9; Khopkar ch.1; NACO STI guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Betamethasone (oral)
posts.summary: VII Systemic corticosteroids · Long-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid (biological half-life 36–54 h)
posts.body:
_Oral · VII Systemic corticosteroids_

**Class:** Long-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid (biological half-life 36–54 h)

## Mechanism of action
- Glucocorticoid receptor agonist like prednisolone, but much more potent and longer acting
- No mineralocorticoid effect

## Pharmacokinetics
- Equivalence: 0.6 mg betamethasone ≈ 5 mg prednisolone (about 25 times hydrocortisone)
- Crosses the placenta (not inactivated by 11β-HSD2) — used to mature fetal lungs

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Oral mini-pulse (OMP): progressive/unstable vitiligo, spreading alopecia areata, extensive lichen planus
- General systemic steroid indications (less often than prednisolone)

## Dose & formulations
- OMP (Pasricha regimen): 5 mg betamethasone (or dexamethasone) as a single morning dose on 2 consecutive days per week (adults); children 0.1 mg/kg on the same schedule
- Continue OMP for about 3–6 months for vitiligo, then taper
- Tablets 0.5 mg (and 1 mg in some brands)

## Adverse effects
- Same as systemic steroids; with OMP mainly weight gain, acne, insomnia, menstrual disturbance, mild Cushingoid features
- Long-acting steroids suppress the HPA axis more than prednisolone if given daily

## Contraindications
- As for systemic steroids

## Drug interactions
- As for prednisolone

## Monitoring
- Weight, BP, glucose during OMP

## Pregnancy & lactation
Crosses the placenta (used deliberately for fetal lung maturity); avoid for skin disease in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- OMP — pulse dosing on 2 days a week reduces side effects but still stops disease activity
- Long-acting: more HPA suppression if given daily
- Not inactivated by the placenta (unlike prednisolone)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.8 (Table 8.2, OMP indications); Wolverton 4e ch.13. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Bilastine
posts.summary: IX Antihistaminics · Second-generation H1 antihistamine (piperidine; newer agent)
posts.body:
_Oral · IX Antihistaminics_

**Class:** Second-generation H1 antihistamine (piperidine; newer agent)

## Mechanism of action
- Highly selective H1 inverse agonist; P-glycoprotein substrate, so very little reaches the brain
- Also some anti-inflammatory effects on mast-cell mediator release

## Pharmacokinetics
- Not metabolised (no CYP involvement); excreted unchanged
- Food and fruit juice greatly reduce absorption — take 1 h before or 2 h after food or juice
- Half-life about 14 h; once daily

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic urticaria and allergic rhinitis
- People who need to drive or operate machinery

## Dose & formulations
- Adults and children over 12 years: 20 mg once daily on an empty stomach (updosing up to 80 mg in urticaria per guidelines)
- Children 6–11 years (over 20 kg): 10 mg daily

## Adverse effects
- Headache, drowsiness (rare), abdominal pain
- No QT effect at standard or 4 times the dose

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- P-gp inhibitors (erythromycin, ketoconazole, cyclosporine, diltiazem) raise levels
- Grapefruit and other fruit juices lower absorption

## Monitoring
- None

## Pregnancy & lactation
Insufficient data — avoid; prefer loratadine or cetirizine.

## Viva points
- Not metabolised — no CYP interactions
- Take on an empty stomach
- Non-sedating; safe for drivers

## Note on sources
Bilastine is in neither book; product data and international urticaria guidelines were used.

_Sources: Not covered in Wolverton 4e or Khopkar; product information and urticaria guidelines (EAACI/GA²LEN) used. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Bleomycin (intralesional)
posts.summary: III Antibiotics · Glycopeptide cytotoxic antibiotic (from Streptomyces verticillus); antineoplastic
posts.body:
_Injectables · III Antibiotics_

**Class:** Glycopeptide cytotoxic antibiotic (from Streptomyces verticillus); antineoplastic

## Mechanism of action
- Binds DNA and iron; produces oxygen free radicals that cause single- and double-strand DNA breaks (G2 phase specific)
- In warts: kills HPV-infected keratinocytes and damages capillaries → haemorrhagic necrosis and eschar
- Skin and lung lack bleomycin hydrolase, the enzyme that inactivates it — hence toxicity in these organs

## Pharmacokinetics
- Intralesional use gives very low systemic levels
- Systemic drug is excreted by the kidneys

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Recalcitrant viral warts (palmoplantar, periungual, common warts)
- Keloids and hypertrophic scars (alternative/adjunct)
- Vascular malformations (sclerotherapy), cystic lymphatic malformations
- Systemic (oncology): squamous cell carcinoma, lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma (intralesional too), germ-cell tumours

## Dose & formulations
- Warts: 1 U/mL (dissolve a 15 U vial in 15 mL normal saline or lignocaine); inject 0.1–0.2 mL into the base of each wart until it blanches
- Keep total dose low per session (usually 1–2 U, a few units at most); repeat every 2–4 weeks if needed
- Vascular malformations: weaker solution 0.2–0.4 mg/mL (Wolverton), every 2–4 weeks for 4–10 sessions
- Reconstituted solution is stable in the refrigerator for some weeks (check local pharmacy guidance)

## Adverse effects
- Pain during and after injection (use lignocaine as diluent or a digital block)
- Black eschar/haemorrhagic crust, then healing in 2–4 weeks
- Periungual/digital injection: nail dystrophy or loss, Raynaud phenomenon, digital necrosis (rare)
- Systemic use (not with IL warts): flagellate hyperpigmentation, pulmonary fibrosis (cumulative over 400 U), Raynaud, scleroderma-like changes, fever, alopecia

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding
- Peripheral vascular disease, Raynaud phenomenon (especially for digital warts)
- Immunosuppression with infection at site; children (relative)

## Drug interactions
- Cisplatin reduces bleomycin clearance (systemic)
- High oxygen concentration (anaesthesia) increases lung toxicity in patients who had systemic bleomycin

## Monitoring
- Review at 2–4 weeks; watch digital circulation after periungual injection

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category D).

## Viva points
- Works via DNA strand breaks from free radicals
- Flagellate pigmentation and lung fibrosis — systemic use only
- Skin and lungs lack bleomycin hydrolase
- IL warts: 1 U/mL, inject until blanching

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.47 (Topical and intralesional chemotherapeutic agents); Khopkar (intralesional agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ceftriaxone
posts.summary: III Antibiotics · Third-generation cephalosporin (β-lactam)
posts.body:
_Injectables · III Antibiotics_

**Class:** Third-generation cephalosporin (β-lactam)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits cell-wall synthesis → bactericidal
- Stable against many β-lactamases; good Gram-negative cover (Neisseria, Haemophilus ducreyi, Enterobacteriaceae) with streptococcal cover

## Pharmacokinetics
- IM or IV; long half-life (6–9 h) → once-daily dosing
- Good CSF penetration with inflamed meninges
- Dual excretion (bile ~40% and urine) — no dose change in renal failure alone

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Gonorrhoea (uncomplicated: urethral, cervical, rectal, pharyngeal) and disseminated gonococcal infection
- Chancroid; PID (with doxycycline + metronidazole)
- Neurosyphilis (alternative when penicillin cannot be used); early syphilis alternative
- Lyme disease (late/neurological), cellulitis, severe skin and soft-tissue infections, meningococcaemia, typhoid

## Dose & formulations
- Uncomplicated gonorrhoea: 500 mg IM single dose (1 g if over 150 kg) — CDC 2020; some guidelines (WHO 2024) use 1 g IM
- Chancroid: 250 mg IM single dose
- Disseminated gonococcal infection: 1 g IV/IM daily
- Neurosyphilis (alternative): 1–2 g IV/IM daily × 10–14 days
- Skin infections: 1–2 g IV daily
- Reconstitute IM dose with 1% lignocaine to reduce pain (never give lignocaine-mixed solution IV)

## Adverse effects
- Injection-site pain, phlebitis
- Hypersensitivity (rash, urticaria, anaphylaxis); cross-reactivity with penicillin is low (about 1–2%)
- Diarrhoea, C. difficile colitis
- Biliary pseudolithiasis (reversible sludge), especially in children with high doses
- Immune haemolytic anaemia (rare); SJS/TEN (rare)

## Contraindications
- Severe immediate hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis) to penicillins or cephalosporins
- Neonates with hyperbilirubinaemia (displaces bilirubin → kernicterus)
- Neonates receiving IV calcium-containing solutions (fatal calcium–ceftriaxone precipitates)

## Drug interactions
- Calcium-containing IV fluids (Ringer lactate) — do not mix in the same line
- Warfarin effect may increase

## Monitoring
- Test of cure for pharyngeal gonorrhoea (7–14 days); test for HIV, syphilis and chlamydia; treat partners

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy (old FDA category B) — the gonorrhoea treatment of choice in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for gonorrhoea (single IM dose)
- Dual excretion — no renal dose adjustment
- Calcium precipitate risk in neonates
- Biliary sludge (pseudolithiasis)

## Note on sources
Gonorrhoea dose differs between guidelines (CDC 500 mg, older guidelines 250 mg, WHO 2024 1 g). Please use whatever dose your department or NACO follows.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9; Khopkar ch.1; CDC STI Treatment Guidelines 2021. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Cetirizine
posts.summary: IX Antihistaminics · Second-generation H1 antihistamine (piperazine; carboxylic acid metabolite of hydroxyzine)
posts.body:
_Oral · IX Antihistaminics_

**Class:** Second-generation H1 antihistamine (piperazine; carboxylic acid metabolite of hydroxyzine)

## Mechanism of action
- Selective peripheral H1 inverse agonist
- Some anti-inflammatory effect: reduces eosinophil migration and late-phase reactions

## Pharmacokinetics
- Rapid onset (within 1 h); half-life about 8–10 h; once daily
- Excreted mostly unchanged in urine — halve the dose in renal impairment
- Levocetirizine is the active R-enantiomer (5 mg = 10 mg cetirizine)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic spontaneous and inducible urticaria (first line)
- Allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis itch (limited), insect bite reactions, mastocytosis

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 10 mg once daily; in urticaria may be increased up to 4 times (40 mg/day) per guidelines
- Children 6 months–2 years: 2.5 mg daily; 2–6 years: 2.5 mg twice daily or 5 mg daily; over 6 years: 10 mg daily

## Adverse effects
- Mild sedation (more than fexofenadine and loratadine; about 10%)
- Headache, dry mouth, fatigue

## Contraindications
- Severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance under 10 mL/min)
- Hypersensitivity to hydroxyzine or piperazines

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol and CNS depressants (mild additive effect)

## Monitoring
- None

## Pregnancy & lactation
One of the preferred antihistamines in pregnancy (with loratadine); compatible with breastfeeding (watch infant drowsiness).

## Viva points
- Metabolite of hydroxyzine
- Renally excreted — adjust in kidney disease
- Most sedating of the second-generation group
- Updosing up to 4 times in urticaria

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.32; Khopkar (Antihistamines). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Colchicine
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Alkaloid from Colchicum autumnale; anti-mitotic, anti-inflammatory
posts.body:
_Oral · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Alkaloid from Colchicum autumnale; anti-mitotic, anti-inflammatory

## Mechanism of action
- Binds tubulin and prevents microtubule polymerisation
- This blocks neutrophil migration, adhesion and degranulation, and inflammasome (NLRP3) activation
- Also an anti-mitotic (metaphase arrest) at higher concentrations

## Pharmacokinetics
- Absorbed in the gut; enterohepatic circulation; metabolised by CYP3A4 and pumped out by P-gp
- Narrow therapeutic index

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Behçet disease (mucocutaneous ulcers, erythema nodosum)
- Leukocytoclastic vasculitis (chronic cutaneous), urticarial vasculitis
- Recurrent aphthous stomatitis, Sweet syndrome, erythema nodosum leprosum (adjunct)
- Dermatitis herpetiformis, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, linear IgA, palmoplantar pustulosis
- Familial Mediterranean fever, gout

## Dose & formulations
- 0.5–0.6 mg once to three times daily (usually 0.5 mg twice daily; Wolverton lists 0.6 mg twice daily)
- Reduce dose in renal/hepatic impairment or the elderly

## Adverse effects
- GI (the commonest, dose-limiting): diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal pain — start low
- Myelosuppression, myopathy and neuropathy (especially with renal impairment or interacting drugs)
- Overdose is often fatal (above 0.8 mg/kg): multiorgan failure, alopecia in survivors
- Reversible azoospermia

## Contraindications
- Severe renal or hepatic impairment
- Combination with strong CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors in patients with renal or hepatic impairment

## Drug interactions
- Clarithromycin, erythromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, cyclosporine, verapamil, diltiazem: raise colchicine levels → fatal toxicity reported
- Statins and fibrates: myopathy

## Monitoring
- CBC, renal function, LFT and CK periodically on long-term use

## Pregnancy & lactation
Can be continued in pregnancy for familial Mediterranean fever (old FDA category C); generally avoid for skin disease. Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Microtubule inhibitor → neutrophil inhibitor
- Main use: Behçet and cutaneous vasculitis
- Diarrhoea is the dose-limiting side effect
- Clarithromycin/cyclosporine interaction can be fatal

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.40; Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Cyclophosphamide injection
posts.summary: V Immunosuppressants · Nitrogen mustard alkylating agent (prodrug)
posts.body:
_Injectables · V Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Nitrogen mustard alkylating agent (prodrug)

## Mechanism of action
- Activated in the liver (CYP2B6, 2C19) to phosphoramide mustard, which cross-links DNA strands (guanine N7) → cell death; cell-cycle non-specific
- Strongly suppresses B cells (antibody production) and T cells
- By-product acrolein causes bladder toxicity

## Pharmacokinetics
- Oral and IV; metabolites excreted in urine — reduce dose in renal failure

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Pemphigus: DCP pulse (dexamethasone–cyclophosphamide; third line in the Derma Desk ladder); also refractory pemphigoid and mucous membrane pemphigoid (ocular)
- Systemic vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, polyarteritis nodosa), lupus nephritis, dermatomyositis with lung disease, systemic sclerosis lung
- Lymphoma/mycosis fungoides (oncology), pyoderma gangrenosum (refractory)

## Dose & formulations
- DCP: 500 mg IV on day 1 of each monthly dexamethasone pulse, plus 50 mg orally daily between pulses
- Vasculitis/lupus (IV pulse): 500–1000 mg/m² (or 15 mg/kg) monthly
- Oral: 1–2 mg/kg/day
- Give in the morning with plenty of fluid (2–3 L/day), frequent voiding; mesna with high IV doses

## Adverse effects
- Bone marrow suppression (nadir 8–14 days)
- Haemorrhagic cystitis (acrolein) and bladder cancer (long-term, cumulative) — prevent with hydration and mesna
- Infertility: premature ovarian failure, azoospermia (consider sperm/oocyte preservation)
- Nausea, vomiting, alopecia (anagen effluvium), nail and skin hyperpigmentation
- Infections (including PJP — consider co-trimoxazole prophylaxis), secondary malignancy (leukaemia, lymphoma, skin cancer)
- SIADH, pulmonary fibrosis, cardiotoxicity (high doses)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding; active serious infection; bone marrow failure
- Urinary outflow obstruction

## Drug interactions
- Allopurinol: increases marrow toxicity
- Enzyme inducers (phenobarbital, rifampicin) increase toxic metabolites
- Succinylcholine: prolonged apnoea (cyclophosphamide inhibits pseudocholinesterase)

## Monitoring
- CBC weekly to 2-weekly during therapy; urine for blood monthly and then for life (bladder cancer risk)
- Renal function, LFT; pregnancy test; fertility counselling

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category D) — teratogenic. Effective contraception during and for some months after treatment.

## Viva points
- Prodrug activated in the liver; acrolein → haemorrhagic cystitis; mesna is the antidote for the bladder
- Lifelong urine checks for bladder cancer
- DCP regimen for pemphigus (Pasricha)
- Fertility counselling before starting

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.19 (Cytotoxic agents); Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs; DCP pulse). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Cyclosporine
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Calcineurin inhibitor (cyclic peptide from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum)
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Calcineurin inhibitor (cyclic peptide from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds cyclophilin inside T cells; the complex inhibits calcineurin
- Calcineurin cannot dephosphorylate NFAT, so NFAT does not enter the nucleus → less IL-2 and other cytokines → T-cell activation blocked
- Also inhibits mast-cell and keratinocyte activation

## Pharmacokinetics
- Microemulsion form (Neoral and generics) has more reliable absorption than the old form (Sandimmune) — do not switch between brands casually
- Metabolised by CYP3A4; excreted in bile
- Grapefruit juice raises levels

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Severe psoriasis — rapid control ('crisis' drug), erythrodermic and generalised pustular psoriasis
- Severe atopic dermatitis (approved in Europe)
- Chronic urticaria (refractory to antihistamines)
- SJS/TEN (early use may reduce mortality; first line in the Derma Desk SJS ladder)
- Pyoderma gangrenosum, Behçet disease, lichen planus, chronic actinic dermatitis, prurigo nodularis, immunobullous diseases (adjunct)

## Dose & formulations
- Psoriasis/atopic dermatitis: 2.5–5 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (Wolverton favours starting at the higher end for rapid control, then tapering)
- Taper by 0.5–1 mg/kg every 2–4 weeks once controlled
- Short courses (intermittent therapy, 12–16 weeks) are preferred; continuous use generally limited to 1–2 years
- Capsules 25, 50, 100 mg; oral solution 100 mg/mL

## Adverse effects
- Nephrotoxicity — the most important; dose- and duration-dependent; early functional (vasoconstriction) then irreversible interstitial fibrosis
- Hypertension (about a quarter of psoriasis patients)
- Hypertrichosis, gingival hyperplasia, sebaceous hyperplasia, follicular keratosis
- Tremor, headache, paraesthesia; hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperuricaemia, hyperlipidaemia
- Increased skin cancer (especially after previous PUVA) and lymphoma; infections

## Contraindications
- Uncontrolled hypertension, abnormal renal function
- Malignancy (except non-melanoma skin cancer, with caution); high cumulative PUVA (above about 200 treatments)
- Concurrent phototherapy; active serious infection; live vaccines

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels (nephrotoxicity): azoles (ketoconazole, itraconazole), macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), diltiazem, verapamil, grapefruit
- CYP3A4 inducers lower levels (rejection/flare): rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, St John's wort
- Additive nephrotoxicity: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides
- Statins (myopathy), potassium-sparing diuretics (hyperkalaemia)

## Monitoring
- Blood pressure and serum creatinine twice at baseline, then every 2 weeks for 1–2 months, then monthly
- If creatinine rises more than 25–30% above baseline (on two readings), reduce dose by 25–50%; stop if it stays high
- Also: K⁺, Mg²⁺, uric acid, lipids, LFT, CBC, urine
- Trough levels are not needed routinely in dermatology

## Pregnancy & lactation
Not teratogenic in humans (old FDA category C); has been used in transplant pregnancies, but prematurity and low birth weight are reported. Avoid breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Calcineurin–NFAT–IL-2 pathway
- Most important side effects: nephrotoxicity and hypertension
- Creatinine rule: more than 25–30% above baseline → reduce dose
- Microemulsion form has better absorption
- Avoid with PUVA history and with phototherapy (skin cancer)

## Note on sources
Wolverton notes that recent guidelines use a 25% creatinine threshold while the traditional dermatology threshold is 30% — both are mentioned.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.17 (Cyclosporine); Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Deflazacort
posts.summary: VII Systemic corticosteroids · Intermediate-acting oxazoline derivative of prednisolone (prodrug)
posts.body:
_Oral · VII Systemic corticosteroids_

**Class:** Intermediate-acting oxazoline derivative of prednisolone (prodrug)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted to its active metabolite (21-desacetyl-deflazacort), which acts on the glucocorticoid receptor like prednisolone

## Pharmacokinetics
- Rapidly absorbed and activated; half-life of the active metabolite about 1–2 h but biological effect 12–36 h
- Equivalence: 6 mg deflazacort ≈ 5 mg prednisolone (ratio about 1.2 : 1)
- Little mineralocorticoid effect

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Same indications as prednisolone — used in India as an alternative in children and patients with diabetes or bone loss concerns
- Approved in the USA for Duchenne muscular dystrophy

## Dose & formulations
- Usual 0.5–1.2 mg/kg/day as a single morning dose (6 mg replaces 5 mg prednisolone)
- Tablets 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 mg

## Adverse effects
- Same class side effects as prednisolone
- It is claimed (in Khopkar and product data) to have fewer effects on bone, glucose and weight, but this advantage is modest and inconsistent
- Weight gain and Cushingoid features are still seen

## Contraindications
- Same as other systemic steroids

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inducers lower levels; CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels

## Monitoring
- Same as prednisolone

## Pregnancy & lactation
Limited data; prednisolone is preferred in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- 6 mg deflazacort = 5 mg prednisolone
- Claimed bone- and glucose-sparing, but it still causes the full range of steroid side effects and is more expensive (Khopkar)

## Note on sources
Deflazacort is not covered in Wolverton; Khopkar and product data were used.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.8 (Oral and injectable steroids); not covered in Wolverton 4e. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Dexamethasone sodium phosphate injection
posts.summary: II Corticosteroids · Long-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid (biological half-life 36–54 h)
posts.body:
_Injectables · II Corticosteroids_

**Class:** Long-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid (biological half-life 36–54 h)

## Mechanism of action
- Potent glucocorticoid receptor agonist (about 25–30 times hydrocortisone) with no mineralocorticoid effect

## Pharmacokinetics
- Water-soluble phosphate ester — IV, IM, intralesional
- Equivalence: 0.75 mg dexamethasone = 5 mg prednisolone
- Crosses the placenta (not inactivated by 11β-HSD2)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Dexamethasone–cyclophosphamide pulse (DCP) and dexamethasone pulse (DP) for pemphigus (Pasricha regimen; third line in the Derma Desk pemphigus ladder)
- Anaphylaxis/angioedema adjunct; acute severe allergic reactions
- SJS/TEN, DRESS (short courses, some centres)
- Cerebral oedema, fetal lung maturation (obstetrics)
- Intralesional/IM use in some Indian practice (less preferred than triamcinolone)

## Dose & formulations
- DCP pulse: dexamethasone 100 mg in 500 mL 5% dextrose over 1–2 h on 3 consecutive days + cyclophosphamide 500 mg IV on day 1; repeated every 4 weeks; oral cyclophosphamide 50 mg daily between pulses
- Phases of DCP: I (pulses until complete remission), II (pulses continue for 9 months with daily oral cyclophosphamide), III (oral cyclophosphamide alone for 9 months), IV (off treatment, follow-up)
- Anaphylaxis adjunct: 4–8 mg IV
- Ampoules 4 mg/mL (2 mL); 8 mg/2 mL

## Adverse effects
- As for pulse steroids: hyperglycaemia, hypertension, hypokalaemia, arrhythmia, psychosis, infection
- Perineal burning/itching with rapid IV injection
- Long-acting — more HPA suppression if given daily

## Contraindications
- As for systemic steroids; active serious infection, systemic fungal infection

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inducer itself (may lower levels of some drugs); enzyme inducers lower its levels

## Monitoring
- As for methylprednisolone pulse: ECG, electrolytes, glucose, BP before and during pulse

## Pregnancy & lactation
Crosses the placenta — used deliberately for fetal lung maturity; avoid for skin disease in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- 0.75 mg dexamethasone = 5 mg prednisolone
- DCP regimen: phases I–IV (Pasricha)
- No mineralocorticoid action

_Sources: Khopkar ch.8 (injectable steroids, DCP/DAP pulse); Wolverton 4e ch.13. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Dolutegravir
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · Integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), second generation
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** Integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), second generation

## Mechanism of action
- Binds the HIV integrase active site and blocks the strand-transfer step
- So viral DNA cannot integrate into the host chromosome
- High genetic barrier to resistance

## Pharmacokinetics
- Taken once daily with or without food; half-life about 14 h
- Metabolised by UGT1A1 (and CYP3A4 to a lesser extent)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Part of the preferred first-line ART regimen in India (TLD: tenofovir 300 mg + lamivudine 300 mg + dolutegravir 50 mg once daily) for adults, adolescents and pregnant women
- Children: with abacavir + lamivudine (weight-band dosing)
- Second-line regimens and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)

## Dose & formulations
- 50 mg once daily (usually within the TLD tablet)
- 50 mg twice daily if taken with rifampicin or when INSTI resistance is suspected

## Adverse effects
- Insomnia, headache, abnormal dreams, depression (uncommon)
- Weight gain
- Small rise in serum creatinine (blocks tubular creatinine secretion; true kidney function is not reduced)
- Hypersensitivity reactions and hepatotoxicity (rare)
- Early concern about neural tube defects with use at conception; later data show the risk is very small — it is now recommended in pregnancy

## Contraindications
- Dofetilide (raised levels)
- Previous hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Polyvalent cations (antacids with Mg/Al, calcium, iron, zinc supplements) chelate it — take dolutegravir 2 h before or 6 h after
- Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin lower levels (double the dose with rifampicin; avoid the others)
- Raises metformin levels — limit the metformin dose (about 1 g/day) and monitor

## Monitoring
- CD4 and viral load per programme
- Weight, mood, renal function (expect a small, stable creatinine rise)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Recommended in pregnancy as part of TLD; give folic acid. Compatible with national breastfeeding guidance for women on ART.

## Viva points
- INSTI — blocks integration of viral DNA
- TLD is the preferred first-line regimen in India
- Separate from zinc, iron, calcium or antacids — relevant when we prescribe zinc
- Creatinine rise without real kidney damage

## Note on sources
Khopkar's edition predates dolutegravir, and Wolverton only lists it, so this post follows current NACO/WHO guidance. Please check.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4 (older edition, before dolutegravir); Wolverton 4e ch.11 (lists the drug); current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Doxycycline
posts.summary: II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines · Second-generation semisynthetic tetracycline (lipophilic)
posts.body:
_Oral · II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines_

**Class:** Second-generation semisynthetic tetracycline (lipophilic)

## Mechanism of action
- Antibacterial: binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA attachment → stops protein synthesis (bacteriostatic)
- Anti-inflammatory (independent of antibacterial action): inhibits matrix metalloproteinases, neutrophil chemotaxis, and pro-inflammatory cytokines
- This anti-inflammatory action is the basis of sub-antimicrobial dosing in rosacea

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed (about 95%); food reduces absorption only slightly, but iron, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc and bismuth chelate it
- Half-life 18–22 h → once- or twice-daily dosing
- Excreted mainly through the gut, so it is the safest tetracycline in renal failure

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne vulgaris (moderate–severe inflammatory) — always with topical benzoyl peroxide or retinoid; limit to 3–4 months
- Rosacea (papulopustular), perioral dermatitis
- Bullous pemphigoid (anti-inflammatory, often with nicotinamide)
- STIs: chlamydia/NGU, LGV, donovanosis, early and late syphilis when penicillin cannot be used
- Community MRSA skin infections, Lyme disease, rickettsial infections, Mycobacterium marinum
- Hidradenitis suppurativa; filariasis (kills Wolbachia); confluent and reticulated papillomatosis

## Dose & formulations
- Acne/rosacea: 50–100 mg once or twice daily
- Sub-antimicrobial: 40 mg modified-release once daily, or 20 mg twice daily (rosacea)
- Chlamydia/NGU: 100 mg twice daily × 7 days; LGV: 100 mg twice daily × 21 days
- Early syphilis (penicillin allergy): 100 mg twice daily × 14 days; late latent: × 28 days
- Donovanosis: 100 mg twice daily for at least 3 weeks and until lesions heal
- Take with a full glass of water, sitting upright, not at bedtime

## Adverse effects
- GI upset; pill oesophagitis (take upright with water)
- Phototoxicity, including photo-onycholysis — the most phototoxic of the commonly used tetracyclines
- Tooth staining and enamel hypoplasia in children under 8 years (less than older tetracyclines)
- Pseudotumor cerebri; vaginal candidiasis
- Rare: hepatotoxicity, hypersensitivity

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (after about 15 weeks) and breastfeeding (long courses)
- Children under 8 years (except short courses for serious infections such as rickettsial disease)
- Concurrent isotretinoin or acitretin; known hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Antacids, iron, calcium, zinc, magnesium, bismuth, milk: reduce absorption — separate by 2–3 h
- Isotretinoin/acitretin: pseudotumor cerebri
- Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, barbiturates: lower doxycycline levels
- Warfarin: effect may increase

## Monitoring
- No routine blood tests for courses used in acne
- Counsel about sun protection and correct swallowing

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (old FDA category D): tooth discolouration and bone effects after about 15 weeks. Short courses in breastfeeding are generally acceptable; avoid long courses.

## Viva points
- Safest tetracycline in renal failure (gut excretion)
- Most phototoxic of the common tetracyclines; photo-onycholysis
- Sub-antimicrobial 40 mg MR works by anti-inflammatory action and does not select resistance
- Never combine with isotretinoin

## Note on sources
Khopkar says doxycycline lacks the anti-inflammatory effect of tetracycline. Wolverton describes clear anti-inflammatory actions (the basis of sub-antimicrobial dosing). We follow Wolverton.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9 (Systemic antibacterial agents); Khopkar ch.1. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Dutasteride
posts.summary: VIII Antiandrogen · Dual 5α-reductase inhibitor (types I and II)
posts.body:
_Oral · VIII Antiandrogen_

**Class:** Dual 5α-reductase inhibitor (types I and II)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits both type I (sebaceous glands, skin) and type II (hair follicle, prostate) 5α-reductase
- Lowers serum DHT by more than 90% — more than finasteride

## Pharmacokinetics
- Very long half-life (about 5 weeks); effect persists for months after stopping
- Metabolised by CYP3A4

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Male androgenetic alopecia (approved in Korea/Japan at 0.5 mg; off-label elsewhere) — slightly more effective than finasteride
- Female pattern hair loss in post-menopausal women (off-label)
- Mesotherapy (intradermal dutasteride) for AGA
- Benign prostatic hyperplasia

## Dose & formulations
- 0.5 mg once daily (some use 0.5 mg 2–3 times a week); soft capsules should not be opened

## Adverse effects
- Sexual side effects (similar to or slightly more than finasteride)
- Gynaecomastia, breast tenderness
- PSA lowered by about 50%

## Contraindications
- Women of childbearing potential and pregnancy; children
- Men should not donate blood for 6 months after the last dose (long half-life)

## Drug interactions
- Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ritonavir, ketoconazole) raise levels

## Monitoring
- Baseline PSA in older men

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category X). Pregnant women should not handle leaking capsules.

## Viva points
- Blocks both isoenzymes — more DHT suppression than finasteride
- Very long half-life — no blood donation for 6 months after stopping

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.34; Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Famciclovir
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Anti-herpes · Diacetyl ester prodrug of penciclovir (guanosine analogue)
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Anti-herpes_

**Class:** Diacetyl ester prodrug of penciclovir (guanosine analogue)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted to penciclovir in the gut wall and liver
- Penciclovir is phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase, then by host kinases, to penciclovir triphosphate, which inhibits viral DNA polymerase
- Not an obligate chain terminator (unlike acyclovir), but stays inside infected cells much longer (intracellular half-life 7–20 h)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Bioavailability about 77%
- Plasma half-life about 2 h, but long intracellular half-life → less frequent dosing
- Renal excretion — reduce dose in renal impairment

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Herpes zoster (start within 72 h)
- Genital herpes: first episode, recurrences, suppression
- Herpes labialis (single dose)
- Recurrent HSV in HIV

## Dose & formulations
- Herpes zoster: 500 mg three times daily × 7 days
- First-episode genital herpes: 250 mg three times daily × 7–10 days
- Recurrent genital herpes: 1 g twice daily for 1 day (or 125 mg twice daily × 5 days)
- Suppression: 250 mg twice daily
- Herpes labialis: 1500 mg single dose
- HIV, recurrent HSV: 500 mg twice daily × 7 days

## Adverse effects
- Headache, nausea, diarrhoea
- Confusion in the elderly (rare)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to famciclovir or penciclovir

## Drug interactions
- Probenecid may raise penciclovir levels
- Few clinically important interactions

## Monitoring
- Renal function for dose adjustment

## Pregnancy & lactation
Old FDA category B; limited human data — acyclovir and valacyclovir are preferred in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Prodrug of penciclovir; long intracellular half-life
- Cross-resistance with acyclovir (both need viral thymidine kinase)
- Single-day treatment options for herpes labialis and recurrent genital herpes

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.11; Khopkar ch.3. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Fexofenadine
posts.summary: IX Antihistaminics · Second-generation H1 antihistamine (active metabolite of terfenadine)
posts.body:
_Oral · IX Antihistaminics_

**Class:** Second-generation H1 antihistamine (active metabolite of terfenadine)

## Mechanism of action
- Selective peripheral H1 inverse agonist; a P-glycoprotein substrate, so it is pumped out of the brain — truly non-sedating

## Pharmacokinetics
- Onset 1–2 h; half-life about 14 h
- Excreted mostly unchanged in faeces and urine; little liver metabolism, so no QT problems (unlike its parent terfenadine)
- Fruit juices (grapefruit, orange, apple) reduce absorption via OATP — take with water

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic urticaria, allergic rhinitis
- Preferred in pilots, drivers and people needing no sedation

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 120–180 mg once daily; urticaria may be updosed up to 360–720 mg/day (Wolverton mentions 180–360 mg)
- Children 6–11 years: 30 mg twice daily

## Adverse effects
- Headache; generally very well tolerated
- No significant sedation even at high doses

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Antacids with aluminium/magnesium and fruit juices reduce absorption
- Erythromycin and ketoconazole raise levels (not clinically important)

## Monitoring
- None

## Pregnancy & lactation
Less data than cetirizine or loratadine; use those first in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Least sedating antihistamine (P-gp efflux)
- Metabolite of terfenadine, but without its QT toxicity
- Avoid fruit juice at the time of dosing

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.32; Khopkar (Antihistamines). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Finasteride
posts.summary: VIII Antiandrogen · 5α-reductase inhibitor (type II isoenzyme selective)
posts.body:
_Oral · VIII Antiandrogen_

**Class:** 5α-reductase inhibitor (type II isoenzyme selective)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits type II 5α-reductase (found in hair follicles, prostate), blocking conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
- Lowers serum DHT by about 70% and scalp DHT by about 60%
- Reverses miniaturisation of androgen-sensitive scalp follicles

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; metabolised in the liver (CYP3A4); half-life 5–6 h, but enzyme inhibition lasts longer

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Male androgenetic alopecia (vertex and mid-scalp) — approved at 1 mg
- Female pattern hair loss in post-menopausal women (off-label, higher doses 2.5–5 mg)
- Hirsutism (off-label, with contraception), frontal fibrosing alopecia (off-label)
- Benign prostatic hyperplasia (5 mg)

## Dose & formulations
- Male AGA: 1 mg once daily; results take 3–6 months, assess at 12 months
- Must be continued — benefit is lost within about 12 months of stopping
- Topical finasteride 0.25% solution is available

## Adverse effects
- Sexual: decreased libido, erectile and ejaculatory dysfunction (about 1–2%; usually reversible)
- Gynaecomastia, breast tenderness
- Depression; 'post-finasteride syndrome' (persistent symptoms after stopping) is reported but unproven
- Lowers PSA by about 50% — double the measured PSA when screening for prostate cancer

## Contraindications
- Women of childbearing potential (unless strict contraception) and pregnancy — risk of feminising a male fetus
- Pregnant women should not handle crushed or broken tablets
- Children

## Drug interactions
- No important interactions

## Monitoring
- None routinely; record baseline PSA in men over 40–50

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated in pregnancy (old FDA category X) — causes hypospadias/ambiguous genitalia in male fetuses. Men on finasteride need no contraception (semen levels are negligible).

## Viva points
- Type II 5α-reductase inhibitor; dutasteride blocks types I and II
- 1 mg for hair; 5 mg for prostate
- PSA is halved — double it
- Pregnant women should not handle broken tablets

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.34 (Antiandrogens and androgen inhibitors); Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Fluconazole
posts.summary: III Antifungals · Triazole antifungal (first generation)
posts.body:
_Oral · III Antifungals_

**Class:** Triazole antifungal (first generation)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-α-demethylase (CYP51), blocking ergosterol synthesis
- Fungistatic; membrane damage from accumulated toxic methylated sterols

## Pharmacokinetics
- Water-soluble; about 90% bioavailable; absorption not affected by food or gastric acid
- Low protein binding; excellent CSF, eye and urine penetration
- Half-life about 30 h → weekly dosing possible
- Excreted unchanged in urine — reduce dose in renal failure

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Vulvovaginal, oropharyngeal and oesophageal candidiasis; candidal intertrigo and paronychia
- Pityriasis versicolor, Malassezia folliculitis
- Dermatophytosis and onychomycosis (alternative)
- Cryptococcosis (including meningitis, with amphotericin B first), coccidioidomycosis
- Prophylaxis in immunocompromised patients

## Dose & formulations
- Vulvovaginal candidiasis: 150 mg single dose; recurrent: 150 mg every 72 h × 3 doses, then weekly for 6 months
- Oropharyngeal candidiasis: 100–200 mg/day × 7–14 days
- Tinea corporis: 150–300 mg once weekly × 2–4 weeks
- Pityriasis versicolor: 300 mg weekly × 2 weeks (or 400 mg single dose)
- Onychomycosis: 150–450 mg once weekly for 6–12 months
- Children: 3–6 mg/kg/day (tinea capitis 6 mg/kg/day)

## Adverse effects
- GI upset, headache
- Hepatotoxicity (usually mild)
- QT prolongation and torsades de pointes
- Alopecia with prolonged high doses
- Rash; fixed drug eruption (common in Indian practice); rarely SJS/TEN

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to azoles
- With QT-prolonging drugs metabolised by CYP3A4 (e.g. cisapride, pimozide, quinidine, erythromycin)
- Pregnancy (high-dose or prolonged use)

## Drug interactions
- Inhibits CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and (moderately) CYP3A4
- Raises levels of warfarin, phenytoin, sulfonylureas, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, some statins, benzodiazepines
- Rifampicin lowers fluconazole levels

## Monitoring
- LFT for courses longer than a few weeks; ECG if other QT risks; renal function for dosing

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid. High-dose or prolonged use in the first trimester is linked to birth defects (old FDA category D); a single 150 mg dose was category C. Compatible with breastfeeding in usual doses.

## Viva points
- Water-soluble azole — best CSF penetration, renal excretion
- Absorption is not acid-dependent (unlike itraconazole)
- Main enzyme inhibited for interactions: CYP2C9 (warfarin, phenytoin)
- Weekly dosing is possible because of the long half-life

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.10; Khopkar ch.2. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Griseofulvin
posts.summary: III Antifungals · Benzofuran fungistatic antibiotic (from Penicillium griseofulvum)
posts.body:
_Oral · III Antifungals_

**Class:** Benzofuran fungistatic antibiotic (from Penicillium griseofulvum)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds microtubule proteins (tubulin) and disrupts the mitotic spindle → arrests fungal cell division in metaphase
- Deposited in keratin precursor cells, so new keratin resists infection
- Active only against dermatophytes; no effect on Candida, Malassezia or deep fungi

## Pharmacokinetics
- Poorly water-soluble; absorption improves with a fatty meal and with smaller particle size
- Microsize and ultramicrosize forms are not interchangeable mg-for-mg (ultramicrosize is better absorbed)
- Half-life 9–24 h; reaches the stratum corneum through sweat; washes out quickly after stopping
- Metabolised in the liver; a CYP inducer

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Tinea capitis — especially Microsporum infections (first choice), and children
- Extensive tinea corporis/cruris when other drugs are unavailable
- Not suitable for onychomycosis (needs 12–18 months, poor cure)
- Rarely used for anti-inflammatory purposes (lichen planus, etc.)

## Dose & formulations
- Children (tinea capitis): microsize 20–25 mg/kg/day, or ultramicrosize 10–15 mg/kg/day, with fatty food, for at least 6–8 weeks
- Adults: microsize 500 mg–1 g/day (ultramicrosize 375–750 mg/day)
- Tinea corporis: 2–4 weeks; tinea pedis: 4–8 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Headache (most common; often settles)
- GI upset, taste disturbance
- Photosensitivity; can precipitate or worsen lupus erythematosus and acute porphyria
- Urticaria, morbilliform rash, fixed drug eruption, rarely SJS/TEN
- Hepatotoxicity, leukopenia, proteinuria (rare)
- Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy; men should not father children during treatment and for 6 months after
- Porphyria, hepatic failure, systemic lupus

## Drug interactions
- Enzyme inducer: reduces efficacy of oral contraceptives, warfarin, cyclosporine
- Phenobarbital reduces griseofulvin absorption
- Alcohol: disulfiram-like reaction

## Monitoring
- CBC and LFT only for prolonged courses
- Advise extra contraception

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category X) — teratogenic and embryotoxic.

## Viva points
- Fungistatic; acts on the mitotic spindle
- Drug of choice for Microsporum tinea capitis; terbinafine is better for Trichophyton tonsurans
- Give with a fatty meal (e.g. milk)
- Ineffective against Candida and Malassezia
- Enzyme inducer — reduces oral contraceptive efficacy

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.10 (Systemic antifungal agents), Table 10.5; Khopkar ch.2. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Histoglobulin (Histoglob PFS)
posts.summary: IV Immunotherapy · Human normal immunoglobulin + histamine dihydrochloride combination (non-specific immunotherapy / 'histaminopexy')
posts.body:
_Injectables · IV Immunotherapy_

**Class:** Human normal immunoglobulin + histamine dihydrochloride combination (non-specific immunotherapy / 'histaminopexy')

## Mechanism of action
- The histamine–immunoglobulin complex is thought to stimulate antibodies that bind histamine
- This raises the blood's capacity to bind and neutralise free histamine (histaminopexy) and lowers responsiveness to histamine
- May also reduce IgE levels and eosinophil counts and dampen mast-cell activation
- Exact mechanism is not fully established

## Pharmacokinetics
- Given by subcutaneous injection; effect builds over the induction course

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chronic spontaneous urticaria not controlled with antihistamines (adjunct)
- Allergic rhinitis, allergic asthma (adjunct)
- Atopic dermatitis (limited evidence)

## Dose & formulations
- One prefilled syringe (PFS) subcutaneously per dose
- Induction: 6 injections at 4-day intervals (days 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 as in the manufacturer's calendar); more injections may be given depending on response
- Maintenance: booster doses at 1, 3 and 6 months
- Continue the patient's antihistamine and taper it according to response

## Adverse effects
- Pain, redness or swelling at the injection site
- Fever, headache, transient flare of itch or urticaria
- Rare: hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis (contains human immunoglobulin) — observe after injection
- Blood-product precautions: very small theoretical risk of transmissible infection

## Contraindications
- Known hypersensitivity to human immunoglobulin or histamine
- IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies
- Acute febrile illness or infection (postpone), uncontrolled asthma attack
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding (insufficient data)

## Drug interactions
- Systemic corticosteroids may blunt the response (some prescribing information advises against simultaneous use)
- Live vaccines: immunoglobulin may reduce response — space as per immunoglobulin guidance

## Monitoring
- Urticaria activity score (UAS7) at baseline and follow-up
- Observe 15–30 min after each injection

## Pregnancy & lactation
No adequate data — avoid.

## Viva points
- Histamine + human immunoglobulin → histaminopexy
- Schedule: 6 SC injections every 4 days, then boosters at 1, 3 and 6 months
- Evidence is limited (small studies); guideline step-up for chronic urticaria is antihistamine updosing → omalizumab → cyclosporine

## Note on sources
Histoglobulin is in neither book. The dosing follows the Histoglob PFS card you shared (6 injections 4 days apart, then boosters at 1, 3 and 6 months).
