_Sources: Not covered in Wolverton or Khopkar; Histoglob PFS prescribing information (Bharat Serums and Vaccines) and dosing card shared by the user. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: HPV vaccine (quadrivalent)
posts.summary: VII Vaccines · Recombinant non-infectious virus-like particle (VLP) vaccine against HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18
posts.body:
_Injectables · VII Vaccines_

**Class:** Recombinant non-infectious virus-like particle (VLP) vaccine against HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18

## Mechanism of action
- L1 capsid protein self-assembles into VLPs (no viral DNA) → strong neutralising antibody response
- Types 6 and 11 cause about 90% of anogenital warts; types 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical cancers
- Prophylactic — does not clear established infection (therapeutic use in warts is off-label)

## Pharmacokinetics
- 0.5 mL IM in the deltoid

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Prevention of cervical, vulvar, vaginal, anal, oropharyngeal cancers and anogenital warts in girls and boys
- Best given before sexual debut (9–14 years)
- Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis prevention
- Off-label: recalcitrant cutaneous and anogenital warts (case series; Wolverton notes some reports of benefit)
- India: indigenous qHPV vaccine (Cervavac) and introduction into the national programme for girls

## Dose & formulations
- 9–14 years: 2 doses (0 and 6–12 months)
- 15–26 years: 3 doses (0, 2 and 6 months) — WHO now also accepts 1–2 doses in younger groups
- Immunocompromised (including HIV): 3 doses
- 9-valent vaccine (Gardasil 9) adds types 31, 33, 45, 52, 58

## Adverse effects
- Injection-site pain, swelling
- Syncope (observe seated for 15 min), headache, fever
- Anaphylaxis very rare (yeast protein)

## Contraindications
- Severe allergy to a previous dose or to yeast
- Pregnancy (defer remaining doses until after delivery; inadvertent dosing is not harmful)

## Drug interactions
- Immunosuppressants may reduce response

## Monitoring
- Observe 15 min for syncope

## Pregnancy & lactation
Not recommended in pregnancy (precaution); safe in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- VLP vaccine — no DNA, cannot cause infection
- 6 and 11 → warts; 16 and 18 → cancer
- 2 doses if started before 15; 3 doses after 15 or if immunocompromised
- Prevents anogenital warts — relevant for STI clinic counselling

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.43 (HPV vaccine in warts); WHO HPV position paper 2022. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Hydrocortisone sodium succinate injection
posts.summary: II Corticosteroids · Short-acting natural glucocorticoid (cortisol) with mineralocorticoid action
posts.body:
_Injectables · II Corticosteroids_

**Class:** Short-acting natural glucocorticoid (cortisol) with mineralocorticoid action

## Mechanism of action
- Glucocorticoid receptor agonist — anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive
- Significant mineralocorticoid effect (salt and water retention) — the right steroid for adrenal insufficiency

## Pharmacokinetics
- Water-soluble succinate ester — rapid onset IV (within 1 h)
- Biological half-life 8–12 h (short-acting)
- Equivalence: 20 mg hydrocortisone = 5 mg prednisolone

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Anaphylaxis — adjunct after adrenaline (prevents late/biphasic reaction; not a first-line drug)
- Acute severe angioedema, severe acute urticaria, acute drug reactions
- Adrenal crisis and stress-dose cover in patients on long-term steroids (surgery, illness)
- Status asthmaticus

## Dose & formulations
- Anaphylaxis: 200 mg IV or IM (adults); children 6–12 years 100 mg, 6 months–6 years 50 mg, under 6 months 25 mg
- Adrenal crisis: 100 mg IV bolus, then 50 mg every 6 h (or 200 mg/24 h infusion)
- Vials 100 mg (reconstitute with sterile water)

## Adverse effects
- Short courses: hyperglycaemia, fluid retention, hypokalaemia, hypertension, mood change
- Rapid IV bolus of large doses: hypotension, arrhythmia (rare)
- Long use: full range of steroid side effects

## Contraindications
- No absolute contraindication in emergencies
- Caution: systemic fungal infection, uncontrolled diabetes, active peptic ulcer

## Drug interactions
- Enzyme inducers lower effect; diuretics add to hypokalaemia; NSAIDs increase GI risk

## Monitoring
- BP, glucose, potassium with repeated doses

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe for emergency use; mostly inactivated by the placenta.

## Viva points
- Only injectable steroid with significant mineralocorticoid effect — drug of choice in adrenal crisis
- In anaphylaxis, steroids are adjuncts — adrenaline is the life-saving drug
- 20 mg hydrocortisone = 5 mg prednisolone

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.13; Khopkar ch.8 (Table 8.4, injectable steroids). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Hydroxyzine
posts.summary: IX Antihistaminics · First-generation (sedating) H1 antihistamine; piperazine class
posts.body:
_Oral · IX Antihistaminics_

**Class:** First-generation (sedating) H1 antihistamine; piperazine class

## Mechanism of action
- Inverse agonist at H1 receptors (stabilises the inactive form)
- Crosses the blood–brain barrier → sedation and anxiolysis
- Also anticholinergic, antiserotonergic and mild antiemetic effects

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; onset 15–30 min; metabolised in the liver to cetirizine (active metabolite)
- Half-life about 20 h in adults (shorter in children, longer in elderly)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Pruritus of atopic dermatitis and other itchy dermatoses — night-time sedation helps
- Urticaria (usually as a night-time add-on to a non-sedating antihistamine)
- Anxiety; pre-procedure sedation

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 10–25 mg at night, up to 25 mg three to four times daily (max 100 mg/day; lower in elderly)
- Children: about 1–2 mg/kg/day in divided doses (syrup 10 mg/5 mL)

## Adverse effects
- Sedation, impaired driving and school performance, next-day hangover
- Anticholinergic: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, blurred vision, confusion in elderly
- QT prolongation at high doses (caution)
- Paradoxical excitation in children

## Contraindications
- Prolonged QT; early pregnancy
- Caution: glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, elderly, hepatic impairment, porphyria

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol and CNS depressants (additive sedation)
- Other QT-prolonging drugs; other anticholinergics

## Monitoring
- None

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in early pregnancy (EMA advice); cetirizine/loratadine preferred. Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- First-generation, crosses BBB
- Its metabolite is cetirizine
- Useful at night for itch-related sleep loss, but sedation lowers daytime performance
- Guidelines recommend second-generation antihistamines as first line for urticaria

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.32 (Antihistamines); Khopkar (Antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Isotretinoin
posts.summary: I Retinoids · First-generation (non-aromatic) retinoid; 13-cis-retinoic acid
posts.body:
_Oral · I Retinoids_

**Class:** First-generation (non-aromatic) retinoid; 13-cis-retinoic acid

## Mechanism of action
- Acts mainly through its metabolites on nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RAR) to change gene transcription
- Shrinks sebaceous glands and cuts sebum output by up to ~90%; this is the only acne drug that does this
- Normalises follicular keratinisation, so fewer microcomedones
- Indirectly reduces C. acnes because the follicle becomes less favourable for it; also anti-inflammatory

## Pharmacokinetics
- Bioavailability about 25%; roughly doubles when taken with a fatty meal (a lidose form, Absorica, is less food-dependent)
- 99% bound to albumin; half-life 10–20 h; main metabolite 4-oxo-isotretinoin
- Metabolised in the liver, excreted in bile and urine; not stored in fat, so it clears in about 1 month

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Severe nodulocystic acne (approved use)
- Moderate acne that fails oral antibiotics, scarring acne, or acne causing marked distress
- Rosacea (papulopustular, phymatous; low dose), Gram-negative folliculitis
- Hidradenitis suppurativa and dissecting cellulitis (limited benefit)
- Sebaceous hyperplasia; chemoprevention of skin cancer in xeroderma pigmentosum (high dose)
- Disorders of keratinisation such as Darier disease and PRP (acitretin usually preferred)

## Dose & formulations
- Acne: 0.5–1 mg/kg/day in 1–2 doses with food
- Aim for a total (cumulative) dose of 120–150 mg/kg; relapse is higher below 120 mg/kg
- Start low (e.g. 0.25–0.5 mg/kg) in severe or nodular acne to avoid an early flare
- Low-dose regimens (≈0.25–0.4 mg/kg/day) are used for moderate acne and rosacea
- Capsules 10, 20, 40 mg

## Adverse effects
- Mucocutaneous (almost universal): cheilitis — the earliest and most constant sign, often used as a marker of adherence; dry skin, dry nose with epistaxis, dry eyes and conjunctivitis, retinoid dermatitis
- Initial flare of acne; excess granulation tissue (pyogenic-granuloma-like) in nail folds or acne lesions
- Hair thinning, paronychia, photosensitivity
- Lipids: raised triglycerides (common); a rapid rise above 800–1000 mg/dL can cause pancreatitis
- Raised transaminases (usually mild and reversible)
- Musculoskeletal: myalgia and back pain; hyperostosis and premature epiphyseal closure with long, high-dose courses
- CNS: headache; pseudotumor cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension), especially with tetracyclines
- Mood change and depression or suicide have been reported; a causal link is not proven, but screen and ask at each visit
- Inflammatory bowel disease: reported, but no causal link shown
- Night blindness (reduced dark adaptation)
- Teratogenic: retinoid embryopathy (CNS, craniofacial, cardiac and thymic defects)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (absolute) and breastfeeding
- Women unable to follow reliable contraception
- Hypersensitivity, including to soy or paraben in some capsule fillers
- Relative: marked hyperlipidaemia, significant liver disease, hypervitaminosis A, concurrent tetracycline

## Drug interactions
- Tetracyclines raise the risk of pseudotumor cerebri — avoid together
- Vitamin A supplements: additive toxicity
- Methotrexate and alcohol: added liver toxicity
- Progestin-only 'mini-pill' is not reliable contraception during therapy
- Carbamazepine levels may fall

## Monitoring
- Women: 2 negative pregnancy tests before starting, then monthly, and 1 month after stopping
- Fasting lipids and LFTs at baseline and after about 1–2 months on the target dose; repeat only if abnormal or the dose rises
- CBC is not routinely needed
- At every visit: mood, headache or visual change, back pain

## Pregnancy & lactation
Absolute contraindication (old FDA category X). Two methods of contraception from 1 month before, throughout, and for 1 month after stopping. No blood donation during treatment or for 1 month after. Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Isotretinoin is the only acne drug that hits all four pathogenic factors: sebum, keratinisation, C. acnes and inflammation
- Cheilitis is the most common side effect; its absence suggests poor adherence
- Do not combine with tetracyclines (pseudotumor cerebri)
- Cumulative dose of 120–150 mg/kg reduces relapse
- Traditional advice was to delay waxing, dermabrasion and laser for 6 months; newer consensus says superficial procedures are probably acceptable — mention both

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.22 (Systemic retinoids); Khopkar (Oral retinoids). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Itraconazole
posts.summary: III Antifungals · Triazole antifungal (first generation; lipophilic)
posts.body:
_Oral · III Antifungals_

**Class:** Triazole antifungal (first generation; lipophilic)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits fungal lanosterol 14-α-demethylase → ergosterol depletion
- Fungistatic; broad spectrum: dermatophytes, Candida, Malassezia, Aspergillus and dimorphic fungi

## Pharmacokinetics
- Capsules need gastric acid and food — take with a full meal; avoid antacids and PPIs (or take with a cola drink)
- Oral solution is better absorbed on an empty stomach; super-bioavailable (SUBA) forms are less food-dependent
- Highly lipophilic and keratophilic; reaches skin via sebum and sweat and stays in nails for 6–9 months after stopping
- Half-life 24–42 h; metabolised by CYP3A4 (active metabolite hydroxy-itraconazole)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Dermatophytosis (tinea corporis, cruris, pedis), onychomycosis (pulse therapy)
- Pityriasis versicolor, Malassezia folliculitis, seborrhoeic dermatitis
- Candidiasis (mucocutaneous, candida onychomycosis)
- Sporotrichosis (drug of choice for cutaneous forms), chromoblastomycosis, histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis
- Aspergillosis (alternative)

## Dose & formulations
- Tinea corporis/cruris: 100–200 mg/day × 2–4 weeks (longer courses at 200 mg/day are often needed in India)
- Onychomycosis pulse: 200 mg twice daily for 1 week each month — 2 pulses for fingernails, 3 for toenails
- Onychomycosis continuous: 200 mg/day × 12 weeks (toenails)
- Pityriasis versicolor: 200 mg/day × 5–7 days
- Sporotrichosis: 100–200 mg/day for 3–6 months
- Children: about 5 mg/kg/day

## Adverse effects
- GI upset, headache, rash
- Hepatotoxicity (rare but can be severe)
- Negative inotropic effect: can cause or worsen congestive heart failure (boxed warning)
- Hypokalaemia, hypertension, oedema (mineralocorticoid-like effect at high doses)
- QT prolongation; peripheral neuropathy (rare)

## Contraindications
- Congestive heart failure or ventricular dysfunction (for nail infections)
- Pregnancy
- Concurrent CYP3A4 substrates with dangerous toxicity: simvastatin, lovastatin, midazolam/triazolam, cisapride, pimozide, quinidine, dofetilide, ergot alkaloids

## Drug interactions
- Potent CYP3A4 inhibitor (and P-glycoprotein inhibitor)
- Raises cyclosporine, tacrolimus, digoxin, warfarin, calcium-channel blockers, some benzodiazepines, colchicine
- Rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine lower itraconazole levels; PPIs/H2 blockers/antacids reduce capsule absorption

## Monitoring
- LFT at baseline and monthly if continuous therapy beyond 1 month
- Ask about heart failure symptoms

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (old FDA category C); women should use contraception during treatment and for 2 months after. Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Capsule absorption needs acid and food; solution on an empty stomach
- Pulse therapy works because the drug persists in the nail for months
- Contraindicated in congestive heart failure
- Potent CYP3A4 inhibitor — statin interaction (rhabdomyolysis)
- Drug of choice for cutaneous sporotrichosis

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.10; Khopkar ch.2. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ivermectin
posts.summary: V Antiparasitic · Macrocyclic lactone (semisynthetic avermectin from Streptomyces avermitilis)
posts.body:
_Oral · V Antiparasitic_

**Class:** Macrocyclic lactone (semisynthetic avermectin from Streptomyces avermitilis)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds glutamate-gated chloride channels in invertebrate nerve and muscle cells (also GABA-gated channels)
- Increases chloride entry → hyperpolarisation → paralysis and death of the parasite
- In mammals these channels are only in the CNS, and P-glycoprotein at the blood–brain barrier keeps ivermectin out — hence its safety

## Pharmacokinetics
- Absorption increases with a fatty meal (often given with food for scabies; the label advises water on an empty stomach)
- Highly lipophilic, widely distributed; half-life about 18 h
- Metabolised in the liver (CYP3A4); excreted in faeces
- Kills mites and lice but not eggs — so a second dose is needed

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Scabies — classic (alternative to permethrin, and for mass treatment, institutions, poor compliance) and crusted (Norwegian) scabies with topical therapy
- Head lice resistant to topical treatment
- Strongyloidiasis (drug of choice), cutaneous larva migrans, larva currens
- Onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis (mass drug administration with albendazole/DEC)
- Demodicosis and rosacea (topical 1% cream mainly)

## Dose & formulations
- Usual dose: 200 µg/kg as a single dose; tablets 3, 6 and 12 mg
- Scabies: 200 µg/kg, repeated after 7–14 days
- Crusted scabies: 200 µg/kg on days 1, 2, 8, 9 and 15 (plus days 22 and 29 in severe cases), with topical permethrin
- Head lice: 400 µg/kg on days 1 and 8 (some use 200 µg/kg)
- Strongyloidiasis: 200 µg/kg for 1–2 days; cutaneous larva migrans: 200 µg/kg for 1–2 days
- Onchocerciasis: 150 µg/kg once (repeat every 6–12 months)

## Adverse effects
- Generally very well tolerated: dizziness, nausea, transient worsening of itch
- Mazzotti reaction in onchocerciasis (fever, itch, lymphadenopathy, hypotension from dying microfilariae)
- Severe encephalopathy in people with very high Loa loa microfilaraemia
- Neurotoxicity in people with P-glycoprotein defects or with P-gp inhibitors

## Contraindications
- Children under 15 kg
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding (avoid, though accidental exposure has not shown clear harm)
- High Loa loa microfilaraemia (endemic areas); conditions with a damaged blood–brain barrier (e.g. meningitis)

## Drug interactions
- Warfarin: INR may rise
- P-gp/CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, cyclosporine, verapamil) may raise CNS exposure

## Monitoring
- No routine blood tests

## Pregnancy & lactation
Not recommended in pregnancy (old FDA category C) or breastfeeding; use permethrin instead.

## Viva points
- Acts on glutamate-gated chloride channels; P-glycoprotein keeps it out of the human brain
- Not ovicidal — repeat the dose after 7–14 days
- Drug of choice for crusted scabies (with topical) and strongyloidiasis
- Avoid in children under 15 kg and in pregnancy

## Note on sources
Wolverton says to repeat the scabies dose in 1 week to 10 days; other guides say 7–14 days. Both fit — 7–14 days is used here.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.12 (Systemic antiparasitic agents); Khopkar ch.5. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Lamivudine + Nevirapine + Zidovudine
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · Fixed-dose triple combination: 2 NRTIs (lamivudine, zidovudine) + 1 NNRTI (nevirapine)
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** Fixed-dose triple combination: 2 NRTIs (lamivudine, zidovudine) + 1 NNRTI (nevirapine)

## Mechanism of action
- NRTIs: chain-terminating nucleoside analogues of HIV reverse transcriptase
- Nevirapine: non-competitive inhibitor that binds a pocket near the reverse transcriptase active site

## Pharmacokinetics
- Nevirapine induces its own metabolism (CYP3A4 and 2B6 autoinduction) over the first 2 weeks
- So the full triple combination is used only after a 2-week lead-in with once-daily nevirapine

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Former first-line ART regimen (the 'ZLN' regimen), now largely replaced by dolutegravir-based TLD
- May still be met in patients started long ago

## Dose & formulations
- Lead-in (14 days): lamivudine 150 mg + zidovudine 300 mg twice daily, with nevirapine 200 mg once daily only
- Then: fixed-dose lamivudine 150 mg + nevirapine 200 mg + zidovudine 300 mg twice daily
- If rash appears during lead-in: do not increase the dose until it resolves; do not extend lead-in beyond 28 days

## Adverse effects
- Nevirapine rash (about 15–20%), mostly in the first 6 weeks; SJS/TEN and DRESS
- Nevirapine hepatotoxicity — higher in women with CD4 above 250 and men with CD4 above 400
- Zidovudine anaemia and neutropenia; melanonychia
- Lamivudine: hepatitis B flare on stopping

## Contraindications
- Previous severe nevirapine rash or hepatitis
- Moderate–severe liver disease
- Severe anaemia (zidovudine)

## Drug interactions
- Nevirapine induces CYP3A4: lowers oral contraceptives, ketoconazole, methadone, protease inhibitors
- Rifampicin lowers nevirapine — avoid together
- Zidovudine: other marrow suppressants

## Monitoring
- LFT at baseline, 2, 4, 8 and 12 weeks (nevirapine)
- Hb/CBC (zidovudine)
- Check skin and mucosa at each visit in the first 6–8 weeks

## Pregnancy & lactation
Used widely in the past; nevirapine-related liver toxicity is higher in women with higher CD4 counts. TLD is now preferred.

## Viva points
- Why the lead-in? Autoinduction — the 2-week once-daily dose lowers the risk of rash and hepatitis
- Nevirapine is one of the commonest causes of SJS/TEN in Indian studies
- Stop permanently if rash comes with fever, blisters, mucosal involvement or hepatitis

## Note on sources
Wolverton gives little detail on ART; Khopkar and NACO used.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4 (Table 4.2); Wolverton 4e ch.3 and ch.67; check current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Lamivudine + Zidovudine
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · Fixed-dose combination of two NRTIs
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** Fixed-dose combination of two NRTIs

## Mechanism of action
- Zidovudine (AZT) is a thymidine analogue; lamivudine (3TC) is a cytidine analogue
- Both are phosphorylated to triphosphates that inhibit HIV reverse transcriptase and terminate viral DNA chains

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed with or without food
- Zidovudine is glucuronidated in the liver (short half-life, twice-daily dosing); lamivudine is excreted by the kidneys

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Alternative NRTI backbone in ART when tenofovir or abacavir cannot be used
- Older first-line regimens (with nevirapine or efavirenz)
- Zidovudine alone: infant prophylaxis in PMTCT (prevention of mother-to-child transmission) programmes

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: lamivudine 150 mg + zidovudine 300 mg twice daily
- Children: weight-band dosing as per NACO tables

## Adverse effects
- Zidovudine: bone marrow suppression — macrocytic anaemia and neutropenia (avoid if Hb below about 8 g/dL)
- Zidovudine: nausea, headache, myopathy, lactic acidosis with hepatic steatosis, lipoatrophy
- Skin and mucosal signs of zidovudine: longitudinal melanonychia, nail and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation
- Lamivudine: generally well tolerated; hepatitis B flare on stopping

## Contraindications
- Severe anaemia (Hb under about 7–8 g/dL) or neutropenia
- Hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Other bone marrow suppressants raise anaemia risk: ganciclovir, co-trimoxazole (high dose), pyrimethamine, interferon, chemotherapy
- Stavudine is antagonistic — never combine with zidovudine
- Probenecid and fluconazole raise zidovudine levels

## Monitoring
- Hb and CBC at baseline, then monthly for the first 3 months, then periodically
- CD4 and viral load per programme; LFT

## Pregnancy & lactation
Zidovudine has the longest safety record in pregnancy; currently TLD is preferred, with zidovudine kept for infant prophylaxis and special cases.

## Viva points
- Zidovudine → anaemia (macrocytic) and neutropenia
- Zidovudine causes longitudinal melanonychia — a common viva photo
- Never combine zidovudine with stavudine (antagonism)

## Note on sources
Wolverton gives little detail on ART; Khopkar and NACO used.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4; Wolverton 4e ch.11; check current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Leucovorin calcium (folinic acid) injection
posts.summary: V Immunosuppressants · Reduced folate (5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate); antidote
posts.body:
_Injectables · V Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Reduced folate (5-formyl-tetrahydrofolate); antidote

## Mechanism of action
- Already in reduced form, so it bypasses the dihydrofolate reductase step blocked by methotrexate
- Restores purine and thymidine synthesis in normal cells ('leucovorin rescue')
- Also enhances 5-FU effect (stabilises thymidylate synthase binding) in oncology

## Pharmacokinetics
- IV, IM or oral; rapidly converted to active folates

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Methotrexate toxicity/overdose (pancytopenia, mucositis, accidental daily dosing) — the antidote
- Planned rescue after high-dose methotrexate (oncology)
- Folate deficiency megaloblastic anaemia when oral folic acid cannot be used
- With 5-FU in colorectal cancer; pyrimethamine/trimethoprim toxicity

## Dose & formulations
- MTX toxicity: give as early as possible (ideally within 24 h; effectiveness falls after 24–48 h)
- Typical: 10–15 mg/m² (or 15–25 mg) IV/IM/orally every 6 h until counts recover and MTX level is below safe threshold; larger doses for high levels
- Ampoules 15 mg/2 mL, 50 mg vials; tablets 15 mg
- Folic acid cannot replace leucovorin in acute toxicity (needs DHFR for activation)

## Adverse effects
- Rare: allergic reactions, fever
- Do not give intrathecally; do not give faster than 160 mg/min IV (calcium content)

## Contraindications
- Pernicious anaemia/B12 deficiency (may correct anaemia while neurological damage progresses)

## Drug interactions
- Reduces efficacy of methotrexate (intended) and of co-trimoxazole for PJP
- Increases 5-FU toxicity
- Anticonvulsants (phenytoin, phenobarbital): levels may fall

## Monitoring
- CBC daily in MTX toxicity; renal function; MTX level where available
- Supportive care: hydration, urine alkalinisation, mouth care, G-CSF if needed

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe when needed.

## Viva points
- Bypasses DHFR → antidote for methotrexate toxicity
- Give within 24 h
- Folic acid prevents side effects of low-dose MTX; leucovorin treats acute toxicity

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.14 (Methotrexate — overdose management); Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Lignocaine (lidocaine) 2% injection
posts.summary: I Local anaesthetics · Amide local anaesthetic (intermediate duration)
posts.body:
_Injectables · I Local anaesthetics_

**Class:** Amide local anaesthetic (intermediate duration)

## Mechanism of action
- The unionised form crosses the nerve membrane; inside, the ionised form blocks voltage-gated sodium channels from within
- No sodium influx → no depolarisation → no nerve conduction
- Small, unmyelinated fibres (pain, temperature, autonomic) are blocked first, then touch, pressure and motor

## Pharmacokinetics
- pKa 7.9 — fast onset (1–2 min by infiltration); works poorly in acidic, infected tissue
- Duration about 30–120 min alone; 2–6 h with adrenaline (vasoconstriction slows absorption)
- Metabolised in the liver (CYP1A2, 3A4); reduce total dose in liver disease and heart failure
- 2% = 20 mg/mL; 1% = 10 mg/mL

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Infiltration anaesthesia for biopsy, excision, electrosurgery, cryo, lasers, IL injections
- Nerve blocks (digital, ring, supraorbital, mental, etc.), field blocks
- Tumescent anaesthesia (very dilute, 0.05–0.1%) for liposuction and large procedures
- Topical forms (gel, EMLA with prilocaine — topicals slot)
- Antiarrhythmic (IV, ventricular arrhythmias)

## Dose & formulations
- Maximum (Wolverton): plain 4.5 mg/kg (up to 300 mg); with adrenaline 7 mg/kg (up to 500 mg)
- Example: 300 mg = 15 mL of 2% plain lignocaine
- Formula: maximum volume (mL) = max dose (mg/kg) × weight (kg) ÷ 10 ÷ % concentration
- Tumescent: up to 35–55 mg/kg because of very slow absorption from fat
- Children: same mg/kg limits; dilute to 0.5–1% to give enough volume

## Adverse effects
- Pain and burning on injection (reduce by buffering with sodium bicarbonate 1 mL 8.4% per 10 mL, warming, slow injection, small needle)
- Systemic toxicity (overdose or intravascular injection) — CNS first: perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, light-headedness, slurred speech → muscle twitching → seizures → coma
- Then cardiovascular: bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmia, cardiac arrest
- Vasovagal reaction (the commonest 'reaction' in practice)
- Adrenaline effects: palpitations, tremor, anxiety, tachycardia
- True allergy to amides is rare (preservative methylparaben may be the cause); esters (procaine, benzocaine — PABA) are more allergenic

## Contraindications
- Known allergy to amide anaesthetics
- Caution: complete heart block, severe liver disease, heart failure
- With adrenaline — caution: uncontrolled hypertension, severe cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, narrow-angle glaucoma; patients on non-selective β-blockers, MAOIs or tricyclics
- Adrenaline in digits/penis: traditionally avoided; Wolverton notes dilute adrenaline is now considered safe in healthy digits (avoid in vascular disease)

## Drug interactions
- β-blockers (propranolol) with adrenaline: unopposed α effect → hypertension and reflex bradycardia
- Cimetidine, propranolol, amiodarone reduce lignocaine clearance
- Other anti-arrhythmics: additive cardiac effects

## Monitoring
- Calculate the maximum dose before starting; aspirate before injecting
- Watch for early CNS symptoms; have resuscitation equipment and 20% lipid emulsion available
- Treatment of toxicity: stop injecting, airway and oxygen, benzodiazepine for seizures, 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy (old FDA category B) and breastfeeding; defer elective procedures to the second trimester; adrenaline in small doses acceptable.

## Viva points
- Amide vs ester: amides have two 'i's in the name (lIdocaIne); esters are metabolised by plasma cholinesterase and cause more allergy (PABA)
- Max dose: 4.5 mg/kg plain, 7 mg/kg with adrenaline
- Signs of toxicity progress from CNS to CVS
- Buffering with bicarbonate reduces pain
- Lipid emulsion is the antidote for systemic toxicity

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.58 (Local anesthetics); Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents / Appendix). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Loratadine
posts.summary: IX Antihistaminics · Second-generation H1 antihistamine (tricyclic, piperidine)
posts.body:
_Oral · IX Antihistaminics_

**Class:** Second-generation H1 antihistamine (tricyclic, piperidine)

## Mechanism of action
- Selective peripheral H1 inverse agonist; poor CNS penetration

## Pharmacokinetics
- Prodrug; metabolised in the liver (CYP3A4, 2D6) to desloratadine (active, longer acting)
- Half-life (with metabolite) about 27 h; once daily

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Urticaria, allergic rhinitis, itch

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 10 mg once daily (updosing to 40 mg in urticaria)
- Children 2–12 years: 5 mg daily (under 30 kg), 10 mg (over 30 kg)
- Liver impairment: 10 mg on alternate days

## Adverse effects
- Headache, fatigue, dry mouth; minimal sedation at standard dose

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; caution in severe liver disease

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin, cimetidine) raise levels without important QT effects

## Monitoring
- None

## Pregnancy & lactation
Preferred antihistamine in pregnancy (with cetirizine); compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Prodrug of desloratadine
- Safe in pregnancy (most data)
- Non-sedating at standard dose

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.32; Khopkar (Antihistamines). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Lymecycline
posts.summary: II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines · Second-generation tetracycline (tetracycline–lysine compound)
posts.body:
_Oral · II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines_

**Class:** Second-generation tetracycline (tetracycline–lysine compound)

## Mechanism of action
- Same as other tetracyclines: binds the 30S ribosome and blocks protein synthesis
- Has anti-inflammatory effects useful in acne

## Pharmacokinetics
- Much more water-soluble and better absorbed than tetracycline; food has less effect on absorption
- Allows once-daily dosing; half-life about 10 h; excreted mainly through the kidneys

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne vulgaris (moderate inflammatory) — with topical benzoyl peroxide or retinoid
- Rosacea (papulopustular)

## Dose & formulations
- 408 mg capsule (equivalent to 300 mg tetracycline base) once daily, usually for 8–12 weeks

## Adverse effects
- GI upset, headache
- Photosensitivity (less than doxycycline)
- Tooth staining in children; pseudotumor cerebri; vaginal candidiasis

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy, breastfeeding, children under 12 (label in Europe/India)
- Significant renal impairment (renally excreted)
- Concurrent oral retinoids

## Drug interactions
- Metal ions and antacids reduce absorption
- Oral retinoids: pseudotumor cerebri
- Warfarin effect may increase

## Monitoring
- No routine blood tests

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding (tetracycline class effect).

## Viva points
- Once-daily tetracycline widely used for acne in Europe and India
- Unlike doxycycline, it is renally excreted — avoid in renal failure

## Note on sources
Neither book has a separate lymecycline section. Please check this one against your notes.

_Sources: Not covered separately in Wolverton or Khopkar; class information from Wolverton ch.9, details from product information. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Menadione (vitamin K3) injection
posts.summary: IX Miscellaneous · Synthetic water-soluble vitamin K analogue (provitamin; menadione sodium bisulfite)
posts.body:
_Injectables · IX Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Synthetic water-soluble vitamin K analogue (provitamin; menadione sodium bisulfite)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted in the liver to active vitamin K2 (menaquinone-4)
- Vitamin K is a cofactor for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S)
- Corrects bleeding from vitamin K deficiency, but acts slowly and weakly compared with vitamin K1

## Pharmacokinetics
- Water-soluble — does not need bile for absorption (useful in obstructive jaundice)
- Onset slower than phytomenadione (vitamin K1); not reliable for reversing warfarin

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Hypoprothrombinaemia due to vitamin K deficiency: obstructive jaundice, malabsorption, long-term broad-spectrum antibiotics, prolonged parenteral nutrition
- Used as a haemostatic in some Indian practice
- Not the drug of choice for warfarin reversal or haemorrhagic disease of the newborn — phytomenadione (vitamin K1) is preferred

## Dose & formulations
- Typically 10 mg IM/IV (menadione sodium bisulfite) as directed by the product
- Vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) for comparison: newborn prophylaxis 1 mg IM at birth; warfarin reversal 1–10 mg slow IV (no faster than 1 mg/min)

## Adverse effects
- Haemolytic anaemia in G6PD deficiency
- Neonates: haemolysis, hyperbilirubinaemia and kernicterus — contraindicated
- Vitamin K injection-site skin reactions (mostly with vitamin K1): itchy eczematous plaques at the injection site (early), and later sclerodermoid plaques with a 'cowboy belt' distribution on the buttocks and thighs (Texier disease)
- Rapid IV vitamin K1: anaphylactoid reactions (flushing, collapse)

## Contraindications
- Neonates and infants; late pregnancy (risk to the newborn)
- G6PD deficiency
- Hypersensitivity

## Drug interactions
- Antagonises warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists
- Long-term antibiotics (cephalosporins) and cholestyramine increase vitamin K needs

## Monitoring
- Prothrombin time/INR

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid menadione in late pregnancy (neonatal haemolysis and jaundice); vitamin K1 is safe.

## Viva points
- Menadione (K3) vs phytomenadione (K1): K1 is preferred in neonates and for warfarin reversal
- Menadione causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency and kernicterus in newborns
- Skin reactions to vitamin K injections: eczematous plaques; Texier disease (pseudo-scleroderma, cowboy-belt pattern)

## Note on sources
Menadione is not covered in Wolverton. Khopkar and standard pharmacology texts were used; please check whether your examiners mean menadione (K3) or phytomenadione (K1).

_Sources: Khopkar (Vitamins and trace elements); pharmacology references; Wolverton 4e (drug eruption sections). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Methotrexate
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Folic acid antagonist (antimetabolite); immunomodulator
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Folic acid antagonist (antimetabolite); immunomodulator

## Mechanism of action
- Competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) → less tetrahydrofolate → less purine and thymidine synthesis → inhibits DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells (S-phase specific)
- At low weekly doses the main effect is anti-inflammatory: polyglutamated MTX inhibits AICAR transformylase → adenosine builds up and acts as an anti-inflammatory signal
- Reduces T-cell activation and keratinocyte proliferation

## Pharmacokinetics
- Oral absorption is variable and saturable at higher doses; subcutaneous route gives more reliable levels (useful above 15–20 mg/week)
- About 50% protein bound (displaced by NSAIDs, sulfonamides, salicylates)
- Stored in cells as polyglutamates; excreted mainly unchanged by the kidneys — reduce dose in renal impairment

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Psoriasis (plaque, erythrodermic, pustular, psoriatic arthritis) — approved
- Atopic dermatitis, chronic urticaria (refractory), alopecia areata
- Immunobullous disease (bullous pemphigoid, pemphigus as steroid-sparing)
- Connective tissue disease: dermatomyositis, morphoea and systemic sclerosis skin, cutaneous lupus
- Sarcoidosis, pityriasis rubra pilaris, pityriasis lichenoides, lymphomatoid papulosis, Mycosis fungoides (early), vasculitis, pyoderma gangrenosum

## Dose & formulations
- Once weekly — never daily (daily dosing errors cause fatal toxicity)
- Psoriasis: start 7.5–15 mg/week (test dose of 2.5–5 mg optional, especially in elderly or renal impairment), increase by 2.5–5 mg to 15–25 mg/week; maximum usually 25–30 mg/week
- Children: 0.2–0.7 mg/kg/week
- Folic acid 1–5 mg daily (except MTX day) or 5 mg weekly reduces GI and liver side effects and cytopenias
- Weekly oral, subcutaneous or IM routes; tablets 2.5, 7.5, 10 mg

## Adverse effects
- GI: nausea, anorexia, stomatitis, oral ulcers
- Bone marrow suppression — pancytopenia is the main cause of death (risk: renal failure, elderly, interacting drugs, no folate, dosing errors)
- Hepatotoxicity: raised enzymes, fibrosis and cirrhosis with long-term use (risk: alcohol, obesity, diabetes, fatty liver, hepatitis B/C)
- Pulmonary: acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis (idiosyncratic) and chronic fibrosis
- Skin: alopecia, ulceration of psoriatic plaques (early sign of overdose), photo-recall, epidermal necrosis
- Teratogenic and abortifacient; reversible oligospermia
- Infections; lymphoma (EBV-related, may regress on stopping)

## Contraindications
- Absolute: pregnancy and breastfeeding; significant liver disease or alcoholism; severe renal impairment; bone marrow failure; active serious infection
- Relative: hepatitis B/C, obesity, diabetes, fatty liver, unreliable patient, immunodeficiency, recent live vaccine

## Drug interactions
- Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole): additive antifolate → severe pancytopenia (most important)
- NSAIDs, salicylates, penicillins, probenecid, PPIs: reduce renal clearance or displace MTX
- Dapsone and other antifolates; retinoids and alcohol (liver); leflunomide
- Phenytoin, sulfonylureas, tetracyclines displace MTX from albumin

## Monitoring
- Baseline: CBC, LFT, renal function, hepatitis B/C, HIV, chest X-ray, pregnancy test, TB screening (IGRA) where relevant
- CBC and LFT weekly–2-weekly for the first month, then every 1–3 months; renal function every 3–6 months
- Liver fibrosis: non-invasive tests (e.g. transient elastography/FibroScan, procollagen III peptide) — liver biopsy only if these suggest fibrosis
- Traditionally biopsy was considered after a cumulative dose of 3.5–4 g in high-risk-free patients (Wolverton reviews this older approach)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Absolute contraindication (old FDA category X). Stop 3 months before conception (women; also commonly advised for men). Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Weekly dosing — check the patient is not taking it daily
- Co-trimoxazole is the most dangerous interaction
- Antidote for overdose: leucovorin (folinic acid) — bypasses DHFR; give as early as possible (covered in slot 3)
- Painful ulceration of psoriatic plaques can be the first sign of toxicity
- Liver monitoring has moved from routine biopsy to non-invasive tests

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.14 (Methotrexate); Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Methoxsalen (8-MOP, oral)
posts.summary: X Photochemotherapy · Psoralen (furocoumarin) photosensitiser; used with UVA (PUVA)
posts.body:
_Oral · X Photochemotherapy_

**Class:** Psoralen (furocoumarin) photosensitiser; used with UVA (PUVA)

## Mechanism of action
- Intercalates between DNA base pairs; after UVA exposure it forms monofunctional adducts and then cross-links between DNA strands
- Result: inhibits DNA synthesis and keratinocyte proliferation; apoptosis of activated T cells; immunosuppression
- In vitiligo: stimulates melanocyte proliferation and migration and melanogenesis

## Pharmacokinetics
- Absorption variable; peak photosensitivity at about 1–2 h (liquid capsules about 1 h, crystalline about 2 h); lasts about 8 h
- Large first-pass metabolism; food slows absorption

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Psoriasis (plaque, palmoplantar, erythrodermic in selected cases)
- Vitiligo (generalised), mycosis fungoides (early stage), chronic hand eczema, atopic dermatitis
- Lichen planus, polymorphous light eruption (prophylactic hardening), urticaria pigmentosa, generalised granuloma annulare, morphoea

## Dose & formulations
- 0.4–0.6 mg/kg orally, 1–2 h before UVA exposure (10 mg tablets/capsules)
- Treatments 2–3 times a week, never on consecutive days (phototoxic reaction peaks at 48–72 h)
- UVA dose started by skin type or minimal phototoxic dose (MPD), increased gradually
- 5-MOP (bergapten) 1.2 mg/kg is an alternative with less nausea and phototoxicity

## Adverse effects
- Nausea (most common), dizziness, headache
- Phototoxic reaction (erythema, blistering, pain); PUVA itch; PUVA lentigines
- Long-term: photoageing, non-melanoma skin cancer (especially SCC, dose-dependent, highest in genitals of men — shield them), melanoma (late)
- Cataract — eye protection with UVA-blocking glasses for 12–24 h after the dose
- Hepatotoxicity (rare)

## Contraindications
- Absolute: pregnancy (relative in many texts), lupus erythematosus, xeroderma pigmentosum, porphyria and other photosensitive disorders, melanoma history, children under 10–12 years
- Relative: previous arsenic or ionising radiation, non-melanoma skin cancer, cataract, liver disease, immunosuppression (cyclosporine), heavy sun damage

## Drug interactions
- Other photosensitising drugs (tetracyclines, thiazides, fluoroquinolones, phenothiazines) increase phototoxicity
- Cyclosporine: much higher skin cancer risk
- Phenytoin and other enzyme inducers lower psoralen levels

## Monitoring
- Baseline eye exam, ANA, LFT (if indicated); yearly eye and skin examination
- Record cumulative UVA dose and number of treatments (risk of SCC rises above about 200 treatments)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (old FDA category C); no clear teratogenicity seen, but use NB-UVB instead.

## Viva points
- DNA cross-linking after UVA activation
- Dose 0.6 mg/kg, 2 h before UVA
- Never on consecutive days — phototoxicity peaks at 48–72 h
- Eye protection for 24 h; shield male genitalia
- Main long-term risk: SCC

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.23 (PUVA photochemotherapy); Khopkar (Psoralens, PUVA and phototherapy). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Methylprednisolone (IV pulse)
posts.summary: II Corticosteroids · Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid; methylprednisolone sodium succinate for IV use
posts.body:
_Injectables · II Corticosteroids_

**Class:** Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid; methylprednisolone sodium succinate for IV use

## Mechanism of action
- At pulse doses, genomic effects are saturated and rapid non-genomic effects on cell membranes add to immunosuppression
- Rapid lymphocyte depletion and suppression of inflammation — gives quick disease control with fewer long-term side effects than prolonged high oral doses

## Pharmacokinetics
- Equivalence: 4 mg methylprednisolone = 5 mg prednisolone
- Minimal mineralocorticoid effect, so preferred for pulse therapy
- Methylprednisolone acetate (depot) is a different, long-acting IM/IL suspension — never give it IV

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Pemphigus vulgaris/foliaceus (severe, not responding), bullous pemphigoid (severe)
- SJS/TEN (early, short course — controversial), DRESS (severe), severe erythema multiforme
- Pyoderma gangrenosum, dermatomyositis (severe/with lung involvement), vasculitis, SLE
- Rapidly progressive alopecia areata (selected), severe type 1 lepra reaction or ENL with neuritis

## Dose & formulations
- Pulse: 500 mg–1 g (about 10–15 mg/kg/day) in 250–500 mL of 5% dextrose or normal saline over 1–3 h, daily for 3 (to 5) consecutive days
- Never as a rapid IV bolus (risk of arrhythmia and sudden death)
- Follow with oral steroid or steroid-sparing drug
- Vials 40, 125, 500 mg, 1 g

## Adverse effects
- Acute: flushing, metallic taste, hyperglycaemia, hypertension, insomnia, mood change, psychosis
- Electrolyte shifts (hypokalaemia), fluid retention
- Cardiac arrhythmia and sudden death (especially with diuretics, low potassium, heart disease, fast infusion)
- Anaphylaxis (rare), seizures, infections; avascular necrosis with repeated pulses

## Contraindications
- Active uncontrolled infection, systemic fungal infection
- Caution: heart disease, renal failure, electrolyte imbalance, uncontrolled diabetes or hypertension, psychiatric disease

## Drug interactions
- Diuretics and amphotericin B (hypokalaemia → arrhythmia)
- Enzyme inducers reduce effect; CYP3A4 inhibitors increase it

## Monitoring
- Before each pulse: BP, pulse, ECG, electrolytes (K⁺), blood glucose, renal function, infection screen, pregnancy test
- During infusion: BP and cardiac monitoring; repeat glucose and K⁺ after

## Pregnancy & lactation
Partly inactivated by the placenta; use only for life-threatening disease in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Pulse = 500 mg–1 g over at least 1 h on 3 consecutive days
- Check K⁺ and ECG before each pulse
- Succinate (IV, soluble) vs acetate (depot, never IV)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.13 (pulse definition); Khopkar ch.8. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Methylprednisolone (oral)
posts.summary: VII Systemic corticosteroids · Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid (biological half-life 12–36 h)
posts.body:
_Oral · VII Systemic corticosteroids_

**Class:** Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid (biological half-life 12–36 h)

## Mechanism of action
- Glucocorticoid receptor agonist; slightly more potent than prednisolone
- Minimal mineralocorticoid effect

## Pharmacokinetics
- Equivalence: 4 mg methylprednisolone ≈ 5 mg prednisolone
- Metabolised in the liver (CYP3A4)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Oral alternative to prednisolone (when less fluid retention is desired)
- Oral step-down after IV methylprednisolone pulses
- IV pulse use (pemphigus, SJS/TEN, pyoderma gangrenosum) — covered in the injectables slot

## Dose & formulations
- Oral: 4–48 mg/day depending on condition (e.g. 0.8 mg/kg/day ≈ 1 mg/kg prednisolone)
- Tablets 4, 8, 16, 32 mg

## Adverse effects
- Same as systemic steroids; less fluid retention than prednisolone

## Contraindications
- As for systemic steroids

## Drug interactions
- CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, macrolides) raise levels; inducers lower them

## Monitoring
- As for prednisolone

## Pregnancy & lactation
Partly inactivated by the placenta; prednisolone is usually preferred.

## Viva points
- 4 mg methylprednisolone = 5 mg prednisolone
- Less mineralocorticoid effect than prednisolone
- Used for IV pulse therapy (slot 3)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.13; Khopkar ch.8. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Metronidazole
posts.summary: II Antibiotics — c) Nitroimidazole · 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobial and antiprotozoal
posts.body:
_Oral · II Antibiotics — c) Nitroimidazole_

**Class:** 5-nitroimidazole antimicrobial and antiprotozoal

## Mechanism of action
- Prodrug: its nitro group is reduced inside anaerobic bacteria and protozoa
- The reduced reactive intermediates damage DNA → cell death (bactericidal)
- Active against anaerobes, Trichomonas, Giardia and Entamoeba; inactive against aerobes

## Pharmacokinetics
- Nearly 100% oral bioavailability; wide distribution including CSF, abscesses, vaginal secretions
- Half-life about 8 h; metabolised in the liver; excreted in urine (can turn urine dark)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Trichomoniasis (patient and partner)
- Bacterial vaginosis; part of PID regimens; vaginal discharge syndrome kits
- Amoebiasis (including cutaneous amoebiasis), giardiasis
- Anaerobic skin infections, infected ulcers, fungating tumours (also topical for odour)
- Rosacea (mainly topical gel); perianal Crohn's disease; dracunculiasis

## Dose & formulations
- Trichomoniasis: 2 g single dose (men); 500 mg twice daily × 7 days (women, preferred)
- Bacterial vaginosis: 500 mg twice daily × 7 days
- Amoebiasis: 750 mg three times daily × 7–10 days
- Anaerobic infections: 400–500 mg three times daily

## Adverse effects
- Metallic taste, nausea, anorexia, dry mouth
- Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (flushing, vomiting, headache, palpitations)
- Dark urine
- Peripheral neuropathy and seizures with high doses or long courses; aseptic meningitis; encephalopathy
- Fixed drug eruption; reversible neutropenia

## Contraindications
- Alcohol during treatment and for 72 h after (some sources say 48 h)
- Recent disulfiram use (within 2 weeks): risk of psychosis
- First trimester: high-dose single-dose regimen best avoided; active neurological disease

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol: disulfiram-like reaction
- Warfarin: markedly increased INR
- Lithium, phenytoin, busulfan, 5-FU: levels may rise
- Phenobarbital, rifampicin: lower metronidazole levels

## Monitoring
- CBC and neurological review if courses exceed 10 days

## Pregnancy & lactation
Old FDA category B; current guidelines allow use in all trimesters for trichomoniasis and BV. For the 2 g single dose in breastfeeding, pause breastfeeding for 12–24 h.

## Viva points
- Prodrug activated only in anaerobes — hence selective toxicity
- Avoid alcohol for 72 h (disulfiram-like reaction)
- Trichomoniasis: always treat the partner
- Commonly causes fixed drug eruption

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9; Khopkar ch.1 and ch.5. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Minocycline
posts.summary: II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines · Second-generation semisynthetic tetracycline — the most lipophilic
posts.body:
_Oral · II Antibiotics — a) Tetracyclines_

**Class:** Second-generation semisynthetic tetracycline — the most lipophilic

## Mechanism of action
- Binds the 30S ribosome and blocks protein synthesis (bacteriostatic)
- Anti-inflammatory: inhibits MMPs, neutrophil chemotaxis and lymphocyte activity
- High lipophilicity → good penetration into the pilosebaceous unit, CNS and skin

## Pharmacokinetics
- Almost completely absorbed; food has little effect; still chelated by metal ions
- Half-life 11–22 h; metabolised mainly in the liver

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acne vulgaris (second choice after doxycycline because of its safety profile)
- Leprosy: part of the ROM regimen (rifampicin, ofloxacin, minocycline) and an alternative drug
- Atypical mycobacteria (especially M. marinum), Nocardia, community MRSA
- Rosacea; anti-inflammatory use in bullous pemphigoid, sarcoidosis, CARP

## Dose & formulations
- Acne: 50–100 mg twice daily, or extended-release 1 mg/kg once daily
- Leprosy: 100 mg daily (alternative regimens); ROM monthly: 100 mg as part of the single monthly dose

## Adverse effects
- Vestibular toxicity (dizziness, vertigo, ataxia) — commoner in women
- Hyperpigmentation — Type I: blue-black in scars and inflamed sites (iron/haemosiderin stains); Type II: blue-grey on normal skin of shins and forearms (iron and melanin); Type III: muddy-brown diffuse in sun-exposed skin (melanin)
- Pigmentation can also affect teeth (even adult teeth), nails, sclera, oral mucosa, thyroid ('black thyroid') and bone
- Autoimmune: drug-induced lupus (often p-ANCA positive), autoimmune hepatitis, serum-sickness-like reaction, polyarteritis-like vasculitis
- Hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS) in the first weeks, pneumonitis
- Less phototoxic than doxycycline; pseudotumor cerebri

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy, breastfeeding, children under 8 years
- Lupus or autoimmune hepatitis history; concurrent oral retinoids

## Drug interactions
- Metal ions and antacids reduce absorption
- Isotretinoin/acitretin: pseudotumor cerebri
- Warfarin effect may increase

## Monitoring
- No routine tests for short courses
- For courses beyond a few months: watch for pigmentation, joint pain, rash, and check LFT/ANA if symptoms

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (old FDA category D). Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Most lipophilic tetracycline → vestibular side effects and best CNS penetration
- Three types of pigmentation — be able to describe them
- Autoimmune side effects: drug-induced lupus and autoimmune hepatitis
- Least phototoxic of the commonly used tetracyclines
- Used in leprosy (ROM)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.9; Khopkar ch.1. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: MMR vaccine
posts.summary: VII Vaccines · Live attenuated viral vaccine (measles, mumps, rubella)
posts.body:
_Injectables · VII Vaccines_

**Class:** Live attenuated viral vaccine (measles, mumps, rubella)

## Mechanism of action
- Attenuated viruses replicate briefly and induce long-lasting humoral and cell-mediated immunity
- Intralesional use in warts: the antigen triggers a delayed-type hypersensitivity (Th1) response with cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF) that also clears distant, untreated warts

## Pharmacokinetics
- 0.5 mL subcutaneous (or IM); seroconversion over 2–3 weeks

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Prevention of measles, mumps and rubella (national schedule: MR at 9–12 months and 16–24 months; MMR in private schedule at 9 months, 15 months, 4–6 years)
- Rubella-susceptible women before pregnancy
- Dermatology: intralesional immunotherapy for multiple or recalcitrant warts (common, plantar, anogenital)

## Dose & formulations
- Prophylaxis: 0.5 mL SC
- Warts: 0.3–0.5 mL injected into the largest (mother) wart, every 2–3 weeks, up to 3–5 sessions (pre-sensitisation not needed)

## Adverse effects
- Pain, swelling, fever, flu-like symptoms
- Transient measles-like rash, parotid swelling, arthralgia (rubella component, adult women)
- Febrile seizures (rare), thrombocytopenia (rare), anaphylaxis (gelatin/neomycin)

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy (avoid pregnancy for 1 month after vaccination)
- Immunosuppression (high-dose steroids, chemotherapy, biologics, advanced HIV)
- Severe allergy to neomycin or gelatin; recent immunoglobulin or blood products (defer 3–11 months)
- Acute febrile illness

## Drug interactions
- Can temporarily suppress tuberculin skin test — do Mantoux on the same day or 4–6 weeks after
- Immunoglobulin products reduce response
- Give other live vaccines the same day or 4 weeks apart

## Monitoring
- Observe 15–30 min after injection

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (live vaccine); inadvertent vaccination is not a reason for termination.

## Viva points
- Live vaccine — avoid in pregnancy and immunosuppression
- Immunotherapy for warts: induces Th1 response, clears distant warts
- Interferes with Mantoux reading

## Note on sources
Wolverton discusses Candida antigen and HPV vaccine more than MMR; MMR wart protocol is from published Indian studies and IADVL practice.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.43 (Topical and intralesional antiviral agents — IL immunotherapy for warts); national immunisation schedule. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Montelukast
posts.summary: IX Antihistaminics · Cysteinyl leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA) — not an antihistamine
posts.body:
_Oral · IX Antihistaminics_

**Class:** Cysteinyl leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA) — not an antihistamine

## Mechanism of action
- Blocks the CysLT1 receptor, so leukotrienes C4, D4 and E4 cannot cause vascular leakage, bronchoconstriction and eosinophil recruitment
- Useful where leukotrienes rather than histamine drive symptoms

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; metabolised by CYP2C8, 2C9 and 3A4; half-life 3–6 h; once daily in the evening

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Add-on in chronic urticaria that does not respond to antihistamines (especially aspirin/NSAID-exacerbated urticaria, delayed pressure urticaria) — evidence modest
- Atopic dermatitis with asthma (limited benefit), allergic rhinitis, asthma
- Mastocytosis

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 10 mg once daily in the evening
- Children: 4 mg (2–5 years), 5 mg (6–14 years) chewable

## Adverse effects
- Headache, GI upset
- Neuropsychiatric events (boxed warning, FDA 2020): sleep disturbance, nightmares, agitation, depression, suicidal thoughts — especially in children
- Churg–Strauss syndrome (EGPA) unmasked when steroids are tapered (rare)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; caution in history of psychiatric illness

## Drug interactions
- Phenobarbital and rifampicin lower levels

## Monitoring
- Ask about mood and sleep, especially in children

## Pregnancy & lactation
Can be used when needed (data from asthma); compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Leukotriene receptor antagonist, not an antihistamine
- Add-on in NSAID-exacerbated urticaria
- Neuropsychiatric boxed warning

## Note on sources
Montelukast is only briefly covered in the books; urticaria guidelines and the FDA label were used.

_Sources: Briefly mentioned in Wolverton (antihistamine/urticaria context) and Khopkar; urticaria guidelines and FDA label used. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF)
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) inhibitor; prodrug of mycophenolic acid
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) inhibitor; prodrug of mycophenolic acid

## Mechanism of action
- Mycophenolic acid reversibly inhibits IMPDH → blocks de novo guanine nucleotide synthesis
- Lymphocytes depend on the de novo pathway (other cells can use the salvage pathway), so the effect is fairly selective for T and B cells
- Also reduces antibody production and adhesion molecule expression

## Pharmacokinetics
- Rapidly converted to mycophenolic acid; glucuronidated in the liver; enterohepatic recirculation
- Enteric-coated mycophenolate sodium (720 mg ≈ 1 g MMF) has fewer GI effects

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Immunobullous diseases: pemphigus vulgaris (second line with rituximab in the Derma Desk ladder), bullous pemphigoid, mucous membrane pemphigoid
- Dermatomyositis, cutaneous lupus, systemic sclerosis (skin and lung), vasculitis
- Atopic dermatitis, psoriasis (modest), pyoderma gangrenosum, lichen planus

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 1–1.5 g twice daily (2–3 g/day); start at 500 mg twice daily and increase over 2–4 weeks
- Children: about 600 mg/m² twice daily
- Tablets 250 and 500 mg; mycophenolate sodium 180 and 360 mg

## Adverse effects
- GI (the commonest): nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps
- Myelosuppression (leucopenia, anaemia), opportunistic infections (CMV, herpes zoster)
- Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (rare); lymphoma and skin cancer risk
- Teratogenic

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy; hypersensitivity
- Active serious infection; caution in peptic ulcer disease and HGPRT deficiency (Lesch–Nyhan, Kelley–Seegmiller)

## Drug interactions
- Antacids, cholestyramine, PPIs, iron: reduce absorption
- Acyclovir/valacyclovir: both levels rise (compete for tubular secretion)
- Azathioprine: do not combine (double myelosuppression)
- Lowers oral contraceptive levels; rifampicin lowers MMF

## Monitoring
- CBC weekly for the first month, every 2 weeks for 2 months, then monthly
- LFT and renal function periodically; pregnancy tests

## Pregnancy & lactation
Contraindicated (old FDA category D; embryopathy including ear, facial and limb defects). Women need two forms of contraception during treatment and for 6 weeks after; men should use condoms during and for 90 days after.

## Viva points
- IMPDH inhibitor — lymphocyte-selective because of dependence on de novo purine synthesis
- GI side effects commonest; enteric-coated sodium salt helps
- Steroid-sparing agent in pemphigus

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.16 (Mycophenolates); Khopkar (Non-steroidal immunosuppressive drugs). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Nevirapine
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds directly to a hydrophobic pocket close to the active site of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase
- Non-competitive inhibition of the enzyme; no phosphorylation needed
- Not active against HIV-2

## Pharmacokinetics
- Over 90% absorbed; crosses the placenta and enters breast milk
- Metabolised by CYP3A4 and 2B6 and induces these enzymes (autoinduction), so the half-life falls from about 45 h to 25–30 h after 2–4 weeks

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Former first-line ART (with zidovudine + lamivudine), now replaced by dolutegravir-based regimens
- Infant prophylaxis in PMTCT (nevirapine syrup) under national programmes

## Dose & formulations
- 200 mg once daily for 14 days (lead-in), then 200 mg twice daily
- Infant prophylaxis: weight-based syrup for 6–12 weeks as per NACO

## Adverse effects
- Rash in about 15–20%, mostly in the first 6 weeks; SJS/TEN and DRESS (hypersensitivity syndrome)
- Hepatotoxicity: can be fulminant; risk higher in women with CD4 above 250 and men with CD4 above 400
- Fever, myalgia, nausea

## Contraindications
- Women with CD4 above 250 and men with CD4 above 400 (when starting)
- Moderate or severe liver disease (Child–Pugh B/C)
- Previous severe rash or hepatitis with nevirapine — never restart

## Drug interactions
- Lowers levels of oral contraceptives, ketoconazole, methadone, protease inhibitors
- Rifampicin lowers nevirapine levels — avoid
- Fluconazole raises nevirapine levels

## Monitoring
- LFT at baseline, 2, 4, 8 and 12 weeks, then periodically
- Skin examination in the first 6–8 weeks; stop if rash with fever, blisters, mucosal involvement, or hepatitis

## Pregnancy & lactation
Has been used in pregnancy, but liver toxicity is higher in women with high CD4 counts. Dolutegravir-based regimens are now preferred.

## Viva points
- Lead-in dosing because of autoinduction
- Rash in the first 6 weeks; one of the commonest causes of SJS/TEN in India
- CD4 thresholds for hepatotoxicity: women above 250, men above 400
- HLA associations with nevirapine hypersensitivity are described (Wolverton ch.3)

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4; Wolverton 4e ch.3, ch.11 and ch.67; check current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Nicotinamide (niacinamide, oral)
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Amide form of vitamin B3
posts.body:
_Oral · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Amide form of vitamin B3

## Mechanism of action
- Precursor of NAD⁺ — restores cellular energy after UV damage, improving DNA repair
- Prevents UV-induced immunosuppression
- Anti-inflammatory: inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis, mast-cell degranulation and PARP; reduces sebum

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; does not cause flushing (unlike nicotinic acid/niacin)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Chemoprevention of non-melanoma skin cancer in high-risk patients (ONTRAC trial: 23% fewer new cancers)
- Bullous pemphigoid (with tetracycline/doxycycline)
- Acne and rosacea (oral and topical), pellagra
- Other neutrophilic or inflammatory dermatoses: linear IgA, dermatitis herpetiformis (adjunct), granuloma annulare, necrobiosis lipoidica

## Dose & formulations
- Skin cancer chemoprevention: 500 mg twice daily
- Bullous pemphigoid: 500 mg three times daily (up to 2 g/day) with doxycycline/tetracycline
- Pellagra: 100 mg every 6 h until symptoms resolve, then maintenance

## Adverse effects
- Generally very safe: mild GI upset, headache
- At very high doses (above 3 g/day): hepatotoxicity

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; caution in liver disease at high doses

## Drug interactions
- Carbamazepine and primidone levels may rise

## Monitoring
- None at usual doses

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe at dietary/standard supplement doses.

## Viva points
- Nicotinamide does not cause flushing — nicotinic acid does
- ONTRAC trial: 500 mg twice daily reduces new skin cancers
- Nicotinamide + tetracycline for bullous pemphigoid

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.40 (Miscellaneous systemic drugs); Khopkar (Vitamins and trace elements). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Pheniramine maleate injection
posts.summary: VI Emergency drugs · First-generation (sedating) H1 antihistamine; alkylamine group
posts.body:
_Injectables · VI Emergency drugs_

**Class:** First-generation (sedating) H1 antihistamine; alkylamine group

## Mechanism of action
- H1 receptor inverse agonist — blocks histamine-mediated itch, wheal, flare and vascular leak
- Anticholinergic and sedative effects

## Pharmacokinetics
- IM or slow IV; onset within 15–30 min; duration 4–6 h

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Adjunct in anaphylaxis (after adrenaline) — relieves itch and urticaria; does not treat airway or shock
- Acute urticaria, angioedema (non-airway), allergic drug reactions, insect bite reactions
- Pre-medication before contrast media or blood products in sensitised patients

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 22.75–45.5 mg (1–2 mL of 22.75 mg/mL) IM or slow IV; repeat up to 2–3 times a day if needed
- Children: about 0.5–1 mg/kg/day in divided doses (avoid in infants)
- Ampoule 22.75 mg/mL (2 mL)

## Adverse effects
- Sedation, dizziness; hypotension with fast IV injection
- Anticholinergic: dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision
- Paradoxical excitation in children, convulsions in overdose

## Contraindications
- Neonates and premature infants; breastfeeding
- Caution: glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, epilepsy, elderly

## Drug interactions
- Alcohol, sedatives, opioids: additive CNS depression
- MAO inhibitors, other anticholinergics

## Monitoring
- Watch BP and level of consciousness after IV use

## Pregnancy & lactation
Use only if needed; prefer second-generation oral antihistamines for routine use.

## Viva points
- Commonly used injectable antihistamine in Indian practice (brand Avil)
- Second-line drug in anaphylaxis — never a substitute for adrenaline
- Inject IV slowly (hypotension)

_Sources: Khopkar (Antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers); Wolverton 4e ch.32 (H1 antihistamines — class). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23)
posts.summary: VII Vaccines · Inactivated polysaccharide vaccine — 23 serotypes of Streptococcus pneumoniae
posts.body:
_Injectables · VII Vaccines_

**Class:** Inactivated polysaccharide vaccine — 23 serotypes of Streptococcus pneumoniae

## Mechanism of action
- Capsular polysaccharides induce antibodies by a T-cell-independent pathway
- Gives no immunological memory, no booster effect, and is poorly immunogenic in children under 2 years
- Conjugate vaccines (PCV13/15/20) link the polysaccharide to a protein → T-cell-dependent, better memory

## Pharmacokinetics
- 0.5 mL IM or SC; antibodies within 2–3 weeks; wane after about 5 years

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Adults 65 years and over
- People at high risk aged 2–64: asplenia, chronic heart/lung/liver/kidney disease, diabetes, HIV
- Dermatology: before or early in immunosuppressive therapy — rituximab, long-term systemic steroids, methotrexate, azathioprine, MMF, cyclophosphamide, JAK inhibitors, biologics
- Give at least 2 weeks before rituximab (rituximab blunts antibody response for 6+ months)

## Dose & formulations
- 0.5 mL IM or SC
- Usual sequence: conjugate vaccine (PCV) first, then PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later; one revaccination with PPSV23 after 5 years in high-risk patients
- If PCV20 or PCV21 is used, PPSV23 is usually not needed (current CDC advice)

## Adverse effects
- Injection-site pain and swelling (more after revaccination)
- Low-grade fever, myalgia
- Severe reactions rare

## Contraindications
- Severe allergy to a previous dose or component
- Defer during acute illness

## Drug interactions
- Immunosuppressants and rituximab reduce response — vaccinate before starting where possible

## Monitoring
- None

## Pregnancy & lactation
Not routinely given; may be given to high-risk women if needed (inactivated).

## Viva points
- Polysaccharide = T-independent = no memory, poor in under-2s
- Vaccinate before rituximab and other immunosuppressants
- PCV first, then PPSV23 ≥8 weeks later

## Note on sources
Adult pneumococcal recommendations changed recently (PCV20/PCV21). Please confirm the current schedule.

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.30 (Rituximab — vaccination before therapy); CDC/ACIP adult schedule. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Prednisolone
posts.summary: VII Systemic corticosteroids · Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid (biological half-life 12–36 h); reference steroid for oral dosing
posts.body:
_Oral · VII Systemic corticosteroids_

**Class:** Intermediate-acting glucocorticoid (biological half-life 12–36 h); reference steroid for oral dosing

## Mechanism of action
- Enters cells and binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor; the complex enters the nucleus
- Genomic effects: switches on anti-inflammatory genes (lipocortin/annexin-1, IκB) and switches off pro-inflammatory genes (NF-κB and AP-1 targets: IL-1, IL-2, TNF-α, COX-2)
- Result: fewer circulating lymphocytes, eosinophils and monocytes; less vascular permeability; reduced antibody production with high doses
- Non-genomic (rapid) effects with high pulse doses

## Pharmacokinetics
- Prednisolone is active itself (prednisone needs conversion in the liver to prednisolone)
- Well absorbed; bound to transcortin and albumin; metabolised in the liver (enzyme inducers raise clearance)
- Equivalence: 5 mg prednisolone = 20 mg hydrocortisone = 4 mg methylprednisolone = 6 mg deflazacort = 0.75 mg dexamethasone = 0.6 mg betamethasone
- Glucocorticoid potency 4 (hydrocortisone = 1); mineralocorticoid effect 0.8

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Immunobullous diseases: pemphigus vulgaris (1–1.5 mg/kg/day initially), bullous pemphigoid (0.5–0.75 mg/kg/day if topical not possible)
- Connective tissue disease: dermatomyositis (1 mg/kg/day), SLE
- Vasculitis, neutrophilic dermatoses (Sweet syndrome, pyoderma gangrenosum)
- Short courses: acute severe allergic contact dermatitis, severe urticaria/angioedema (short), DRESS, erythema nodosum leprosum and type 1 lepra reaction
- Lichen planus (extensive), sarcoidosis, alopecia areata (selected)

## Dose & formulations
- Short courses: 0.5–1 mg/kg/day for 1–3 weeks, then taper
- Give as a single morning dose (mimics normal cortisol rhythm, less HPA suppression); divided doses for severe disease
- Alternate-day dosing for maintenance reduces HPA suppression and side effects
- Taper slowly once disease is controlled; below physiological dose (about 5–7.5 mg/day) taper more slowly
- Courses under 2–3 weeks can usually be stopped without taper

## Adverse effects
- Metabolic: hyperglycaemia/steroid diabetes, weight gain, Cushingoid features, hyperlipidaemia, hypokalaemia
- Bone: osteoporosis and fractures, avascular necrosis of femoral head, growth retardation in children
- Eye: posterior subcapsular cataract, glaucoma
- GI: peptic ulcer (mainly with NSAIDs), pancreatitis
- CNS: insomnia, mood change, psychosis
- Infections (TB reactivation, strongyloides hyperinfection, opportunistic); poor wound healing
- HPA axis suppression and adrenal crisis on sudden withdrawal
- Skin: striae, atrophy, purpura, steroid acne, hirsutism, delayed healing
- Hypertension, fluid retention; myopathy (proximal)

## Contraindications
- Absolute: systemic fungal infection, herpes simplex keratitis, hypersensitivity
- Relative: active TB, uncontrolled diabetes or hypertension, peptic ulcer, osteoporosis, psychosis, recent live vaccines, pregnancy (prefer lowest dose)

## Drug interactions
- Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) lower steroid levels — dose may need doubling
- CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir) raise levels
- NSAIDs: GI ulcer risk
- Diuretics/amphotericin B: hypokalaemia
- Live vaccines: avoid with immunosuppressive doses

## Monitoring
- Baseline: weight, BP, glucose, lipids, electrolytes, eye exam, TB screen, bone density (if long-term), stool for strongyloides in endemic areas
- Follow-up: BP, weight, glucose, electrolytes regularly; eye exam every 6–12 months; bone density annually if long-term
- Prevention: calcium + vitamin D, bisphosphonate if long-term (≥3 months, ≥7.5 mg/day), PPI if ulcer risk, deworming (albendazole) in endemic areas

## Pregnancy & lactation
Prednisolone is mostly inactivated by placental 11β-HSD2, so it is the preferred steroid in pregnancy; slight risk of cleft palate with first-trimester use and growth restriction with high doses. Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Know the equivalence table
- Morning single dose; alternate-day dosing to spare the HPA axis
- Prophylaxis for long-term use: calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonate, PPI if needed, deworming
- Prednisone is a prodrug; prednisolone is active (use in liver disease)
- Placenta inactivates prednisolone — preferred in pregnancy (dexamethasone and betamethasone cross)

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.13 (Systemic corticosteroids); Khopkar ch.8 (Oral and injectable steroids), Table 8.2. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Pregabalin + Nortriptyline
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Fixed-dose combination: gabapentinoid (pregabalin) + tricyclic antidepressant (nortriptyline)
posts.body:
_Oral · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Fixed-dose combination: gabapentinoid (pregabalin) + tricyclic antidepressant (nortriptyline)

## Mechanism of action
- Pregabalin binds the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels in nerve endings → less release of glutamate, substance P and noradrenaline → reduces neuropathic pain and neuropathic itch
- Nortriptyline (secondary-amine TCA, metabolite of amitriptyline) blocks reuptake of noradrenaline (and serotonin) → strengthens descending pain-inhibiting pathways; fewer anticholinergic effects than amitriptyline
- The two act at different points, so lower doses of each can be used

## Pharmacokinetics
- Pregabalin: well absorbed, not metabolised, excreted by kidneys — reduce in renal impairment; no CYP interactions
- Nortriptyline: metabolised by CYP2D6; long half-life (about 30 h)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN)
- Neuropathic itch: brachioradial pruritus, notalgia paraesthetica, post-zoster itch, scalp dysaesthesia
- Leprosy neuritis-related neuropathic pain, diabetic neuropathy
- Pregabalin alone: uraemic pruritus, chronic prurigo, burning mouth (adjunct)

## Dose & formulations
- Common Indian FDC: pregabalin 75 mg + nortriptyline 10 mg, one tablet at bedtime; may increase to twice daily
- Pregabalin alone: start 75 mg twice daily (or 75 mg at night), up to 150–300 mg/day (max 600 mg/day); halve in renal impairment
- Start low and go slow in the elderly; taper slowly when stopping

## Adverse effects
- Pregabalin: dizziness, drowsiness, weight gain, peripheral oedema, blurred vision; misuse and dependence potential; withdrawal on abrupt stop
- Nortriptyline: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, postural hypotension, sedation
- Nortriptyline: arrhythmias and QT prolongation; overdose is dangerous (cardiotoxic)
- Suicidal thoughts (antidepressant class warning)

## Contraindications
- Recent myocardial infarction, heart block or arrhythmia (TCA)
- Use of MAO inhibitors within 14 days
- Narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention, severe liver disease
- Caution: elderly (falls), renal impairment, history of substance misuse, suicidal risk

## Drug interactions
- Other CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines): more sedation and respiratory depression
- SSRIs, tramadol, linezolid with TCA: serotonin syndrome
- CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, terbinafine) raise nortriptyline levels
- Other QT-prolonging and anticholinergic drugs

## Monitoring
- ECG before starting in patients over 40–50 or with cardiac history
- Renal function for pregabalin dosing; mood and suicidal ideation; weight

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid in pregnancy unless clearly needed (possible malformation signal with pregabalin; TCA neonatal withdrawal). Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- Pregabalin: α2δ calcium-channel ligand
- Nortriptyline: fewer anticholinergic effects than amitriptyline
- Terbinafine (CYP2D6 inhibitor) raises nortriptyline levels
- Used for PHN and neuropathic itch

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.35 (Psychotropic agents) and ch.39 (Drugs for the skinternist; pregabalin); Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Propranolol
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Non-selective β-adrenergic blocker
posts.body:
_Oral · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Non-selective β-adrenergic blocker

## Mechanism of action
- In infantile haemangioma: early vasoconstriction (lighter colour, softer within days), then inhibition of angiogenic signals (VEGF, bFGF) and induction of apoptosis of endothelial cells
- Also blocks the renin–angiotensin system in haemangioma tissue

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; large first-pass metabolism; lipophilic (crosses BBB); half-life 3–6 h
- Hypoglycaemia risk: blocks glycogenolysis and masks its warning signs

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Infantile haemangioma — first-line systemic therapy: ulcerated, function-threatening (eye, airway, ear), disfiguring (face, nose, lip), segmental (PHACE), or multiple with liver involvement
- Best started early (proliferative phase, ideally before 5 months of age)
- Off-label: performance anxiety, rosacea flushing, essential tremor

## Dose & formulations
