- Infantile haemangioma: start 0.5–1 mg/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses, increase over 1–2 weeks to 2–3 mg/kg/day (Wolverton: 1–3 mg/kg/day divided twice or three times daily)
- Give with or just after feeds (avoid hypoglycaemia); stop during illness or poor feeding
- Continue for at least 6 months (often until 12 months of age), then taper
- Oral solution 20 mg/5 mL or 40 mg/5 mL; in India often prepared from tablets

## Adverse effects
- Hypoglycaemia (especially with poor feeding or vomiting) — the most important in infants
- Bradycardia, hypotension
- Bronchospasm/wheeze
- Sleep disturbance, cold hands and feet, GI upset
- Rebound growth of haemangioma after stopping

## Contraindications
- Cardiogenic shock, sinus bradycardia, heart block above first degree, heart failure
- Bronchial asthma or bronchospasm, hypoglycaemia tendency
- Premature infants under 5 weeks corrected age, weight under 2 kg (caution)
- PHACE syndrome with significant brain vessel abnormalities — careful assessment before starting (stroke risk)

## Drug interactions
- Other antihypertensives and calcium-channel blockers (verapamil — bradycardia)
- Insulin and oral hypoglycaemics (masking of hypoglycaemia)
- CYP2D6 inhibitors raise levels

## Monitoring
- Baseline: history and examination of heart and lungs, heart rate and BP; ECG if bradycardia or family history of arrhythmia
- Heart rate and BP 1–2 h after the first dose and after each dose increase
- Counsel parents on hypoglycaemia signs

## Pregnancy & lactation
Used in pregnancy for maternal indications (may cause fetal growth restriction and neonatal bradycardia/hypoglycaemia). Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- First-line systemic treatment for problematic infantile haemangioma
- Give with feeds — hypoglycaemia is the main risk
- Check heart rate and BP after starting and after dose increases
- Screen for PHACE syndrome in large segmental facial haemangiomas

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.70 (Dermatologic drug therapy in children), ; Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Ritonavir
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART) · HIV protease inhibitor (PI); used today mainly as a pharmacokinetic booster
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Antiretroviral (ART)_

**Class:** HIV protease inhibitor (PI); used today mainly as a pharmacokinetic booster

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits HIV protease, which cleaves the gag-pol polyprotein → immature, non-infectious virus particles
- At low dose (100 mg) it strongly inhibits CYP3A4 (and P-gp), so it is used to 'boost' levels of other PIs (lopinavir, atazanavir, darunavir)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Take with food; metabolised by CYP3A4 (and also induces some enzymes such as glucuronidation, CYP1A2, 2C9 and 2C19)
- Highly protein bound

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Booster in second-line ART: lopinavir/ritonavir 400/100 mg twice daily, atazanavir/ritonavir 300/100 mg once daily, darunavir/ritonavir
- Full-dose ritonavir as the only PI is no longer used because of poor tolerance

## Dose & formulations
- Booster dose: 100 mg once or twice daily with the partner PI
- Heat-stable tablet formulations; take with food

## Adverse effects
- GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; altered taste; perioral and peripheral paraesthesia
- Metabolic: hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, insulin resistance
- Lipodystrophy: central fat gain (buffalo hump, increased abdominal fat) with peripheral lipoatrophy
- Hepatitis, pancreatitis; PR/QT prolongation

## Contraindications
- Co-administration with CYP3A4 substrates that are dangerous at high levels: simvastatin, lovastatin, midazolam (oral), pimozide, ergot alkaloids, amiodarone, sildenafil for pulmonary hypertension, colchicine in renal/liver impairment

## Drug interactions
- Dermatology-relevant: inhaled, intranasal or injected corticosteroids (fluticasone, budesonide, intralesional or intra-articular triamcinolone) → iatrogenic Cushing syndrome and adrenal suppression
- Raises cyclosporine, tacrolimus, colchicine (fatal toxicity reported), itraconazole and some antihistamines
- Lowers oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol) levels and voriconazole levels
- Rifampicin lowers PI levels — avoid

## Monitoring
- Lipids and glucose; LFT
- Review all co-prescribed drugs, including steroid injections and creams over large areas

## Pregnancy & lactation
Boosted PIs (e.g. atazanavir/ritonavir, lopinavir/ritonavir) are used in pregnancy when needed.

## Viva points
- Ritonavir is mostly a 'booster' through CYP3A4 inhibition
- Triamcinolone injection or inhaled fluticasone with ritonavir → Cushing syndrome
- PI-related lipodystrophy and dyslipidaemia

## Note on sources
Wolverton gives little detail on ART; Khopkar and NACO used.

_Sources: Khopkar ch.4; Wolverton 4e ch.11 and ch.66 (Drug interactions); check current NACO guidelines. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Sodium bicarbonate injection
posts.summary: VI Emergency drugs · Alkalinising agent (systemic buffer)
posts.body:
_Injectables · VI Emergency drugs_

**Class:** Alkalinising agent (systemic buffer)

## Mechanism of action
- Bicarbonate combines with hydrogen ions → carbonic acid → CO₂ (breathed out) and water → raises blood pH
- Alkalinises urine; shifts potassium into cells
- In local anaesthesia: raises solution pH so more drug is unionised → faster onset and much less injection pain

## Pharmacokinetics
- Available as 7.5% (≈0.9 mEq/mL) and 8.4% (1 mEq/mL) solutions; hypertonic

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Buffering lignocaine before injection (dermatology use): 1 mL 8.4% NaHCO₃ to 10 mL lignocaine (with or without adrenaline)
- Severe metabolic acidosis (e.g. pH below 7.1), hyperkalaemia (adjunct), tricyclic antidepressant overdose (QRS widening)
- Urinary alkalinisation in methotrexate toxicity and salicylate poisoning
- Not given routinely in cardiac arrest

## Dose & formulations
- Buffering: 1 : 10 with lignocaine — use within about a week (adrenaline breaks down faster in alkaline solution); prepare fresh where possible
- Metabolic acidosis: 1 mEq/kg slow IV, then guided by blood gases
- Hyperkalaemia/TCA overdose: 50–100 mEq IV slowly

## Adverse effects
- Metabolic alkalosis, hypernatraemia, fluid overload
- Hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia (tetany)
- Severe tissue necrosis if extravasated (hypertonic)
- Paradoxical CSF acidosis (CO₂ crosses BBB)

## Contraindications
- Metabolic or respiratory alkalosis, hypocalcaemia, chloride loss from vomiting
- Caution: heart failure, renal failure, hypernatraemia

## Drug interactions
- Incompatible with calcium salts and catecholamines in the same line (precipitates/inactivates)
- Alkaline urine increases excretion of salicylates and methotrexate, decreases excretion of amphetamines

## Monitoring
- Arterial blood gas, sodium, potassium, calcium during IV use

## Pregnancy & lactation
Use when indicated.

## Viva points
- Buffered lignocaine (1:10) — less pain, faster onset
- Urine alkalinisation in MTX toxicity
- Not routine in CPR

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.58 (buffering local anaesthetics) and ch.14 (MTX toxicity). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: STI kits (NACO colour-coded kits)
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Pre-packed syndromic treatment kits supplied free under the National AIDS Control Programme (NACO) — 7 colour-coded kits
posts.body:
_Oral · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Pre-packed syndromic treatment kits supplied free under the National AIDS Control Programme (NACO) — 7 colour-coded kits

## Mechanism of action
- Syndromic case management: treats all the common organisms that cause a given syndrome at the first visit, without waiting for lab tests
- Each kit is a single complete course, which improves adherence; partners get the same kit

## Pharmacokinetics
- See each component drug (azithromycin, cefixime, secnidazole, fluconazole, benzathine penicillin, doxycycline, acyclovir, metronidazole)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Kit 1 — Grey: urethral discharge, anorectal discharge, cervicitis → azithromycin 1 g single dose + cefixime 400 mg single dose
- Kit 2 — Green: vaginal discharge (vaginitis: trichomonas, bacterial vaginosis, candida) → secnidazole 2 g single dose + fluconazole 150 mg single dose
- Kit 3 — White: genital ulcer disease, non-herpetic (syphilis, chancroid) → benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose (with sterile water and syringe) + azithromycin 1 g single dose
- Kit 4 — Blue: genital ulcer disease, non-herpetic, for penicillin allergy → doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 15 days + azithromycin 1 g single dose
- Kit 5 — Red: genital ulcer disease, herpetic → acyclovir 400 mg three times daily × 7 days
- Kit 6 — Yellow: lower abdominal pain (PID) → cefixime 400 mg single dose + metronidazole 400 mg twice daily × 14 days + doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 14 days
- Kit 7 — Black: inguinal bubo (LGV, chancroid) → doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 21 days + azithromycin 1 g single dose

## Dose & formulations
- Given as the full kit to the patient, with an identical kit (or appropriate treatment) for each partner
- Pregnancy: avoid doxycycline kits (blue, black, yellow) — use erythromycin/azithromycin alternatives as per NACO; secnidazole avoided in the first trimester

## Adverse effects
- As for the individual drugs: GI upset (azithromycin, metronidazole, doxycycline), disulfiram-like reaction (metronidazole/secnidazole with alcohol), Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction and anaphylaxis risk (benzathine penicillin), photosensitivity (doxycycline)

## Contraindications
- Kit 3 (white): penicillin allergy → use kit 4 (blue)
- Doxycycline kits in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children under 8
- Avoid alcohol with kits containing metronidazole or secnidazole

## Drug interactions
- See component drugs

## Monitoring
- Follow-up at 7 days (14 days for ulcers and PID) to check response
- Offer HIV and syphilis testing, condoms, partner notification and counselling (the '4 Cs': compliance, counselling, condoms, contact tracing)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Adjust in pregnancy (no doxycycline); syphilis in pregnancy → benzathine penicillin (desensitise if allergic).

## Viva points
- Know each colour and its contents — a favourite viva question
- Grey = urethral discharge; Green = vaginal discharge; White = non-herpetic ulcer; Blue = non-herpetic ulcer with penicillin allergy; Red = herpetic ulcer; Yellow = lower abdominal pain; Black = bubo
- Syndromic approach — treat the patient and partner at the first visit
- 4 Cs of STI management

## Note on sources
The kit contents follow NACO's standard 7-kit scheme. The exam list names 5 colours (white, green, blue, yellow, black), but all 7 are included because grey and red are commonly asked too. Please check against the latest NACO technical guidelines in case your hospital supply differs.

_Sources: NACO National Guidelines on Prevention, Management and Control of RTI including STI (colour-coded kits); not covered in Wolverton or Khopkar. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Terbinafine
posts.summary: III Antifungals · Allylamine antifungal
posts.body:
_Oral · III Antifungals_

**Class:** Allylamine antifungal

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits squalene epoxidase, an early step in ergosterol synthesis
- Toxic build-up of squalene inside the cell → fungicidal against dermatophytes
- Ergosterol deficiency adds a fungistatic effect (mainly against yeasts)

## Pharmacokinetics
- 70–80% absorbed; food does not matter
- Highly lipophilic and keratophilic; reaches the stratum corneum via sebum and the nail via the matrix
- Persists in nails for weeks to months after stopping; long terminal half-life
- Metabolised in the liver; inhibits CYP2D6

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Dermatophytosis: tinea corporis, cruris, pedis and manuum
- Onychomycosis caused by dermatophytes (drug of choice)
- Tinea capitis — especially Trichophyton tonsurans (less effective for Microsporum)
- Some activity in sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis; poor against Candida and Malassezia orally

## Dose & formulations
- Adults: 250 mg once daily
- Tinea corporis/cruris: 2–4 weeks (often longer in India due to resistance — follow current national consensus)
- Onychomycosis: fingernails 6 weeks, toenails 12 weeks
- Tinea capitis (children): 10–20 kg 62.5 mg; 21–40 kg 125 mg; over 40 kg 250 mg daily, for 2–6 weeks (T. tonsurans)

## Adverse effects
- GI upset, headache
- Taste disturbance (can last weeks), loss of smell
- Rash, urticaria; rarely SJS/TEN, AGEP, DRESS
- Induction or worsening of subacute cutaneous lupus; worsening of psoriasis
- Hepatotoxicity — rare but can be severe (cholestatic or hepatitic; liver failure reported)
- Neutropenia, depression (rare)

## Contraindications
- Chronic or active liver disease
- Severe renal impairment (clearance under 50 mL/min — avoid or reduce dose)
- Lupus erythematosus (relative)

## Drug interactions
- CYP2D6 inhibition: raises levels of tricyclic antidepressants, some SSRIs, beta-blockers (metoprolol), codeine activation reduced
- Rifampicin lowers terbinafine levels; cimetidine raises them

## Monitoring
- Baseline LFT (as advised by the label); repeat if courses exceed 6 weeks or symptoms of liver injury
- CBC if course exceeds 6 weeks

## Pregnancy & lactation
Old FDA category B, but because it is not urgent, treatment of onychomycosis is postponed until after pregnancy and breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- The only commonly used oral antifungal that is fungicidal
- Squalene epoxidase inhibition — not CYP450 dependent
- Inhibits CYP2D6, not CYP3A4 (unlike azoles)
- Squalene epoxidase gene mutations explain terbinafine resistance in T. indotineae seen in India

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.10, Table 10.5; Khopkar ch.2. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Thalidomide
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Glutamic acid derivative; immunomodulatory drug (IMiD)
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Glutamic acid derivative; immunomodulatory drug (IMiD)

## Mechanism of action
- Binds cereblon (part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase), changing which proteins are degraded
- Reduces TNF-α production (by speeding TNF mRNA breakdown); shifts Th1 responses
- Anti-angiogenic (explains teratogenicity — limb defects) and sedative

## Pharmacokinetics
- Slowly absorbed; half-life about 5–7 h
- Broken down mainly by non-enzymatic hydrolysis — few CYP interactions

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) — drug of choice for severe/recurrent ENL
- Cutaneous lupus (refractory discoid/subacute), Behçet disease and aphthous ulcers (especially HIV)
- Prurigo nodularis, actinic prurigo, Jessner lymphocytic infiltrate, sarcoidosis, graft-versus-host disease
- Multiple myeloma (oncology)

## Dose & formulations
- ENL: 100–400 mg/day at bedtime (start 100 mg; higher doses split), taper to the lowest effective dose (e.g. 50–100 mg) once controlled
- Lupus, prurigo, aphthae: 50–100 mg/day at night
- Capsules 50, 100 mg

## Adverse effects
- Teratogenic — phocomelia and other limb, ear, heart, GI defects even after a single dose in early pregnancy (days 20–36 after conception)
- Peripheral neuropathy (sensory, often irreversible; dose- and duration-related)
- Sedation, dizziness, constipation, oedema
- Venous thromboembolism (especially with steroids or chemotherapy)
- Rash, bradycardia, neutropenia, hypothyroidism

## Contraindications
- Pregnancy and women unable to use reliable contraception
- Existing peripheral neuropathy; breastfeeding

## Drug interactions
- CNS depressants (alcohol, sedatives): more sedation
- Drugs causing neuropathy (dapsone, metronidazole, isoniazid): more neuropathy
- Drugs raising clot risk (oral contraceptives, steroids)

## Monitoring
- Pregnancy tests before, weekly in the first month, then monthly
- Baseline and periodic nerve conduction studies or clinical sensory examination
- Watch for signs of thrombosis

## Pregnancy & lactation
Absolute contraindication (old FDA category X). Women: two contraceptive methods from 4 weeks before until 4 weeks after. Men must use condoms (drug is present in semen) during treatment and for 4 weeks after. Restricted-distribution programme in many countries.

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for severe ENL
- Teratogenicity — phocomelia; sensitive period days 20–36 after conception
- Peripheral neuropathy — monitor
- Mechanism: cereblon binding, TNF-α reduction, anti-angiogenesis

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.40 (Miscellaneous systemic drugs); Khopkar (Miscellaneous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Tofacitinib
posts.summary: VI Immunosuppressants · Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor — mainly JAK1 and JAK3 (pan-JAK at higher doses)
posts.body:
_Oral · VI Immunosuppressants_

**Class:** Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor — mainly JAK1 and JAK3 (pan-JAK at higher doses)

## Mechanism of action
- Blocks JAK enzymes that pass on signals from cytokine receptors
- So STAT proteins are not activated, and responses to IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-7, IL-15, IL-21 and interferons are reduced
- Dampens T-cell, B-cell and NK-cell function

## Pharmacokinetics
- Well absorbed; half-life about 3 h (twice daily or once-daily extended release)
- Metabolised by CYP3A4 (70%) and kidneys (30%)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Approved: rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ulcerative colitis
- Off-label in dermatology: alopecia areata, vitiligo (with phototherapy), refractory dermatomyositis, atopic dermatitis, sarcoidosis, lichen planopilaris, psoriasis
- In the Derma Desk ladders it is a later-line option (e.g. alopecia areata, vitiligo)

## Dose & formulations
- 5 mg twice daily (or 11 mg extended release once daily); 10 mg twice daily used in some trials and off-label for alopecia areata
- Reduce to 5 mg once daily with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or moderate–severe renal/hepatic impairment

## Adverse effects
- Infections: upper respiratory, herpes zoster (notable risk), TB reactivation, opportunistic infections
- Boxed warnings (ORAL Surveillance study, patients over 50 with cardiovascular risk): major cardiac events, thrombosis (DVT/PE), malignancy (lung cancer, lymphoma), and death
- Raised lipids, LFT and creatine kinase; cytopenias (lymphopenia, neutropenia, anaemia)
- Acne, headache, GI perforation (rare)

## Contraindications
- Active serious infection including TB; severe hepatic impairment
- Lymphocytes under 500/mm³, neutrophils under 1000/mm³, Hb under 9 g/dL
- Pregnancy; caution if over 50 with cardiovascular risk factors or smokers, history of thrombosis or cancer

## Drug interactions
- Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole) → reduce dose; inducers (rifampicin) → avoid
- Do not combine with biologics or potent immunosuppressants such as cyclosporine or azathioprine
- Live vaccines — avoid; give recombinant zoster vaccine beforehand

## Monitoring
- Baseline: CBC, LFT, lipids, renal function, TB screen (IGRA), hepatitis B/C, HIV
- CBC and LFT at 4–8 weeks, then every 3 months; lipids at 4–8 weeks
- Skin check; cardiovascular risk review

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (limited data; animal teratogenicity). Stop at least 4 weeks before planned conception. Avoid in breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- JAK-STAT pathway — 'cytokine signal blocker'
- Herpes zoster risk — consider the recombinant zoster vaccine
- Boxed warning from ORAL Surveillance: MACE, thrombosis, malignancy, death
- Oral JAK inhibitor; topical 2% ointment is in the topicals slot

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.18 (PDE-4 and JAK inhibitors); Khopkar edition predates JAK inhibitors. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Triamcinolone acetonide injection
posts.summary: II Corticosteroids · Intermediate-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid; insoluble depot suspension
posts.body:
_Injectables · II Corticosteroids_

**Class:** Intermediate-acting fluorinated glucocorticoid; insoluble depot suspension

## Mechanism of action
- Glucocorticoid receptor agonist (5 times hydrocortisone); the acetonide crystals dissolve slowly, giving a local depot lasting weeks
- In keloids: reduces fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis, increases collagenase

## Pharmacokinetics
- Suspension — shake well; never give IV
- Local effect lasts 3–6 weeks; some systemic absorption (HPA suppression possible with large doses)
- Vials 10 mg/mL and 40 mg/mL

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Intralesional (IL): keloids and hypertrophic scars, alopecia areata (patchy), discoid lupus, lichen planus (hypertrophic), lichen simplex chronicus, prurigo nodularis, granuloma annulare, sarcoidosis, nodulocystic acne, psoriasis plaques and nail psoriasis, necrobiosis lipoidica, chalazion
- Intramuscular: short-term control of severe allergic or inflammatory dermatoses (used sparingly)

## Dose & formulations
- IL concentrations: face and acne cysts 2.5 mg/mL; alopecia areata 2.5–10 mg/mL (5 mg/mL commonly); thick plaques 5–10 mg/mL; keloids 10–40 mg/mL
- Dilute with normal saline or lignocaine; inject 0.05–0.1 mL per site, about 1 cm apart, into the dermis (subcutaneous injection causes fat atrophy); keloids are injected into the body of the lesion
- Repeat every 3–6 weeks; keep the total per session modest (e.g. up to about 20–40 mg total for scalp)
- IM: 40–80 mg into the gluteus (deep), not more often than every 4–6 weeks

## Adverse effects
- Local: atrophy (dermal and fat), hypopigmentation (especially in dark skin), telangiectasia, injection-site infection, crystal deposits
- Rare but serious: blindness from retinal artery embolism after periocular/nasal/scalp injection — inject slowly with low pressure, aspirate
- Systemic (large doses/IM): HPA suppression, Cushingoid features, menstrual irregularity, hyperglycaemia
- IM: fat atrophy at gluteal site, abscess

## Contraindications
- Infection at the injection site; known hypersensitivity
- IV injection
- Caution: on ritonavir/cobicistat (Cushing syndrome)

## Drug interactions
- Ritonavir, cobicistat, itraconazole (strong CYP3A4 inhibitors): iatrogenic Cushing and adrenal suppression even after IL/joint injection

## Monitoring
- Photograph lesions; check for atrophy before repeat injections
- Glucose in diabetics after large doses

## Pregnancy & lactation
Small IL doses are acceptable; avoid large IM doses.

## Viva points
- Concentrations by site: face 2.5, AA 5, keloid 10–40 mg/mL
- Inject into the dermis, not fat
- Atrophy and hypopigmentation are the commonest side effects; blindness the most feared
- Ritonavir interaction

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.45 (Topical corticosteroids — IL use) and ch.13; Khopkar ch.22 (Topical and intralesional corticosteroids). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Tuberculin PPD (Mantoux test)
posts.summary: VII Vaccines · Purified protein derivative of M. tuberculosis — diagnostic antigen for delayed-type hypersensitivity
posts.body:
_Injectables · VII Vaccines_

**Class:** Purified protein derivative of M. tuberculosis — diagnostic antigen for delayed-type hypersensitivity

## Mechanism of action
- In people previously sensitised to mycobacteria (infection or BCG), memory T cells react to intradermal PPD
- Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity → induration peaks at 48–72 h

## Pharmacokinetics
- Intradermal injection forms a 6–10 mm wheal (bleb)

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Screening for latent TB before biologics, JAK inhibitors, long-term steroids, methotrexate and other immunosuppressants (IGRA preferred after BCG)
- Supporting diagnosis of cutaneous TB (lupus vulgaris, TBVC, scrofuloderma usually strongly positive)
- Assessing cell-mediated immunity (anergy in sarcoidosis, HIV, lepromatous leprosy)
- Dermatology off-label: intralesional immunotherapy for warts (PPD 10 TU into the largest wart every 2 weeks)

## Dose & formulations
- Mantoux: 0.1 mL (5 TU PPD-S or 2 TU PPD RT23 used in India) intradermal on the volar forearm
- Read at 48–72 h: measure induration (not redness) across the forearm
- Positive: ≥5 mm in HIV, immunosuppressed (including ≥15 mg prednisolone/day), recent contacts; ≥10 mm in others at risk (and in India generally); ≥15 mm in people with no risk factors

## Adverse effects
- Local itching, redness; rarely blistering or ulceration in highly sensitive people
- Lymphangitis (rare); anaphylaxis very rare

## Contraindications
- Previous severe reaction to tuberculin (blistering, necrosis)
- Known active TB — not needed

## Drug interactions
- False negatives: recent live vaccine (MMR, varicella — do test the same day or 4–6 weeks later), immunosuppressants, HIV, sarcoidosis, malnutrition, overwhelming TB, measles, Hodgkin disease, very young or old
- False positives: BCG vaccination, non-tuberculous mycobacteria
- Booster phenomenon: repeat test may be positive because the first test re-awakens immunity (two-step testing)

## Monitoring
- Read at 48–72 h by trained staff

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- Measure induration, not erythema
- Lupus vulgaris — strongly positive
- Causes of false-negative and false-positive results
- IGRA is preferred in BCG-vaccinated people before biologics

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.26 (TNF inhibitors — TB screening); Khopkar (Antituberculous agents). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Valacyclovir
posts.summary: IV Antivirals — Anti-herpes · L-valyl ester prodrug of acyclovir
posts.body:
_Oral · IV Antivirals — Anti-herpes_

**Class:** L-valyl ester prodrug of acyclovir

## Mechanism of action
- Rapidly converted to acyclovir by first-pass intestinal and hepatic metabolism
- Then acts like acyclovir: viral thymidine kinase → triphosphate → inhibits viral DNA polymerase

## Pharmacokinetics
- Bioavailability about 55% (3–5 times that of acyclovir) → fewer daily doses
- Gives plasma acyclovir levels similar to IV acyclovir at high doses
- Renal excretion as acyclovir — reduce dose in renal impairment

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Herpes zoster (start within 72 h)
- Genital herpes: first episode, recurrences, suppression (also reduces transmission to partner)
- Herpes labialis (single-day treatment)
- HSV-associated erythema multiforme suppression

## Dose & formulations
- Herpes zoster: 1 g three times daily × 7 days
- First-episode genital herpes: 1 g twice daily × 7–10 days
- Recurrent genital herpes: 500 mg twice daily × 3 days, or 1 g once daily × 5 days
- Suppression: 500 mg–1 g once daily
- Herpes labialis: 2 g twice daily for 1 day (12 h apart)

## Adverse effects
- Headache, nausea, abdominal pain
- CNS toxicity (confusion, hallucinations) in elderly or renally impaired patients
- Very high doses (8 g/day) in advanced HIV/transplant: thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS)

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity to valacyclovir or acyclovir

## Drug interactions
- As for acyclovir: probenecid, cimetidine, mycophenolate, nephrotoxic drugs

## Monitoring
- Renal function in the elderly or those with kidney disease

## Pregnancy & lactation
Considered safe (old FDA category B). Compatible with breastfeeding.

## Viva points
- A prodrug with 3–5 times better bioavailability than acyclovir
- Once-daily suppression; reduces genital herpes transmission
- TTP/HUS reported at very high doses in immunocompromised patients

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.11; Khopkar ch.3. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) 60,000 IU
posts.summary: VIII Vitamins · Fat-soluble vitamin (secosteroid prohormone)
posts.body:
_Injectables · VIII Vitamins_

**Class:** Fat-soluble vitamin (secosteroid prohormone)

## Mechanism of action
- Converted in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D (storage form, measured in blood), then in the kidney to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol, active)
- Calcitriol acts on the vitamin D receptor: increases calcium and phosphate absorption, regulates bone
- Skin effects: regulates keratinocyte differentiation, boosts innate immunity (cathelicidin), dampens Th1/Th17 responses

## Pharmacokinetics
- Stored in fat; long half-life of 25(OH)D (about 2–3 weeks) allows weekly or monthly dosing
- Oral 60,000 IU (sachet, capsule, chewable) is well absorbed and preferred
- IM injections (usually 300,000 or 600,000 IU) are absorbed slowly and unpredictably — reserve for malabsorption or poor compliance

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Vitamin D deficiency (common in India): especially patients on strict photoprotection (xeroderma pigmentosum, porphyria, lupus), long-term steroids, anticonvulsants, dark skin with little sun
- Bone protection with long-term systemic steroids (with calcium)
- Adjunct (evidence modest): atopic dermatitis, chronic urticaria, psoriasis, vitiligo, alopecia areata in deficient patients
- Rickets, osteomalacia

## Dose & formulations
- Deficiency (adults): 60,000 IU once weekly orally for 8 weeks, then 60,000 IU monthly for maintenance
- Children: weight/age-based (e.g. 60,000 IU weekly for 6 weeks over 1 year of age; lower in infants)
- IM (if needed): 300,000–600,000 IU single dose ('stoss' therapy) — not repeated within 3 months
- Deficiency: 25(OH)D below 20 ng/mL; insufficiency 20–29 ng/mL; sufficient 30–100 ng/mL

## Adverse effects
- At usual doses — safe
- Toxicity (25(OH)D over about 150 ng/mL): hypercalcaemia → nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, thirst, confusion, kidney stones, nephrocalcinosis, arrhythmia

## Contraindications
- Hypercalcaemia, vitamin D toxicity
- Caution: granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, TB — macrophages make calcitriol → hypercalcaemia), kidney stones, severe renal failure (needs active form)

## Drug interactions
- Thiazide diuretics: hypercalcaemia
- Digoxin: hypercalcaemia increases toxicity
- Anticonvulsants, rifampicin, long-term steroids increase vitamin D needs
- Orlistat and cholestyramine reduce absorption

## Monitoring
- Serum 25(OH)D at baseline and 3 months after loading; serum calcium (especially with high doses or sarcoidosis)

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe at recommended doses; deficiency should be corrected in pregnancy.

## Viva points
- 60,000 IU weekly × 8 weeks, then monthly
- Measure 25(OH)D, not 1,25(OH)₂D
- Sarcoidosis — risk of hypercalcaemia
- Patients on strict photoprotection need supplements

## Note on sources
The exam list puts 60,000 IU under injectables, but 60,000 IU is mainly an oral dose in India (injections are 300,000/600,000 IU). Both are covered.

_Sources: Khopkar (Vitamins and trace elements); Endocrine Society and Indian vitamin D guidance. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Voriconazole
posts.summary: III Antifungals · Second-generation triazole (fluconazole derivative)
posts.body:
_Oral · III Antifungals_

**Class:** Second-generation triazole (fluconazole derivative)

## Mechanism of action
- Inhibits fungal 14-α-demethylase → ergosterol depletion
- Broad spectrum: Aspergillus (fungicidal), Fusarium, Scedosporium, Candida (including fluconazole-resistant C. krusei and C. glabrata), dimorphic fungi
- No activity against Mucorales (mucormycosis)

## Pharmacokinetics
- About 96% bioavailable — take 1 h before or after meals
- Non-linear (saturable) kinetics; metabolised by CYP2C19, 2C9 and 3A4
- CYP2C19 poor metabolisers (more common in Asians) have higher levels and more toxicity
- Good CNS penetration

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Invasive aspergillosis (drug of choice)
- Fusarium and Scedosporium infections; candidaemia and resistant oesophageal candidiasis
- Rarely in dermatology: refractory chromoblastomycosis or deep fungal infections in the immunocompromised

## Dose & formulations
- Oral: 200 mg every 12 h (100 mg every 12 h if under 40 kg)
- IV: 6 mg/kg every 12 h × 2 doses (loading), then 4 mg/kg every 12 h
- Adjust by trough level (target about 1–5.5 µg/mL)

## Adverse effects
- Visual disturbance (blurring, colour change, photophobia) in about 30% — transient
- Phototoxicity (skin-related highlight): exaggerated sunburn, cheilitis, pseudoporphyria, lentigines and accelerated photoageing
- Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (and melanoma) with long-term use, especially in transplant recipients
- Periostitis and fluorosis (fluoride content) with long courses — bone pain, raised alkaline phosphatase
- Hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, hallucinations and encephalopathy

## Contraindications
- Concurrent rifampicin, rifabutin, carbamazepine, long-acting barbiturates, efavirenz (standard dose), high-dose ritonavir, sirolimus, ergot alkaloids, pimozide, quinidine
- Pregnancy

## Drug interactions
- Raises tacrolimus, cyclosporine, sirolimus, warfarin, statins, benzodiazepines
- Enzyme inducers drastically lower voriconazole levels

## Monitoring
- Trough levels, LFT, electrolytes, ECG
- Regular full-skin examination and strict sun protection on long courses; eye review if visual symptoms persist
- Fluoride level or bone scan if bone pain

## Pregnancy & lactation
Avoid (old FDA category D — teratogenic in animals). Effective contraception during treatment.

## Viva points
- Drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis; inactive against Mucor
- Phototoxicity and skin cancer (SCC) with long-term use — key dermatology point
- Periostitis due to fluoride
- CYP2C19 polymorphism affects levels

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.10; Khopkar ch.2. Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Zinc acetate (oral zinc)
posts.summary: XI Miscellaneous · Trace element supplement (zinc salt)
posts.body:
_Oral · XI Miscellaneous_

**Class:** Trace element supplement (zinc salt)

## Mechanism of action
- Zinc is a cofactor for over 300 enzymes — needed for epithelial repair, immune function and wound healing
- Anti-inflammatory: inhibits neutrophil chemotaxis and TNF-α; reduces sebum and C. acnes inflammation
- Immunomodulatory — boosts cell-mediated immunity (used in warts and leishmaniasis)

## Pharmacokinetics
- Absorbed in the small intestine; food (phytates), iron and calcium reduce absorption
- Zinc acetate and gluconate are better tolerated than zinc sulfate

## Indications in dermatology & STI
- Acrodermatitis enteropathica (inherited — lifelong) and acquired zinc deficiency
- Acne (modest benefit), hidradenitis suppurativa (adjunct), rosacea
- Viral warts (immunomodulation), alopecia areata (in deficiency), leg ulcers in deficient patients
- Wilson disease (zinc acetate approved — blocks copper absorption)

## Dose & formulations
- Acrodermatitis enteropathica: 1–3 mg/kg/day of elemental zinc
- Adults (acne/warts): about 10 mg/kg/day zinc sulfate (up to 600 mg/day) in divided doses, or 30–90 mg elemental zinc/day
- Wilson disease: zinc acetate 50 mg elemental zinc three times daily
- Check how much elemental zinc a tablet gives: zinc acetate ≈ 30%, zinc sulfate ≈ 23%, zinc gluconate ≈ 14%

## Adverse effects
- Nausea, epigastric pain, metallic taste (take with food if needed)
- Long-term high doses: copper deficiency → anaemia, neutropenia, neuropathy
- Lowers HDL

## Contraindications
- Hypersensitivity; caution in copper deficiency

## Drug interactions
- Reduces absorption of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones and dolutegravir — separate by at least 2 h
- Iron and calcium compete for absorption
- Penicillamine absorption reduced

## Monitoring
- Serum zinc and alkaline phosphatase (zinc-dependent) in deficiency; copper level and CBC on long courses

## Pregnancy & lactation
Safe at recommended doses.

## Viva points
- Acrodermatitis enteropathica — SLC39A4 (ZIP4) mutation; triad of periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia and diarrhoea; responds dramatically to zinc
- Chronic high-dose zinc causes copper deficiency
- Separate zinc from tetracyclines and dolutegravir

_Sources: Wolverton 4e ch.40 (zinc sulfate); Khopkar (Vitamins and trace elements). Facts summarised in our own words; Wolverton followed where books differ._

posts.title: Adson-Brown forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Adson-type forceps whose tips carry two rows of many fine interlocking teeth, for delicate tissue.
posts.body:
![Adson-Brown forceps](instruments/adson-brown-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Brown-Adson forceps_

Adson-type forceps whose tips carry two rows of many fine interlocking teeth, for delicate tissue.

## Parts
- Adson-pattern handle
- Two rows of fine interlocking teeth at the tip

## Uses / indications
- Gentle handling of superficial, delicate tissue and skin edges

## How to hold
Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Many small teeth spread the grip, so less crush than 1x2 teeth

posts.title: Adson forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Small, light thumb forceps with wide ridged handle tapering to a fine tip, used for handling skin.
posts.body:
![Adson forceps](instruments/adson-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Adson tissue forceps_

Small, light thumb forceps with wide ridged handle tapering to a fine tip, used for handling skin.

## Parts
- Broad ridged handle for controlled grip
- Long tapered narrow ends
- Tips plain or with small interlocking teeth

## Types / variants
- Toothed (1x2) and non-toothed
- Adson-Brown variant - see separate entry

## Uses / indications
- Holding skin edges during suturing (relatively atraumatic) - except eyelids
- Suture removal
- Handling punch grafts
- Holding recipient plugs in hair transplant (PPT1)

## How to hold
Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Workhorse forceps of dermatosurgery

posts.title: Allis forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Ring-handled locking forceps with interdigitating teeth for a secure grip on tissue to be removed.
posts.body:
![Allis forceps](instruments/allis-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Allis tissue forceps_

Ring-handled locking forceps with interdigitating teeth for a secure grip on tissue to be removed.

## Parts
- Two straight blades, separated except at the tip
- Interdigitating teeth at the tip
- Ratchet lock near the handle (3 catches)
- Blades riveted together - the joint acts as fulcrum

## Uses / indications
- Corn enucleation
- Cyst excision (holding the cyst/tissue being removed)

## How to hold
Thumb and ring finger in the rings, index finger along the shanks for control; ratchet engaged/released by pressing the rings together and apart.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Traumatic - hold only tissue that will be removed (PPT1)

posts.title: Artery forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Ring-handled locking clamp with blunt serrated tapering jaws used to catch bleeders and grasp tissue.
posts.body:
![Artery forceps](instruments/artery-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Haemostatic forceps, Hemostat, Mosquito forceps, Kelly clamp, Crile / Rochester-Pean forceps_

Ring-handled locking clamp with blunt serrated tapering jaws used to catch bleeders and grasp tissue.

## Parts
- Ring handles
- Ratchet lock
- Box joint
- Blunt tapering jaws with transverse serrations

## Types / variants
- Straight or curved
- Mosquito (Halsted/Hartmann) - smallest, 3-5 inch
- Kelly - 5-7 inch, serrations on distal part of jaw only
- Crile / Rochester-Pean - largest, serrations along entire jaw

## Uses / indications
- Catching bleeding vessels
- Holding the free end of a suture
- Blunt dissection of lipoma and cysts
- Crushing the pedicle of pedunculated lesions (acrochordon, DPN)
- Removing nail plate in partial nail avulsion
- Three-point traction during circumcision
- Plucking hairs for trichogram

## How to hold
Thumb and ring finger in the rings, index finger along the shanks for control; ratchet engaged/released by pressing the rings together and apart.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Size order: Mosquito < Kelly < Crile/Pean
- Medium and small sizes are most used in dermatosurgery (PPT1)

posts.title: Bard-Parker handle
posts.summary: Blades & scalpels · Flat reusable handle onto whose grooved tip a disposable surgical blade is mounted to form a scalpel.
posts.body:
![Bard-Parker handle](instruments/bard-parker-handle.jpg)

_Also called: BP handle, Scalpel handle_

Flat reusable handle onto whose grooved tip a disposable surgical blade is mounted to form a scalpel.

## Parts
- Long flat body (often with metric ruler)
- Grooved, tapered blunt tip that receives the blade

## Types / variants
- No. 3 handle - small blades 10, 11, 12, 15 (Khopkar)
- No. 4 handle - large blades 20-25
- Longer versions marked L (3L, 4L)
- Other handles: No. 7, Siegel (round-bodied, held like a pen), Beaver (PPT1)

## Uses / indications
- Mounting a surgical blade for incision, excision, shave and other procedures

## How to hold
Pencil grip for fine dermatological incisions; table-knife grip for long firm cuts; violin-bow grip for long light strokes.

## Method of use
1. Attach: hold blade with artery forceps/needle holder, slide its slot onto the grooved tip until it clicks
2. Remove: lift the blade heel with the forceps and push it off the tip away from you

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Never load or unload blades with fingers
- Seminar lists blade 9 also fitting No. 3; Khopkar says 10, 11, 12, 15

posts.title: Castroviejo needle holder
posts.summary: Needle holders · Small spring-handled needle holder with a lock, for fine needles in delicate surgery.
posts.body:
![Castroviejo needle holder](instruments/castroviejo-needle-holder.jpg)

_Also called: Castro needle holder, Micro needle holder_

Small spring-handled needle holder with a lock, for fine needles in delicate surgery.

## Parts
- Spring (non-ring) textured handles
- Fine straight or curved tips
- Locking catch (not a ratchet)

## Uses / indications
- Fine suturing with 6-0 and smaller sutures
- Delicate surgery such as mini hair grafts and acne scar revision (Khopkar)

## How to hold
Held like a pencil between thumb and index/middle fingers; spring action opens and closes the jaws.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

posts.title: Castroviejo scissors
posts.summary: Scissors · Delicate spring-handled micro-scissors with small cutting tips.
posts.body:
![Castroviejo scissors](instruments/castroviejo-scissors.jpg)

_Also called: Castroviejo iris scissors, Castroviejo spring scissors_

Delicate spring-handled micro-scissors with small cutting tips.

## Parts
- Spring (non-ring) handles
- Small, fine cutting tips

## Types / variants
- Straight or curved

## Uses / indications
- Surgery on mucosa and thin-skinned areas such as eyelids
- Harvesting suction blister grafts
- Cutting thin split-thickness / blister grafts (PPT1)

## How to hold
Held like a pencil; squeeze the spring handles to cut.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

posts.title: Chalazion clamp
posts.summary: Biopsy & excision · Screw-tightened ring clamp that isolates and compresses tissue to give a bloodless field.
posts.body:
![Chalazion clamp](instruments/chalazion-clamp.jpg)

_Also called: Desmarres chalazion clamp, Lid clamp_

Screw-tightened ring clamp that isolates and compresses tissue to give a bloodless field.

## Parts
- Two arms joined at one end, free at the other
- Screw to approximate the arms and hold them in position
- Free ends expanded: one a flat plate, the other a ring/perforated plate with a large flat thin rim

## Types / variants
- Various sizes (e.g. 16, 20, 24 mm rings)
- Braid, Desmarres and Weis patterns (PPT1)

## Uses / indications
- Mucocele excision / deroofing
- Haemostasis during excision of lip pyogenic granuloma or other neoplasm
- Reducing bleeding during tongue biopsy
- Ear lobe surgery and repair
- Oral mucosal and minor salivary gland biopsy; scrotal surgery; lesions on ala nasi (PPT1)

## How to hold
Place ring over the lesion, plate on the opposite side, tighten screw; the clamp then holds itself.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Originally an eyelid (chalazion) instrument; dermatologists use it on lip, tongue, ear lobe

posts.title: Cheatle forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Long L-shaped forceps without teeth or lock, kept in antiseptic to pick up sterile items.
posts.body:
![Cheatle forceps](instruments/cheatle-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Cheatle's sterilizer forceps, Transfer forceps_

Long L-shaped forceps without teeth or lock, kept in antiseptic to pick up sterile items.

## Parts
- Somewhat L-shaped arms without teeth or lock
- Proximal rings for thumb and ring finger (or one ring and a V-bend)
- Sinuous distal part with curved serrated jaws

## Uses / indications
- Picking up sterile instruments, gauze and dressing material from trays/drums

## How to hold
Thumb and ring finger in rings; keep tips pointing down so fluid does not run back onto the handle.

## Sterilisation & care
Distal part kept immersed in antiseptic (e.g. Savlon) in its jar; autoclave periodically.

## Viva points & tips
- Must be stored in a bottle of Savlon / antiseptic
- Never touch the patient with it

posts.title: Comedone extractor
posts.summary: Curettes & extractors · Double-ended steel instrument with perforated cups used to press out comedone contents.
posts.body:
![Comedone extractor](instruments/comedone-extractor.jpg)

_Also called: Comedone expressor, Comedo extractor, Unna/Schamberg/Saalfield comedone extractor_

Double-ended steel instrument with perforated cups used to press out comedone contents.

## Parts
- Central handle
- Two hemispherical cups, one at each end
- Central perforation in each cup with blunt margins
- Sinuous (S-curved) shape for better handling and localised pressure

## Types / variants
- Saalfield extractor
- Schamberg extractor

## Uses / indications
- Expression of open and closed comedones in acne
- Expression of contents of nevus comedonicus and senile (solar) comedones

## How to hold
Held at the central handle like a pen; cup kept perpendicular to the skin.

## Method of use
1. Place the cup perforation over the plugged follicular opening of an open comedone
2. Apply gentle, firm pressure perpendicularly downward
3. Comedone contents extrude through the hole and collect in the cup
4. For closed comedones first nick the surface with a sterile lancet or needle, then express the same way

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Pressure must be perpendicular, not sliding, to avoid trauma and scarring
- Closed comedones need an artificial opening first

posts.title: Common pin
posts.summary: Office aids · Ordinary pin whose head, tip and shaft each serve as simple bedside diagnostic tools.
posts.body:
Ordinary pin whose head, tip and shaft each serve as simple bedside diagnostic tools.

## Parts
- Head
- Body (shaft)
- Tip

## Uses / indications
- Head: crude touch sensation in leprosy and neurological conditions
- Head: eliciting deep dermal tenderness
- Head: showing the feeding vessel of a spider angioma
- Head: demonstrating scales - scratch sign (pityriasis versicolor), carpet-tack / cat's-tongue sign (DLE, pemphigus foliaceus), Auspitz sign (psoriasis), wafer-like scale (pityriasis lichenoides chronica)
- Head: stroking skin for dermographism and Darier's sign
- Head: chemical cauterisation
- Tip: pain sensation in leprosy, HSAN, congenital insensitivity to pain
- Tip: extracting mites
- Shaft: lifting the buried distal end of an ingrowing hair in pseudofolliculitis

## Viva points & tips
- Use a fresh sterile pin for each patient when breaking skin

posts.title: Cotton swab stick
posts.summary: Office aids · Wooden stick with a cotton tip used to collect specimens, apply agents and perform simple procedures.
posts.body:
_Also called: Cotton-tipped applicator, Ear bud_

Wooden stick with a cotton tip used to collect specimens, apply agents and perform simple procedures.

## Parts
- Cotton tip
- Wooden stick (ear buds or ready-made sterile plastic swabs as alternatives)

## Uses / indications
- Cotton tip: smears and culture swabs of discharges
- Applying peels (glycolic acid, TCA, phenol, salicylic acid)
- Chemical cauterisation (TCA, phenol)
- Cryotherapy by dipstick method
- Applying podophyllin to genital warts; acetowhitening for subclinical warts
- Cervical swabs; specimens for PCR
- Haemostasis in hair transplantation
- Spreading ointment on suture lines; applying topical lotions (e.g. psoralen in vitiligo)
- Nikolsky sign on mucosa
- Stick end: chemical cauterisation of small lesions (DPN, filiform wart, verruca plana, molluscum)
- Stick: extraction of guinea worm

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave; ready-made swabs for specimen collection are gamma-irradiated.

posts.title: Cryotherapy unit
posts.summary: Cryo / electro / light devices · Liquid-nitrogen container with spray tips and probes used to freeze and destroy lesions.
posts.body:
![Cryotherapy unit](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Wart_cryotherapy.jpg/640px-Wart_cryotherapy.jpg)

_Photo: Tonicthebrown, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons_

_Also called: Cryocan, Cryo-spray unit, Cryojet, Cryoprobe, Cryoroller_

Liquid-nitrogen container with spray tips and probes used to freeze and destroy lesions.

## Parts
- Insulated canister for liquid nitrogen with trigger valve
- Spray tips / cones / cylinders (open and closed methods)
- Closed cryoprobes - flat, pointed, rounded
- Accessories: eye protection (Jaeger retractor, goggles), cotton plugs, tongue depressor, thermocouple needles, chamois bag for CO2

## Types / variants
- Dipstick (cotton bud) method
- Cryospray - open (spot, paintbrush, spiral, rotatory) and closed (cones)
- Cryoprobe
- Cryoroller - metal roller dipped in LN2 (acne scars, keloids)
- Forceps technique - for pedunculated lesions
- Intralesional cryo through spinal needle (thick keloids)
- Cryoslush - solid CO2 with acetone (acne, scars)

## Uses / indications
- Benign: warts, molluscum, keloid, hypertrophic scar, pyogenic granuloma, skin tags, SK, mucous/myxoid cyst, angioma
- Premalignant: leukoplakia, Bowen's, actinic keratosis, erythroplasia of Queyrat
- Malignant: BCC (not morphoeic), SCC, LMM, palliation
- Softening keloid before intralesional steroid
- Cooling during laser; frozen section; topical anaesthesia (ethyl chloride); cutaneous myiasis

## Contraindications
- Cold intolerance, Raynaud's, cryoglobulinaemia, cold urticaria
- Undiagnosed lesion
- Multiple myeloma, agammaglobulinaemia, CTD
- Atherosclerosis
- Concurrent immunosuppressives

## Method of use
1. Fill unit with LN2 to 2 inches below brim; wait 3-4 min for pressure
2. Mark lesion margin; spray at centre from about 1 cm
3. Let ice ball thaw completely before 2nd freeze-thaw cycle
4. Probe size about 3/4 of lesion size; remove probe only after thawing

## Sterilisation & care
Accessories: dry heat, autoclave or 2% glutaraldehyde.

## Viva points & tips
- Liquid nitrogen -196 C (spray), about -20 C on swab
- Melanocytes die at -4 to -8 C, so hypopigmentation is common
- Thaw time is about twice freeze time; fast freeze, slow thaw kills best
- James Arnott - father of cryosurgery

posts.title: Curved scissors
posts.summary: Scissors · Sharp scissors with curved blades that give better reach and visibility in deeper dissection.
posts.body:
![Curved scissors](instruments/curved-scissors.jpg)

_Also called: Curved dissecting scissors_

Sharp scissors with curved blades that give better reach and visibility in deeper dissection.

## Parts
- Two blades pivoting on a rivet/screw that acts as fulcrum; ring handles
- Curved sharp blades

## Uses / indications
- Cutting tissue
- Negotiating difficult-to-reach areas during deeper dissection

## How to hold
Tripod grip: thumb and ring finger in the rings (only up to the distal phalanx), index finger resting near the screw joint for stability.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Straight scissors give mechanical advantage for tough tissue; curved give more directional mobility and visibility (seminar)

posts.title: Cusco's self-retaining vaginal speculum
posts.summary: Diagnostic · Bivalve speculum resembling a bird's beak that is locked open by a screw, freeing the examiner's hands.
posts.body:
![Cusco's self-retaining vaginal speculum](instruments/cuscos-speculum.jpg)

_Also called: Cusco's speculum, Bivalve speculum, Duck-bill speculum_

Bivalve speculum resembling a bird's beak that is locked open by a screw, freeing the examiner's hands.

## Parts
- Two blades, concave inside with rounded free margins, riveted together
- Handles at right angles to blades
- Screw lock to hold blades apart

## Types / variants
- Small, intermediate (most used), large
- Small for nulliparous, large for multiparous/prolapse

## Uses / indications
- Visualising cervix
- Pap smear, cervical biopsy, swab collection
- Chemical cauterisation / cryotherapy of cervical warts
- IUCD insertion, colposcopy (seminar)

## Method of use
1. Insert with blades closed (Khopkar: oriented vertically)
2. After full insertion rotate 90 degrees (Khopkar: anticlockwise) so handle points down
3. Press handles to open blades and tighten the screw
4. Before removal loosen the screw, close the blades and withdraw

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Self-retaining: hands free for procedures; patient need not move to table edge
- Disadvantage: anterior and posterior walls are hidden by the blades
- Seminar wording: enter at 9 o'clock then rotate to 6/12 o'clock - follow Khopkar's description
- Seminar/PPT: preferred in cryosurgery as it shields the vaginal walls; not ideal for vaginal surgery

posts.title: DeBakey forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Atraumatic thumb forceps with fine longitudinal serrations on the jaws.
posts.body:
![DeBakey forceps](instruments/debakey-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: DeBakey atraumatic forceps_

Atraumatic thumb forceps with fine longitudinal serrations on the jaws.

## Parts
- Long handle
- One jaw with two parallel rows of serrations, the other with a single central row (longitudinal)

## Uses / indications
- Atraumatic holding of delicate tissue and vessels

## How to hold
Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Originally a vascular forceps; non-toothed

posts.title: Dermatome
posts.summary: Blades & scalpels · Disposable or powered device that harvests split-thickness skin grafts of set thickness.
posts.body:
_Also called: Powered skin graft harvester_

Disposable or powered device that harvests split-thickness skin grafts of set thickness.

## Types / variants
- Simon Davol dermatome - small rechargeable unit for small grafts
- Brown (electric) dermatome - adjustable split-thickness graft depth, about 0.2-0.75 mm (0.008-0.030 inch)

## Uses / indications
- Harvesting split-thickness skin grafts

## Viva points & tips
- Graft thickness corrected from source (Khopkar prints 3-8 mm) to the standard split-thickness range of about 0.2-0.75 mm

posts.title: Dermoscope
posts.summary: Diagnostic · Hand-held illuminated magnifier that shows subsurface skin structures not visible to the naked eye.
posts.body:
![Dermoscope](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Dermatoscope.jpg)

_Photo: Northerncedar, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons_

_Also called: Dermatoscope, Epiluminescence microscope, Skin surface microscope, Episcope_

Hand-held illuminated magnifier that shows subsurface skin structures not visible to the naked eye.

## Parts
- Achromatic lens (variable magnification)
- In-built illumination - halogen or LED
- Power: lithium/AA battery, rechargeable handle
- Optional camera/software for image capture

## Types / variants
- Without image capture (e.g. Delta 10, Mini 2000)
- With image capture (e.g. Dermlite Foto, Delta 20, Video episcope)
- With capture and analysis (e.g. MoleMax, FotoFinder)
- Contact (glass plate + linkage fluid) vs non-contact polarised

## Uses / indications
- Pigmented lesions - naevi, early melanoma
- Psoriasis, lichen planus, dermatofibroma, Darier's disease, cicatricial alopecia, seborrhoeic keratosis, urticarial vasculitis
- Follicular density of donor area before hair transplant
- Nail-fold capillaroscopy (small plates)

## Method of use
1. Contact: apply linkage fluid, place glass plate on lesion
2. Non-contact: cross-polarised lens held just above skin

## Sterilisation & care
Contact plates: 2% glutaraldehyde, methylated spirit, boiling or autoclaving.

## Viva points & tips
- Non-contact avoids cross-infection but gives less illumination and resolution

posts.title: Dissecting forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Non-locking V-shaped spring forceps used to hold tissue during dissection, suturing and dressing.
posts.body:
![Dissecting forceps](instruments/dissecting-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Thumb forceps, Tissue forceps, Pick-ups, Plain / toothed forceps_

Non-locking V-shaped spring forceps used to hold tissue during dissection, suturing and dressing.

## Parts
- Two blades/arms fused at one end and free at the other
- Tips plain (serrated) or toothed
- No ratchet or lock

## Types / variants
- Plain (non-toothed) - transverse serrations, less traumatic; for nerves, biopsy tissue and delicate structures
- Toothed - usually 2 teeth on one jaw interlocking with 1 on the other (1x2); firmer grip, more traumatic; for dermis and cyst walls

## Uses / indications
- Holding tissue during dissection, suturing and dressing
- Plain: delicate structures, biopsy specimens
- Toothed: skin/dermis, cyst wall

## How to hold
Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Do not crush the epidermis - pick up dermis
- Plain = less traumatic; toothed = better grip but more traumatic

posts.title: Dressing forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Long, serrated non-locking forceps used to handle dressings.
posts.body:
![Dressing forceps](instruments/dressing-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Dressing thumb forceps_

Long, serrated non-locking forceps used to handle dressings.

## Parts
- Long thin handles
- Wider, flatter tip than tissue forceps
- Serrated (or smooth) tip, no teeth

## Uses / indications
- Holding medicated dressings and gauze during wound care

## How to hold
Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Khopkar: serrated; seminar: may be smooth or serrated

posts.title: Dressing scissors
posts.summary: Scissors · Straight scissors with one thick blunt blade and one sharp blade, for cutting dressings and sutures.
posts.body:
![Dressing scissors](instruments/dressing-scissors.jpg)

_Also called: Straight scissors, Bandage scissors, Lister bandage scissors_

Straight scissors with one thick blunt blade and one sharp blade, for cutting dressings and sutures.

## Parts
- Two blades pivoting on a rivet/screw that acts as fulcrum; ring handles
- Lower blade thick and blunt (slides under the dressing, protects skin)
- Upper blade sharp - cuts as the scissors close

## Types / variants
- Straight dressing scissors
- Lister bandage scissors (angled)

## Uses / indications
- Cutting dressings and bandages without injuring skin
- Cutting sutures

## How to hold
Tripod grip: thumb and ring finger in the rings (only up to the distal phalanx), index finger resting near the screw joint for stability.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

posts.title: Electrocautery / electrosurgical unit
posts.summary: Cryo / electro / light devices · Device converting mains current into high-frequency oscillating current that destroys, coagulates or cuts tiss
posts.body:
_Also called: Electrocautery, Electrosurgery, Spark-gap cautery_

Device converting mains current into high-frequency oscillating current that destroys, coagulates or cuts tissue.

## Parts
- Power regulator (output 1-10)
- Sockets: monopolar (low/high), bipolar, epilation
- Terminal: monoterminal or biterminal
- Electrode probes - pointed, bent, straight, blade, ball, wire, Teflon-coated, forceps electrode
- Ground/dispersive plate
- Foot pad / switch

## Types / variants
- Spark gap - damped wave: fulguration, desiccation, coagulation (most used in India)
- Vacuum tube - pure wave: electrosection
- Solid state - all/blended waves: coagulation and cutting
- Electrofulguration (no touch, 1-3 mm gap; power 1-2): verruca plana, DPN, milia
- Electrodesiccation (touch; power 5-7): SK, warts, pyogenic granuloma, acrochordon, xanthelasma, superficial BCC
- Electrocoagulation (power 7-10, ground plate): telangiectasia, BCC, nail matrix ablation, bleeders
- Electrosection (cutting, 5-10 mm/s): keloid, acne keloidalis, rhinophyma

## Uses / indications
- Destruction of benign/superficial lesions
- Haemostasis
- Cutting (electrosection)

## Contraindications
- Cardiac pacemaker
- Keloidal tendency
- History of seizures

## Method of use
1. Clean electrode with blade/sand paper or wet gauze
2. Choose mode and power
3. Do not forcibly pull off eschar

## Sterilisation & care
Probes are self-sterilising from heat; disposable electrodes may be preferred.

## Viva points & tips
- Keep alcohol/ether away; let spirit evaporate fully
- Use smoke evacuator within 2 cm or mask (HPV, HBV, HIV in plume)
- Avoid infiltrating anaesthetic over telangiectasia (blanches vessels)
- William Bovie - father of modern electrosurgery

posts.title: Electrolysis (galvanic) epilator
posts.summary: Cryo / electro / light devices · Direct-current device that generates caustic sodium hydroxide in the follicle to destroy the hair bulb.
posts.body:
_Also called: Electrolysis, Chemolysis, Galvanic electroepilation_

Direct-current device that generates caustic sodium hydroxide in the follicle to destroy the hair bulb.

## Parts
- DC (galvanic) source
- Treating needle electrode on cathode (negative)
- Dispersive electrode on anode (positive) held against skin

## Uses / indications
- Permanent hair removal (electroepilation)

## Method of use
1. Insert cathode needle into the hair follicle
2. Patient holds/contacts the anode
3. Current ionises tissue water and salt: NaOH forms at cathode and destroys the bulb

## Viva points & tips
- Products: NaOH (lye) and H2 at cathode; HCl and Cl2 at anode

posts.title: Epilation forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Small forceps with serrated tips used to pluck hairs and remove sutures.
posts.body:
![Epilation forceps](instruments/epilation-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Hair-plucking forceps, Tweezers_

Small forceps with serrated tips used to pluck hairs and remove sutures.

## Parts
- Small spring body
- Serrated tips

## Types / variants
- Barraquer - rounded tip
- Berg - angled tip

## Uses / indications
- Epilation
- Suture removal

## How to hold
Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

posts.title: Filter paper
posts.summary: Office aids · Absorbent paper used for simple bedside tests and for collecting and preserving specimens.
posts.body:
Absorbent paper used for simple bedside tests and for collecting and preserving specimens.

## Uses / indications
- Checking dapsone adherence in leprosy - urine drop on filter paper dipped in Ehrlich's reagent
- Sweat tests: ninhydrin (pink) and bromophenol blue (blue) in leprosy and other neuropathies (diabetes, alcohol, HSAN, porphyria)
- Patch testing liquid allergens (formaldehyde, propylene glycol)
- Documenting Auspitz sign
- Collecting and keeping hair, skin scrapings and nail clippings
- Wrapping tattoo pigments for autoclaving

posts.title: Glass slide
posts.summary: Office aids · Plain microscope slide used for diascopy and for preparing smears and mounts.
posts.body:
_Also called: Microscope slide, Diascope_

Plain microscope slide used for diascopy and for preparing smears and mounts.

## Uses / indications
- Diascopy (vitropression): purpura vs erythema; nevus depigmentosus vs nevus anemicus; apple-jelly nodules in lupus vulgaris, sarcoidosis
- Therapeutic diascopy: blanching the superficial part of a vascular malformation so laser reaches the deeper part
- Testing compressibility of vascular malformations
- Smears: imprint, tissue, crush, slit-skin smear for Gram, AFB, Giemsa/Wright stain; KOH (10-20%) mount
- Tzanck smear in calcinosis cutis (irregular deep blue basophilic granules)
- Elastosis perforans serpiginosa - elastic fibres in keratotic plug (KOH and stain)
- Transferring suction blister grafts from donor to recipient site
- Preparing hair mounts

## Method of use
1. Diascopy: press the slide firmly on the lesion and look for blanching or residual colour

posts.title: Hair transplant forceps
posts.summary: Hair & nail · Fine forceps designed to grasp follicular grafts without crushing them, for extraction and implantation.
posts.body:
![Hair transplant forceps](instruments/hair-transplant-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Graft extraction forceps, Implantation forceps_

Fine forceps designed to grasp follicular grafts without crushing them, for extraction and implantation.

## Types / variants
- Extraction forceps - fine sharp tips to pull follicles from donor area
- Implantation forceps - insert grafts into recipient slits
- Jeweller's, Foerster, Castroviejo and Adson hair-transplant patterns
- Plain, groove, hex tips; straight or curved (seminar figures)

## Uses / indications
- Follicular unit extraction (FUE)
- Follicular unit transplantation (FUT/strip) graft handling and implantation

## How to hold
Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Hold the graft by the perifollicular tissue, never the bulb
- Not a separate Khopkar entry; Khopkar lists ring forceps and jeweller's forceps for hair transplantation (p409)

posts.title: Humby's knife
posts.summary: Blades & scalpels · Hand-held skin-graft knife with an adjustable roller guard for cutting split-thickness grafts.
posts.body:
![Humby's knife](instruments/humbys-knife.jpg)

_Also called: Humby skin graft knife, Skin graft harvester_

Hand-held skin-graft knife with an adjustable roller guard for cutting split-thickness grafts.

## Parts
- Handle at one end
- Long flat metal blade
- Adjustable screws to set graft thickness
- Roller that flattens the skin ahead of the blade

## Types / variants
- Modifications: Braithwaite, Watson, Cobbett (PPT1)

## Uses / indications
- Harvesting split-thickness skin grafts (e.g. for stable vitiligo, ulcers)

## How to hold
Held at the handle with the blade nearly flat to stretched, lubricated donor skin; cut with a to-and-fro sawing movement.

## Method of use
1. Set graft thickness by the screws (check the gap against a blade edge)
2. Lubricate and stretch donor skin with boards
3. Advance with to-and-fro oscillating strokes, roller leading

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde

## Viva points & tips
- Watson modification is the most commonly used (PPT1)

posts.title: Hypodermic needle
posts.summary: Miscellaneous · Disposable hollow needle that doubles in dermatology as an extractor, cutting tool, hook and injection device.
posts.body:
![Hypodermic needle](instruments/hypodermic-needle.jpg)

_Also called: Injection needle_

Disposable hollow needle that doubles in dermatology as an extractor, cutting tool, hook and injection device.

## Parts
- Hub (colour-coded by gauge)
- Shaft / cannula
- Bevel with cutting tip

## Types / variants
- 18G to 30G (higher gauge = finer needle)
- Hub colour indicates gauge

## Uses / indications
- Intramuscular, intravenous, subcutaneous injections
- Intralesional injection: corticosteroid, 5-fluorouracil, bleomycin, interferon, sodium stibogluconate
- Intramatricial steroid injection in nail psoriasis and nail lichen planus
- Infiltration anaesthesia before procedures
- Aspiration/drainage of bullae (e.g. bullous pemphigoid), vesicles, seroma or haematoma under grafts
- Extraction of milia (rice-grain contents also confirm diagnosis), comedones, molluscum
- Puncturing closed comedones before extraction
- Distinguishing a papule from a small vesicle
- Ear and nose piercing
- Chemical cauterisation of sebaceous cyst / steatocystoma (Khopkar) and xanthelasma (seminar)
- Subcision of acne scars
- Intradermal tests: prick, Mantoux, pathergy, Kveim, Frei, Ito-Reenstierna, Montenegro, histamine/pilocarpine, ASST
- Needling in vitiligo and molluscum
- Drainage of paronychial or small abscess, acne pustule
- Slit making in hair transplantation; transferring mini-punch grafts in vitiligo
- Intralesional cryotherapy, FNAC
- As a hook: nerve biopsy, knot opening, suture cutting

## How to hold
Mounted on a syringe for injections; used bare (or bent tip) as a lancet, extractor or hook.

## Sterilisation & care
Commercially pre-packed and sterilised by gamma irradiation; single use.

## Viva points & tips
- Khopkar lists chemical cauterisation of sebaceous cyst/steatocystoma; the seminar lists xanthelasma
- Classify uses as needle as extractor / cutting instrument / hook / injecting device for viva

posts.title: Intense pulsed light (IPL)
posts.summary: Cryo / electro / light devices · Non-laser xenon flash-lamp source emitting broad-spectrum light (500-1200 nm) that is filtered for the target.
posts.body:
_Also called: IPL_

Non-laser xenon flash-lamp source emitting broad-spectrum light (500-1200 nm) that is filtered for the target.

## Parts
- Xenon flash lamp
- Cut-off filters

## Uses / indications
- Hair reduction
- Non-ablative rejuvenation
- Hyperpigmentation (mixed type)

## Viva points & tips
- Not a laser: non-coherent, polychromatic; filters let one machine do many tasks

posts.title: Iontophoresis unit
posts.summary: Cryo / electro / light devices · Galvanic device that drives charged drug ions or tap-water ions into skin with direct current.
posts.body:
_Also called: Iontophoresis_

Galvanic device that drives charged drug ions or tap-water ions into skin with direct current.

## Parts
- DC source with current control (0-3.8 mA)
- Treating and indifferent electrodes
- Trays/pads

## Uses / indications
- Palmoplantar hyperhidrosis
- Drug delivery: tretinoin (scars), glycolic acid, retinoids for melasma, sodium salicylate (warts), zinc oxide (ulcer), iodide (scars), idoxuridine (herpes labialis)
- Patch testing, pilocarpine (sweat) test

## Contraindications
- Anaesthetic skin
- Cuts, wounds, ulcers
- Dermatitis

## Method of use
1. Clean area with spirit
2. Place the drug under the electrode of the same charge: positively charged drug under the anode, negatively charged drug under the cathode; the other electrode is the indifferent one
3. Tap-water iontophoresis for hyperhidrosis: both palms/soles in water trays, one on each electrode, with polarity reversed midway through the session
4. Raise current slowly 0-3.8 mA with continuous circular/stroking movement of the electrode; full face takes about 20-25 min
5. End point mild erythema; reduce to zero and reverse polarity briefly

## Viva points & tips
- Principle: like charges repel - cations are driven into skin from the anode, anions from the cathode (corrected from source: Khopkar's acidic-agent/cathode wording dropped)
- Grease abrasions; stop and reverse current if pain/burning
- Complications: erythema, urticaria, burns, irritant/allergic dermatitis

posts.title: Iris forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Fine, narrow-bladed forceps with gradually tapering tips for delicate grafting work.
posts.body:
![Iris forceps](instruments/iris-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Fine forceps_

Fine, narrow-bladed forceps with gradually tapering tips for delicate grafting work.

## Parts
- Narrow blades tapering gradually (more gradual than Adson)
- Plain or fine-toothed tip
- Spring forceps - no lock or ratchet

## Types / variants
- Straight or curved
- Graefe, Stevens, Bishop-Harmon, Foerster, Gill, Tuebingen patterns (PPT1)
- Bishop-Harmon: fenestrated handle, fine tips (sometimes 1x2 teeth), horizontal or crisscross serrations (seminar)

## Uses / indications
- Miniature punch grafting
- Acne scar surgery
- Split-thickness and blister grafting (PPT1)

## How to hold
Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Corrected from source: Khopkar/PPT2 mention a 'lock'; iris forceps have no lock
- Originally an ophthalmic forceps for handling the iris
- Bishop-Harmon is grouped here (PPT1 lists it as an iris forceps type; seminar gives a separate slide)

posts.title: Iris scissors
posts.summary: Scissors · Small, sharp-pointed scissors with a long rivet-to-tip distance and short shank for fine dissection.
posts.body:
![Iris scissors](instruments/iris-scissors.jpg)

_Also called: Fine dissecting scissors_

Small, sharp-pointed scissors with a long rivet-to-tip distance and short shank for fine dissection.

## Parts
- Two blades pivoting on a rivet/screw that acts as fulcrum; ring handles
- Long rivet-to-tip distance, short shank
- Sharp fine tips
- One blade may be serrated for tissue grip

## Types / variants
- Straight or curved
- Plain or serrated blade
- Usually 3.5-4.5 inch

## Uses / indications
- Fine dissection in dermatosurgery
- Serrated variant for thin skin
- Cutting delicate tissue and mucous membranes, skin biopsy, enucleation of cyst/lipoma (PPT1)

## How to hold
Tripod grip: thumb and ring finger in the rings (only up to the distal phalanx), index finger resting near the screw joint for stability.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Originally ophthalmic; do not use for cutting sutures or dressings - blunts the tips

posts.title: Jeweller's forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Plain-handled forceps that taper rapidly to very fine points, for atraumatic micro-handling.
posts.body:
![Jeweller's forceps](instruments/jewellers-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Watchmaker's forceps, Micro forceps_

Plain-handled forceps that taper rapidly to very fine points, for atraumatic micro-handling.

## Parts
- Elongated plain handles
- Rapid taper to a fine tip

## Types / variants
- Straight, curved or angled

## Uses / indications
- Atraumatic handling of skin grafts
- Hair transplantation (graft implantation)
- Suture removal
- Grasping small bleeders during electrocoagulation

## How to hold
Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

posts.title: Lasers
posts.summary: Cryo / electro / light devices · Devices emitting coherent, collimated, monochromatic light that selectively destroys target chromophores.
posts.body:
_Also called: LASER - Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation_

Devices emitting coherent, collimated, monochromatic light that selectively destroys target chromophores.

## Parts
- Gain (lasing) medium
- Optical resonator - 100% and partially reflecting mirrors
- Power/pumping source (electrical, flash lamp, chemical, diode)
- Cooling system and plume evacuator

## Types / variants
- Solid (ruby, Nd:YAG, Er:YAG, alexandrite, diode)
- Liquid (dye/PDL)
- Gas (argon, krypton, excimer, CO2)
- Vapour (copper, gold)

## Uses / indications
- Hair reduction: long-pulsed Nd:YAG 1064 (dark skin), diode 800, alexandrite 755, IPL
- Pigment and tattoos: Q-switched Nd:YAG 1064/532, ruby 694, alexandrite 755
- Vascular: PDL 585 nm, alexandrite, Nd:YAG, argon-pumped dye, krypton, copper vapour
- Ablative resurfacing: CO2 10,600 nm, Er:YAG 2940 nm
- Psoriasis/vitiligo: excimer 308 nm
- Acne, scars, keloids, warts

## Viva points & tips
- Mechanism: selective photothermolysis; photothermal, photomechanical, photoacoustic effects
- Know terms: fluence (J/cm2), irradiance, pulse duration, thermal relaxation time, spot size
- Precautions: no combustibles, goggles for all, plume evacuator, no reflective instruments

posts.title: Blue and red light devices
posts.summary: Cryo / electro / light devices · LED light sources (blue about 400 nm, red 660 nm) that photoactivate porphyrins in acne and photodynamic thera
posts.body:
_Also called: LED light therapy, Blue light, Red light_

LED light sources (blue about 400 nm, red 660 nm) that photoactivate porphyrins in acne and photodynamic therapy.

## Types / variants
- Blue light - peak about 400 nm (Soret band)
- Red light - 660 nm LED, deeper penetration

## Uses / indications
- Inflammatory and non-inflammatory acne
- Photodynamic therapy (with 5-ALA)

## Viva points & tips
- P. acnes porphyrins are photo-excited and kill the bacteria

posts.title: Liposuction cannula
posts.summary: Miscellaneous · Hollow blunt metal tube with side openings at the tip, attached to syringe or suction to remove fat.
posts.body:
![Liposuction cannula](instruments/liposuction-cannula.jpg)

_Also called: Fat aspiration cannula_

Hollow blunt metal tube with side openings at the tip, attached to syringe or suction to remove fat.

## Parts
- Distal tip with one or more openings where fat enters
- Hollow metal tube (channel)
- Proximal end that attaches to syringe or suction device

## Types / variants
- Different diameters and lengths
- Short cannulas for face; long for back and outer thigh

## Uses / indications
- Liposuction / fat harvesting (e.g. for fat grafting)

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Large cannula: more dead cells, more complications; small cannula: better fat take (seminar figure)

posts.title: Loupes
posts.summary: Diagnostic · Binocular magnifying devices (about 2-4x) worn during examination and surgery.
posts.body:
![Loupes](instruments/loupes.jpg)

_Also called: Surgical loupes, Binocular magnifier, Head loupe_
