Binocular magnifying devices (about 2-4x) worn during examination and surgery.

## Types / variants
- Head-band and spectacle-mounted
- Magnification about 2x to 4x

## Uses / indications
- Better visualisation for suturing and spotting bleeding points
- Biopsy, excision, hair transplant and reconstructive surgery
- Better posture and less eye strain in long procedures

posts.title: Magnifying lens
posts.summary: Office aids · Hand lens (2x-7x), with or without its own light, for studying fine surface details of lesions.
posts.body:
_Also called: Hand lens, Self-illuminating magnifier_

Hand lens (2x-7x), with or without its own light, for studying fine surface details of lesions.

## Types / variants
- Self-illuminating (built-in torch)
- Non-illuminating
- Magnification 2x to 7x

## Uses / indications
- Studying fine morphology of skin lesions
- Nits and lice (pediculosis capitis, pubic lice); lice in clothing seams (pediculosis corporis)
- Scabies burrows and mites
- Auspitz sign, nail pits, Wickham's striae (lichen planus vs lichenoid drug rash)
- Black dots in warts and black-dot tinea capitis
- Umbilication in molluscum, penicilliosis
- Carpet-tack sign in DLE, seborrhoeic keratosis, Darier's disease, pemphigus foliaceus
- Nail-fold telangiectasia in collagen vascular disease
- Furrow in the ridged margin of porokeratosis
- Exclamation-mark hairs in alopecia areata
- Can act as a diascope when no glass slide is available

posts.title: Manual dermabrader
posts.summary: Dermabrasion & resurfacing · Hand-held abrader with a toothed, slightly curved rectangular tip, devised by Dr Rustom Maneksha.
posts.body:
![Manual dermabrader](instruments/manual-dermabrader.jpg)

_Also called: Maneksha's manual dermabrader, Dermabrader_

Hand-held abrader with a toothed, slightly curved rectangular tip, devised by Dr Rustom Maneksha.

## Parts
- Handle with or without thumb rest
- Slightly curved, expanded rectangular tip
- Sharp teeth in regular rows and columns on the convex surface

## Types / variants
- Tip sizes 3-25 mm

## Uses / indications
- Vitiligo: abrading recipient area for suction blister or split-thickness grafts; stimulating melanocyte proliferation and migration
- Lichen amyloidosis, lichen simplex chronicus
- Spot dermabrasion of acne scars
- Full-face dermabrasion for rejuvenation
- Debulking rhinophyma
- Multiple adenoma sebaceum
- Tattoo removal
- Freshening edges in ear lobe repair

## How to hold
Gripped with four fingers around the handle and thumb on the thumb rest; skin stretched with the other hand.

## Method of use
1. Stretch and anaesthetise the area
2. Abrade with firm back-and-forth strokes
3. End point: pin-point bleeding (papillary dermis)

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Indian innovation - Maneksha's dermabrader is a favourite viva spot

posts.title: Mayo scissors
posts.summary: Scissors · Heavy, robust scissors for cutting thick tissue such as fascia and cartilage.
posts.body:
![Mayo scissors](instruments/mayo-scissors.jpg)

Heavy, robust scissors for cutting thick tissue such as fascia and cartilage.

## Parts
- Two blades pivoting on a rivet/screw that acts as fulcrum; ring handles
- Short heavy blades, sturdier than Metzenbaum

## Types / variants
- Straight or curved

## Uses / indications
- Cutting thick tissue (fascia, cartilage)
- Straight Mayo commonly used to cut sutures in general surgery

## How to hold
Tripod grip: thumb and ring finger in the rings (only up to the distal phalanx), index finger resting near the screw joint for stability.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Mayo = short handle, heavy blades; Metzenbaum = long handle, fine blades

posts.title: Measuring tape
posts.summary: Office aids · Flexible tape used to measure lesions and body dimensions for documentation and follow-up.
posts.body:
_Also called: Tape measure_

Flexible tape used to measure lesions and body dimensions for documentation and follow-up.

## Uses / indications
- Size of ulcers, plaques, lymph nodes for description and monitoring
- Limb hypertrophy (Klippel-Trenaunay, lymphoedema), muscle atrophy (leprosy, hereditary motor neuropathy), limb girth in mycetoma
- Induration after Mantoux and other intradermal tests
- Chest expansion in scleroderma
- Hip/waist ratio in lipodystrophy
- Upper:lower segment ratio and arm span in Marfan syndrome

posts.title: Molluscum curette
posts.summary: Curettes & extractors · Double-ended curette with a small round or oval cutting loop, used to scoop out superficial lesions.
posts.body:
![Molluscum curette](instruments/molluscum-curette.jpg)

_Also called: Molluscum extractor, Dermal curette, Fox curette, Piffard curette_

Double-ended curette with a small round or oval cutting loop, used to scoop out superficial lesions.

## Parts
- Central handle
- Round or oval loop with cutting edge at either end

## Types / variants
- Fox curette - round cutting edge
- Piffard curette - oval cutting edge
- Rein round curette (PPT1)
- Loop sizes 1-10 mm; 3-4 mm most commonly used

## Uses / indications
- Extraction of molluscum contagiosum
- Curettage of seborrheic keratosis, stucco keratosis, verruca plana and actinic keratosis

## How to hold
Pencil (fountain-pen) grip between thumb, index and middle finger, or potato-peeler grip with the handle in the distal interdigital fold of the index finger and thumb as a stable base; stretch the skin with the other hand.

## Method of use
1. Stretch the skin around the lesion with the other hand
2. Engage the lesion edge with the loop
3. Scoop out with a single firm stroke, keeping the curette at an angle to the skin

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Two holding techniques asked in viva: pencil/fountain-pen and potato-peeler (seminar p10)
- Curette removes soft lesional tissue preferentially; normal dermis resists

posts.title: Motorised dermabrader
posts.summary: Dermabrasion & resurfacing · Motor-driven handpiece that spins diamond fraises or wire brushes to abrade skin at controlled speed.
posts.body:
![Motorised dermabrader](instruments/motorized-dermabrader.jpg)

_Also called: Micromotor, Hand engine, Dermabrasion machine, Diamond fraise, Wire brush_

Motor-driven handpiece that spins diamond fraises or wire brushes to abrade skin at controlled speed.

## Parts
- Motor / control unit with foot pedal
- Rotating handpiece
- Attachments: diamond fraise or wire brush

## Types / variants
- Diamond fraises - diamond chips bonded to steel wheels; regular, coarse, extra-coarse (coarser = deeper)
- Wire brushes - short steel wires; abrade deeper than fraises
- Burrs of various shapes (ball, pear, cylinder, cone, wheel)
- Bell hand engines, dental burrs

## Uses / indications
- Same indications as manual dermabrasion (vitiligo recipient site, scars, rhinophyma, amyloidosis)
- Driving FUE punches in hair transplant
- Bone/nail burring (osteophyte removal) - seminar

## Method of use
1. Choose fraise/brush by depth needed
2. Set speed; depth depends on burr type, speed, pressure, duration and skin condition

## Sterilisation & care
Fraises/brushes: autoclave; handpiece per manufacturer

## Viva points & tips
- Speed: Khopkar 3000-30,000 rpm (seminar text garbled as '3,000 and 0,000 rpm')
- Wire brush abrades deeper than diamond fraise

posts.title: Nail nipper / nail splitter
posts.summary: Hair & nail · Stout plier-like cutter used to cut the nail plate in nail surgery.
posts.body:
![Nail nipper / nail splitter](instruments/nail-nipper.jpg)

_Also called: Nail nipper, Nail splitter, English anvil nail splitter, Thwaites nail splitter_

Stout plier-like cutter used to cut the nail plate in nail surgery.

## Parts
- Stout handles (often spring-loaded)
- Strong blades with sharp cutting edges
- Splitter: one wedge-shaped blunt (anvil) blade and one sharp cutting blade

## Types / variants
- Nail nipper - both blades cutting
- Nail splitter - anvil + cutting blade

## Uses / indications
- Cutting the nail plate during partial nail avulsion

## How to hold
Held in the palm like pliers; in a splitter the blunt anvil blade goes under the nail plate.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Khopkar distinguishes nipper (both edges sharp) from splitter (anvil + sharp); seminar/PPT treat them as one

posts.title: Nail spatula
posts.summary: Hair & nail · Double-ended instrument with flat curved plates used to separate the nail plate from surrounding tissue.
posts.body:
![Nail spatula](instruments/nail-spatula.jpg)

_Also called: Nail elevator_

Double-ended instrument with flat curved plates used to separate the nail plate from surrounding tissue.

## Parts
- Central handle
- Flat, rectangular, curved plates at either end

## Uses / indications
- Separating nail plate from nail bed
- Separating proximal nail fold from nail plate
- Lifting dressing from skin or punch grafts

## How to hold
Pencil grip; advance the plate under the nail with gentle to-and-fro movements.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

posts.title: Needle holder
posts.summary: Needle holders · Ring-handled locking instrument with short strong jaws that grips the suture needle.
posts.body:
![Needle holder](instruments/needle-holder.jpg)

_Also called: Needle driver, Mayo-Hegar needle holder_

Ring-handled locking instrument with short strong jaws that grips the suture needle.

## Parts
- Short jaws, smooth or serrated, with a central groove
- Ratchet lock (Khopkar: in the proximal part)
- Shanks and ring handles

## Types / variants
- Mayo-Hegar - heavy, for larger needles (2-0, 3-0)
- Crile-Wood - finer, rounded tip for delicate needles
- Gillies - combined design, not ratcheted
- Ryder - small, fine tips for 4-0/5-0 needles (PPT1)
- Castroviejo - see separate entry

## Uses / indications
- Grasping and driving the needle during suturing
- Instrument tying of knots

## How to hold
Finger (ring) grip with thumb and ring finger in rings and index finger on the shank, or palm (thenar) grip with rings in the palm for speed. Grasp the needle at the junction of its middle and posterior thirds (2/3:1/3 rule), near the jaw tip.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Do not grip the swaged end - it bends/breaks
- Khopkar places the lock proximally; the seminar says near the jaws - follow Khopkar

posts.title: Patch test kit
posts.summary: Diagnostic · Allergen series and occlusive chambers used to demonstrate type IV contact allergy.
posts.body:
![Patch test kit](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Skin_patch_allergy_test_02.jpg/640px-Skin_patch_allergy_test_02.jpg)

_Photo: Smirkybec, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons_

_Also called: Finn chambers, TRUE test, Indian standard series_

Allergen series and occlusive chambers used to demonstrate type IV contact allergy.

## Parts
- Allergens in petrolatum or other vehicles
- Chambers: Al-test discs, Finn chambers (8 mm aluminium), plastic chambers
- Micropore/hypoallergenic tape

## Types / variants
- Indian standard series (CODFI) plus cosmetic and footwear series
- TRUE test - ready-to-use 20 allergens
- Chemotechnique series (International, European)

## Uses / indications
- Confirming allergic contact dermatitis
- Photopatch testing for photoallergy

## Method of use
1. Apply to upper back (or outer arm/thigh)
2. Keep dry for 48 h; remove at 48 h
3. First reading about 30 min after removal; late readings 48-72 h later and at day 4-7 (ICDRG grading)

## Viva points & tips
- Stop systemic steroids (>20 mg/day) and immunosuppressants before testing
- Plastic Finn chambers for metals (nickel, cobalt, mercury)
- Jadassohn - father of patch testing (1895)
- False positives: angry back, irritants, excess concentration

posts.title: Power punch
posts.summary: Biopsy & excision · Punch shaft mounted on a motorised handpiece that rotates it at set speed.
posts.body:
![Power punch](instruments/power-punch.jpg)

_Also called: Machine-held punch, Motorised punch_

Punch shaft mounted on a motorised handpiece that rotates it at set speed.

## Parts
- Hand machine / micromotor handpiece
- Punch shaft with circular cutting edge

## Types / variants
- Sizes 1.5-4.5 mm

## Uses / indications
- Same as hand punches
- Follicular unit extraction (FUE) in hair transplantation
- Rapid harvesting of multiple punch grafts

## Method of use
1. Mount punch on handpiece
2. Set rotational speed (2000-10,000 rpm per Khopkar)
3. Apply perpendicular to skin to required depth

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Speed is adjustable, giving faster and more uniform cuts than manual punches

posts.title: Prick test kit
posts.summary: Diagnostic · Kit of allergen solutions, lancets and stencil used to demonstrate type I (immediate) hypersensitivity.
posts.body:
![Prick test kit](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Skin_prick_testing_for_allergies.jpg/640px-Skin_prick_testing_for_allergies.jpg)

_Photo: National Institutes of Health, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons_

_Also called: Skin prick test_

Kit of allergen solutions, lancets and stencil used to demonstrate type I (immediate) hypersensitivity.

## Parts
- Allergen solutions in small dropper bottles
- Positive (histamine) and negative (saline) controls
- Blood lancets
- Stencil for measuring wheal

## Uses / indications
- Diagnosis of respiratory allergy, chronic urticaria and other IgE-mediated allergy

## Method of use
1. Place allergen drops about 1 inch apart on flexor forearm or back (back preferred in children)
2. Prick superficially through each drop without drawing blood; wipe lancet between pricks
3. Read at 20 minutes against controls with the stencil

## Viva points & tips
- Stop antihistamines, steroids, mast-cell stabilisers beforehand
- Emergency kit (hydrocortisone, adrenaline, chlorpheniramine, bronchodilator) must be ready

posts.title: Radiofrequency surgical unit
posts.summary: Cryo / electro / light devices · Electrosurgery at very high frequency (500-4000 kHz) giving precise cutting/coagulation with little lateral he
posts.body:
_Also called: Radiofrequency, RF surgery, Radiosurgery_

Electrosurgery at very high frequency (500-4000 kHz) giving precise cutting/coagulation with little lateral heat damage.

## Types / variants
- Cut mode (pure wave): skin tags, naevi, cysts, shave of xanthelasma, verruca plana
- Cut-and-coagulate (blended): curettage, SK, keloids, warts, BCC, Bowen's, SCC, Paget's, debulking rhinophyma, large pyogenic granuloma
- Coagulation mode: pyogenic granuloma, haemangioma, telangiectasia

## Uses / indications
- Same as electrocautery, with choice of mode

## Viva points & tips
- Advantages: less lateral spread, better scars, less infection, easier bleeding control
- Disadvantages: expensive, fragile costly probes

posts.title: Ring forceps
posts.summary: Hair & nail · Fine forceps like iris forceps but without teeth or serrations, with a curved fine tip.
posts.body:
Fine forceps like iris forceps but without teeth or serrations, with a curved fine tip.

## Parts
- Iris-forceps-like body
- No teeth, no serrations
- Curved fine tip

## Uses / indications
- Hair transplantation

## How to hold
Hold like a pen with the first three fingers (between thumb and middle finger, index finger steadying); grasp dermis rather than epidermis to avoid crushing the wound edge.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

posts.title: Scoop
posts.summary: Curettes & extractors · Double-ended instrument with shallow oval spoons, used to scoop out cavity contents and granulation tissue.
posts.body:
![Scoop](instruments/scoop.jpg)

_Also called: Volkmann double-ended scoop, Volkmann spoon_

Double-ended instrument with shallow oval spoons, used to scoop out cavity contents and granulation tissue.

## Parts
- Central handle
- Oval, spoon-shaped shallow pointed expansion at either end
- Spoon edges sharp (PPT1)

## Types / variants
- Small, medium and large sizes; small to medium most used

## Uses / indications
- Scooping out contents of cysts, abscesses and ulcers
- Removal of hyperplastic granulation tissue around an ingrown toenail
- Ulcer debridement, corn enucleation (seminar)
- Nail surgery; applying cell pellet in cell-based vitiligo surgery (PPT1)

## How to hold
Pencil (fountain-pen) grip between thumb, index and middle finger, or potato-peeler grip with the handle in the distal interdigital fold of the index finger and thumb as a stable base; stretch the skin with the other hand.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Larger and deeper than a molluscum curette
- Considered a modification of the curette (PPT1)

posts.title: Silver's knife
posts.summary: Blades & scalpels · Smaller version of Humby's knife that takes a disposable shaving (razor) blade.
posts.body:
![Silver's knife](instruments/silvers-knife.jpg)

_Also called: Silver skin graft knife, Miniature dermatome_

Smaller version of Humby's knife that takes a disposable shaving (razor) blade.

## Parts
- Handle
- Clamp holding an ordinary disposable shaving blade
- Screws to adjust graft thickness

## Uses / indications
- Harvesting small, thin split-thickness grafts
- Grafts from awkward areas (dorsa of hands, face, scalp) where Humby's knife cannot reach

## How to hold
Like Humby's knife, held flat to the stretched skin with gentle sawing strokes.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde

## Viva points & tips
- Cheap: uses ordinary razor blades

posts.title: Sim's anterior vaginal wall retractor
posts.summary: Diagnostic · Long thin instrument with angled, serrated oval fenestrated ends that lifts the anterior vaginal wall.
posts.body:
![Sim's anterior vaginal wall retractor](instruments/sims-anterior-vaginal-wall-retractor.jpg)

_Also called: Sims vaginal wall retractor_

Long thin instrument with angled, serrated oval fenestrated ends that lifts the anterior vaginal wall.

## Parts
- Central elongated metal shaft
- Expanded oval fenestrated loops at both ends, angled to the shaft (about 15 degrees, facing opposite directions)
- Serrations on the loops for grip

## Uses / indications
- Used with Sim's speculum during gynaecological examination and procedures
- Retracting anterior vaginal wall to see cervix and fornices

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

posts.title: Sim's speculum
posts.summary: Diagnostic · Double-ended curved-plate vaginal speculum that depresses the posterior wall.
posts.body:
![Sim's speculum](instruments/sims-speculum.jpg)

_Also called: Sims double-bladed speculum_

Double-ended curved-plate vaginal speculum that depresses the posterior wall.

## Parts
- Two curved blades (plates) of different sizes
- Vertical handle in between
- Trough / central depression along the length

## Types / variants
- Sizes 26/31, 31/36, 36/42 mm
- Single- or double-ended

## Uses / indications
- Visualising anterior and lateral vaginal walls, fornices, cervix and os
- Differentiating cervical from vaginal discharge
- Seeing strawberry cervix (trichomoniasis)
- Collecting discharge: wet mount (Trichomonas), KOH/Gram (Candida), clue cells (Gardnerella)
- Pap smear
- Treating cervical/vaginal warts (podophyllin, cryotherapy)
- Acetowhitening test with 3-5% acetic acid

## Method of use
1. Warm in water before use
2. Patient in left lateral (Sims) position
3. Insert one blade vertically, then rotate 90 degrees to depress posterior wall
4. Lift anterior wall with Sim's retractor; discharge pools in the central trough

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Disadvantages: patient brought to table edge; clinician's hands are not free (needs assistant/retractor)

posts.title: Skin biopsy punch
posts.summary: Biopsy & excision · Cylindrical circular blade on a handle that cuts a full-thickness core of skin.
posts.body:
![Skin biopsy punch](instruments/skin-biopsy-punch.jpg)

_Also called: Biopsy punch, Hand-held punch, Keyes punch_

Cylindrical circular blade on a handle that cuts a full-thickness core of skin.

## Parts
- Handle (metal or plastic)
- Cylindrical shaft with sharp circular cutting tip
- Stylet with guard in metal punches (gauges graft depth and protects the tip)

## Types / variants
- Metal reusable punches - tapering or cylindrical tips; some with interchangeable tips on one handle
- Disposable plastic-handle punches
- Sizes 1.5-10 mm (Khopkar); 1-8 mm (PPT1)
- Power (machine) punches - see separate entry

## Uses / indications
- Diagnostic, therapeutic and prognostic skin biopsy
- Excisional biopsy of small naevus, solitary molluscum, pyogenic granuloma, digitate wart
- Punch grafting in localised stable vitiligo
- Lipoma excision by narrow-hole extrusion technique
- Hair transplantation
- Acne scar surgery: punch excision, punch elevation, punch grafting
- Punch excision of small tattoos and melanocytic naevi
- Nail matrix/nail bed biopsy (PPT1)

## How to hold
Held vertically between thumb and index finger like a pencil, perpendicular to the skin.

## Method of use
1. Stretch skin perpendicular to the relaxed skin tension lines
2. Press and rotate the punch in one direction until the subcutis is reached
3. Lift the core gently (skin hook/needle), cut the base with scissors
4. Close with suture or let heal by secondary intention

## Sterilisation & care
Metal punches: autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde, boiling. Disposable plastic punches: 2% glutaraldehyde.

## Viva points & tips
- Remove the stylet before biopsy and flush the hollow during cleaning
- Up to 3 mm punches are used on the face for cosmetic reasons
- 3.5 or 4 mm is the usual diagnostic size (PPT1)

posts.title: Skin graft spreader
posts.summary: Miscellaneous · Straight metal rod of uniform diameter with blunt ends used to spread thin grafts.
posts.body:
Straight metal rod of uniform diameter with blunt ends used to spread thin grafts.

## Parts
- Straight metallic rod, uniform diameter
- Blunt ends

## Uses / indications
- Spreading suction blister or split-thickness grafts over the recipient area

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

posts.title: Skin hook
posts.summary: Miscellaneous · Handle ending in one or more fine hooks that lift skin edges with less trauma than forceps.
posts.body:
![Skin hook](instruments/skin-hook.jpg)

_Also called: Frazier hook, Cottle hook, Rake retractor, Guthrie hook, Joseph double hook_

Handle ending in one or more fine hooks that lift skin edges with less trauma than forceps.

## Parts
- Handle
- Hook(s) - one to six prongs

## Types / variants
- Frazier - single hook
- Cottle - double-pronged
- Rakes - multi-pronged
- Guthrie - 2-4 flattened prongs (PPT1)
- Joseph - double U-shaped hook (PPT1)

## Uses / indications
- Holding skin margins during suturing, especially thin skin (eyelids)
- Retracting skin margins during deeper dissection and undermining
- Holding vital structures such as nerves during procedures/biopsy
- Rakes for retracting large wound areas
- Repair of dog-ears; everting wound edges while undermining (seminar)

## How to hold
Held like a pencil; hook inserted into the dermis of the wound edge and lifted gently.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Preferred to forceps because they do not crush tissue
- Sharp hooks can injure the operator - handle carefully

posts.title: Sponge holding forceps
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Long ring-handled locking forceps with fenestrated oval jaws for holding gauze swabs.
posts.body:
![Sponge holding forceps](instruments/sponge-holding-forceps.jpg)

_Also called: Foerster forceps_

Long ring-handled locking forceps with fenestrated oval jaws for holding gauze swabs.

## Parts
- Long shanks with ring handles and ratchet
- Oval fenestrated jaws
- Transverse serrations on inner jaw surface

## Types / variants
- Straight or curved

## Uses / indications
- Holding cotton/gauze swabs to paint the operative site with antiseptic before surgery

## How to hold
Thumb and ring finger in the rings, index finger along the shanks for control; ratchet engaged/released by pressing the rings together and apart.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

posts.title: Suction blister apparatus
posts.summary: Miscellaneous · Suction machine or syringe assembly that raises epidermal blisters for epidermal grafting in vitiligo.
posts.body:
_Also called: Suction blister set-up, Syringe suction technique_

Suction machine or syringe assembly that raises epidermal blisters for epidermal grafting in vitiligo.

## Parts
- Suction machine: suction pump, vacuum gauge, glass cup with non-traumatic rim
- Syringe technique: 20/50/100 ml disposable syringes with pistons removed, three-way cannula (Disofix), 50-100 ml syringe for negative pressure

## Types / variants
- Suction machine (250-500 mmHg)
- Syringe technique

## Uses / indications
- Raising suction blisters for epidermal (blister-roof) grafting in stable vitiligo

## Method of use
1. Clean donor site (anterolateral thigh, flexor forearm, abdomen); shave hair
2. Interconnect syringes via three-way cannulas, open ends on skin
3. Withdraw piston of the end syringe to create negative pressure; close the three-way
4. Blister forms in 1-2 h from dermo-epidermal separation

## Sterilisation & care
Glass cups must be sterilised; syringes are disposable.

## Viva points & tips
- Syringe method: cheap, less painful, no sterilisation, easy
- Blister grafts: good colour match, no pebbling; suitable for eyelids, lips, glans
- Machine: expensive, bulky, needs special cups

posts.title: Surgical blade
posts.summary: Blades & scalpels · Disposable steel blade with a slot that fits a Bard-Parker handle; shape and number decide its use.
posts.body:
![Surgical blade](instruments/surgical-blade.jpg)

_Also called: Scalpel blade, BP blade_

Disposable steel blade with a slot that fits a Bard-Parker handle; shape and number decide its use.

## Parts
- Belly with one sharp cutting edge
- Blunt back (spine)
- Linear slot that fits the handle groove
- Tip

## Types / variants
- No. 11 - triangular, pointed tip
- No. 15 - small, rounded belly (most used in dermatosurgery); 15C/15D finer
- Nos. 20-24 - large, rounded belly
- Nos. 10, 12 also fit No. 3 handle

## Uses / indications
- No. 11: stab incision, drainage of abscess, shave biopsy
- No. 15: slit-skin smear (leprosy, leishmaniasis); incisions on thin skin such as eyelids and face
- Nos. 20-24: incision and excision; Tzanck smear; molluscum smear; paring of warts and corns

## How to hold
As for the scalpel - pencil grip for precision.

## Sterilisation & care
Commercially pre-sterilised by gamma irradiation (cold sterilisation); single use.

## Viva points & tips
- Higher number = larger blade within each handle range
- 15 is the workhorse blade for skin surgery

posts.title: Suture materials
posts.summary: Miscellaneous · Threads used to close wounds, graded from 11-0 (finest) to 3 (thickest).
posts.body:
_Also called: Sutures_

Threads used to close wounds, graded from 11-0 (finest) to 3 (thickest).

## Types / variants
- Absorbable: catgut, polyglycolic acid (Dexon), polyglactin 910 (Vicryl), polydioxanone (PDS), poliglecaprone (Monocryl)
- Non-absorbable: silk, nylon (Ethilon), polyester (Mersilene), polypropylene (Prolene), polybutester
- Monofilament: gut, nylon, polypropylene
- Multifilament: silk, cotton, linen, braided nylon, polyglactin
- Natural vs synthetic

## Uses / indications
- 3-0/4-0: scalp, back, extremities, facial wounds under tension
- 5-0: face, scrotum
- 6-0: eyelids
- Most dermatosurgery uses 3-0 to 6-0

## Sterilisation & care
Gamma irradiation (factory pre-sterilised).

## Viva points & tips
- Sizes thicker than 1-0 carry the '#' prefix
- Other closure aids: cyanoacrylate glue, fibrin glue, closure tapes (Steri-Strip), staples; tincture benzoin as tactifier

posts.title: Suture removal scissors
posts.summary: Scissors · Small scissors with a hooked or notched lower blade that slips under a stitch to cut it.
posts.body:
![Suture removal scissors](instruments/suture-removal-scissors.jpg)

_Also called: Stitch scissors, Spencer stitch scissors, Forgesy scissors_

Small scissors with a hooked or notched lower blade that slips under a stitch to cut it.

## Parts
- Two blades pivoting on a rivet/screw that acts as fulcrum; ring handles
- Small hook / concavity on one blade

## Types / variants
- Spencer
- Forgesy

## Uses / indications
- Safe, quick removal of sutures

## How to hold
Tripod grip: thumb and ring finger in the rings (only up to the distal phalanx), index finger resting near the screw joint for stability.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde or boiling

## Viva points & tips
- Specialised (fine) scissors should not be used for cutting sutures - use these instead

posts.title: Suturing needle
posts.summary: Miscellaneous · Curved or straight needle that carries suture through tissue; classified by curvature and cross-section.
posts.body:
_Also called: Surgical needle_

Curved or straight needle that carries suture through tissue; classified by curvature and cross-section.

## Parts
- Needle point
- Body
- Shank (eyed or swaged)

## Types / variants
- Shank: closed eye (suture threaded) or swaged (suture attached)
- Curvature: 1/4, 3/8, 1/2, 5/8 circle
- Conventional cutting - third edge on inner curve
- Reverse cutting - third edge on outer curve; preferred for skin under tension
- Round-bodied - no cutting edge; mucosa, subcutaneous sutures
- Straight needles - round or cutting

## Uses / indications
- Suturing skin, mucosa and subcutaneous tissue

## How to hold
Held in a needle holder at the junction of middle and posterior thirds.

## Sterilisation & care
Autoclave, hot air oven, 2% glutaraldehyde, boiling (swaged suture-needles come gamma-sterilised).

## Viva points & tips
- Conventional cutting needles tend to cut through the wound margin; reverse cutting avoids this

posts.title: Semmes-Weinstein monofilament
posts.summary: Diagnostic · Colour-coded nylon filaments that bend at a fixed force, used to test protective touch sensation.
posts.body:
_Also called: SW monofilament, Graded nylon monofilaments_

Colour-coded nylon filaments that bend at a fixed force, used to test protective touch sensation.

## Parts
- Nylon 612 filament of set diameter
- Holder; colour code for force

## Types / variants
- Green 0.05 g - normal
- Blue 0.2 g - diminished light touch
- Purple 2 g - diminished protective sensation
- Red 4 g - loss of protective sensation
- Orange 7.5 g - only deep pressure
- About 20 grades exist

## Uses / indications
- Screening for sensory neuropathy
- Measuring sensory loss in leprosy, diabetes and other neuropathies
- Detecting silent neuritis in leprosy (test every 2 weeks for 4 months, then monthly)

## How to hold
Hold perpendicular to the skin and press until the filament bends into a 'C'.

## Method of use
1. Test hands at 7 sites (3 ulnar, 3 median, 1 radial)
2. Test feet at the standard 10 sites: plantar 1st, 3rd and 5th metatarsal heads; plantar distal hallux, 3rd and 5th toes; medial and lateral midfoot; heel; dorsum between 1st and 2nd toes
3. Ask the patient (eyes closed) if felt
4. Failure at any tested point = positive

## Viva points & tips
- Designed by Josephine Semmes and Sidney Weinstein
- Inability to feel the purple filament = loss of protective sensation
- Foot test sites corrected from source to the standard 10-site examination

posts.title: Towel clip
posts.summary: Forceps & clamps · Small ring-handled locking clip with curved pointed tips that fixes drapes in place.
posts.body:
![Towel clip](instruments/towel-clip.jpg)

posts.title: Undermining scissors

## Types / variants

posts.title: Wood's lamp
posts.summary: Diagnostic · Hand-held long-wave UVA source whose induced fluorescence helps diagnose skin, hair and systemic conditions.
posts.body:
![Wood's lamp](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Wood%27s_UV_lamp.JPG/640px-Wood%27s_UV_lamp.JPG)

_Photo: Seawind60, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons_

_Also called: Wood's light, UVA (black light) lamp_

Hand-held long-wave UVA source whose induced fluorescence helps diagnose skin, hair and systemic conditions.

## Parts
- High-pressure mercury arc lamp
- Wood's filter (barium silicate with 9% nickel oxide)
- Many models: white light and magnifying lens
- AC power supply; output <1 mW/cm2; peak 365 nm (320-400 nm)

## Uses / indications
- Pityriasis versicolor - golden yellow
- Tinea capitis: M. canis, M. audouinii, M. distortum, M. ferrugineum - blue-green; M. gypseum - dull yellow; T. schoenleinii - dull blue
- Pseudomonas - greenish (pyoverdin); erythrasma - coral red (coproporphyrin III)
- Vitiligo - chalky/bright blue-white; nevus depigmentosus vs nevus anemicus
- Typing melasma (epidermal accentuates)
- Porphyrias - pink fluorescence of urine, teeth, tears etc.; acne - orange-red (P. acnes porphyrins)
- Scabies burrows (tetracycline/fluorescein)
- Checking even application of peel or barrier cream
- Therapeutic: vitiligo when UV source unavailable (long exposures)
- Non-dermatological: forged currency/signatures, semen detection, cracks in metal

## How to hold
Held 4-5 inches (10-13 cm) from the skin in a dark room.

## Method of use
1. Darken the room (or use a hood)
2. Pre-warm the lamp for about 1 minute
3. Hold 4-5 inches from the lesion
4. Examine before the patient washes the area

## Viva points & tips
- Invented by physicist Robert W. Wood (1903)
- False negative: washing removes water-soluble coproporphyrin in erythrasma
- False positive: white coat (light blue), scales, salicylic ointment (green), petrolatum (bluish-purple)

posts.title: Comedone extraction
posts.summary: Manual removal of open and closed comedones, often before peels
posts.body:
Comedone extraction removes keratin plugs from blackheads and whiteheads. It gives quick cosmetic improvement and helps topical therapy work, but it does not prevent new comedones. It is often done before or along with a salicylic or glycolic peel.

## Indications
- Open comedones (blackheads) and closed comedones (whiteheads)
- Macrocomedones that do not respond to retinoids
- Before chemical peels in comedonal acne
- Favre–Racouchot (solar comedones)

## Contraindications
- Inflamed papules, pustules or nodules (do not squeeze)
- Active infection, herpes or dermatitis on the face
- Keloid tendency (relative)
- Bleeding disorder (relative)

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: discomfort, redness, PIH, and small chance of scarring
- Counsel that topical retinoids must continue; extraction alone does not cure acne
- Start a topical retinoid 2–4 weeks before to loosen comedones
- Clean the face and, if possible, soften with warm compresses for 5 minutes

## Equipment
- Comedone extractors (Unna, Schamberg, or Saalfeld)
- 26G needle or No. 11 blade for closed comedones
- Spirit swabs, gauze, gloves
- Magnifying lamp

## Procedure step by step
1. Clean the face with spirit and let it dry.
2. **Open comedones**: place the extractor loop centred over the plug and press down and slightly sideways with gentle, even pressure.
3. **Closed comedones**: make a tiny nick or opening over the top with the needle bevel, then press with the extractor.
4. **Endpoint**: the whole plug is out and the follicular opening is empty.
5. If the plug does not come out with gentle pressure, leave it. Repeated forceful pressing leads to inflammation and PIH.
6. Wipe each site with spirit.
7. Move from one area to the next systematically (forehead, nose, cheeks, chin).

## Post-procedure care
- Calming moisturiser; sunscreen during the day
- Avoid makeup for 12–24 hours
- Restart topical retinoid after 24–48 hours
- Do not pick or self-squeeze at home

## Complications & management
- Erythema: settles within hours
- Inflamed papules: topical antibiotic (clindamycin) or benzoyl peroxide
- PIH: sunscreen, azelaic acid
- Scarring: with excess force; avoid
- Bleeding: pressure

## Sessions & follow-up
- Repeat every 3–4 weeks as needed, often with peels
- Continue retinoid maintenance for prevention

_Draft — awaiting review by Dr. Nisha_

posts.title: Dermatosis papulosa nigra removal (RF / electrocautery)
posts.summary: Light-touch radiofrequency or cautery removal of DPN in brown skin
posts.body:
Dermatosis papulosa nigra (DPN) is a variant of seborrhoeic keratosis common in skin types IV–VI. It presents as small, dark papules on the face and neck. Removal is purely cosmetic, so the goal is to remove the lesion with minimal heat to the surrounding skin and avoid PIH or hypopigmentation.

## Indications
- Cosmetic removal of DPN on the face, neck and upper trunk
- Pedunculated lesions catching on clothing or jewellery

## Contraindications
- Uncertain diagnosis (melanocytic naevus, BCC, melanoma) — biopsy first
- Pacemaker or ICD: avoid RF; use electrocautery (heated tip) instead
- Active infection or herpes at site
- Keloid tendency (relative)
- Pregnancy (relative, defer cosmetic procedures)
- Unrealistic expectations; patients who cannot avoid the sun

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: temporary darkening or lightening, small scab, recurrence of new lesions, rare scarring
- **Test spot**: treat 2–3 lesions first and review at 4 weeks in patients prone to PIH
- Topical anaesthetic (EMLA) for 45–60 minutes under occlusion; local infiltration rarely needed
- Remove makeup; wipe with alcohol and **let it dry fully** (flammable)
- Photograph

## Equipment
- RF unit with fine needle electrode, or electrocautery unit with a fine wire tip
- Fine iris scissors for pedunculated lesions
- Smoke evacuator and surgical mask
- Saline gauze, antibiotic ointment, sunscreen

## Procedure step by step
1. Ensure the skin is dry and that no oxygen is near.
2. Start at the lowest power and increase gradually until the lesion responds.
3. **RF**: use a fine needle electrode in fulguration or coagulation mode; touch lightly to the surface of the papule.
4. **Electrocautery**: touch the heated tip lightly onto the surface.
5. **Endpoint**: the lesion turns light grey or white and slightly shrinks. Do not go down to the surrounding skin.
6. Wipe the treated lesion with saline gauze; the coagulated lesion often comes off.
7. For pedunculated lesions: snip at the base with scissors and touch the base lightly with the electrode.
8. Use the smoke evacuator throughout.

## Post-procedure care
- Antibiotic ointment twice a day until scabs fall (5–7 days)
- Do not pick the scabs
- Strict sunscreen for 4–6 weeks
- Avoid scrubs and retinoids for 1 week

## Complications & management
- PIH: common; azelaic acid or hydroquinone, sunscreen; fades in weeks to months
- Hypopigmentation: from excess heat; lower power next time
- Scar: from deep treatment; avoid
- Infection: topical antibiotic
- Recurrence: new lesions appear with age

## Sessions & follow-up
- Usually one session, with touch-up at 4–6 weeks
- Treat in batches if there are many lesions

_Draft — awaiting review by Dr. Nisha_

posts.title: Excimer 308 nm
posts.summary: Targeted 308 nm excimer light/laser for localised vitiligo, psoriasis and AA
posts.body:
The excimer (XeCl) device delivers 308 nm monochromatic UVB to small areas. Because only lesional skin is treated, higher doses can be given with less erythema to normal skin and lower cumulative exposure. Response is usually faster than with whole-body NB-UVB.

## Indications
- Vitiligo: face and neck respond best; trunk and limbs moderately; acral sites (fingers, wrists, feet) respond poorly
- Localised plaque, scalp and palmoplantar psoriasis
- Patchy alopecia areata
- Localised atopic dermatitis, prurigo nodularis

## Contraindications
- Photosensitivity disorders (lupus, porphyria, xeroderma pigmentosum, PLE that is not controlled)
- Photosensitising drugs
- Melanoma or non-melanoma skin cancer at the treatment site
- Relative: history of skin cancer, actinic damage at site, pregnancy (consult), unable to attend twice weekly

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: twice-weekly visits for several months; erythema, blistering, perilesional tanning; uncertain response at acral sites
- Mark and photograph target lesions with a scale
- Review drug history for photosensitisers
- Psoriasis: determine MED on uninvolved skin or use the manufacturer's skin-type chart
- Explain that combined therapy (tacrolimus or topical steroid) improves results

## Equipment
- Excimer device with calibrated hand-piece; spot size per manufacturer
- UV-protective goggles for patient and operator
- Dose log sheet per lesion site

## Procedure step by step
1. Clean the area; remove thick scale or ointment.
2. Patient and operator put on goggles.
3. **Starting doses (vitiligo)**: about 100 mJ/cm² face and neck; 150–200 mJ/cm² trunk and limbs; 250–300 mJ/cm² hands and feet.
4. **Psoriasis**: start from MED-based dosing (multiples of the MED according to plaque thickness).
5. Place the hand-piece flat on the skin and deliver the pulses in a grid, without overlapping or leaving gaps; keep a small margin onto normal skin.
6. Treat twice a week, on non-consecutive days.
7. Increase by 10–20% per session until there is a **faint erythema at 24–48 h** (the endpoint); then hold that dose.
8. Record dose per site every session.

## Post-procedure care
- Apply tacrolimus 0.1% or a mid-potency topical steroid as prescribed
- Sunscreen on uninvolved surrounding skin; avoid extra sun on treatment days
- Report blistering, painful redness or itching

## Complications & management
- Marked erythema: hold the dose at the next session
- **Blister**: skip the session; when healed, restart 20–25% lower than the blistering dose
- **Missed sessions**: reduce the dose by 10–25% depending on the gap
- Perilesional hyperpigmentation: reassure; fades
- Koebnerisation from blisters in vitiligo: avoid overdosing

## Sessions & follow-up
- First response is expected at 8–12 sessions
- Formal assessment at 24 sessions; continue up to about 6 months if repigmentation is progressing
- Stop if there is no response at 24 sessions
- Photographs every 8 sessions

_Draft — awaiting review by Dr. Nisha_

posts.title: Glycolic acid peel
posts.summary: Time-dependent AHA peel for melasma, photoageing and acne; needs neutralisation
posts.body:
Glycolic acid (GA) is the smallest alpha-hydroxy acid. It penetrates quickly and loosens corneocyte cohesion. How deeply it acts depends on concentration, pH, free-acid content and **contact time**, so it must be timed and neutralised. Clinic peels range from 20% to 70%.

## Indications
- Melasma and facial melanoses (with topical depigmenting agents)
- PIH, superficial acne scars, comedonal acne
- Photoageing: fine lines, dullness, rough texture
- Pre-treatment before medium-depth or combination peels

## Contraindications
- Active infection, dermatitis, open wounds or recent sunburn at the site
- Oral isotretinoin in the past 6 months (relative; individualise)
- Recent waxing, laser or dermabrasion (within 1–2 weeks)
- Pregnancy (relative; most clinicians defer)
- Keloidal tendency, poor sun-protection compliance, unrealistic expectations

## Pre-procedure
- Written consent covering erythema, stinging, flaking, PIH and the rare risk of epidermolysis
- **Priming 2–4 weeks**: sunscreen + hydroquinone 2–4% or a modified Kligman's regimen; tretinoin improves uniform penetration
- Stop retinoids 3–5 days before the peel
- Antiviral prophylaxis if there is a history of facial herpes
- Test patch in the preauricular area at the starting concentration
- Baseline photographs

## Equipment
- GA 20%, 35%, 50%, 70% (note the pH and buffering on the label)
- Neutraliser: 8–15% sodium bicarbonate solution, or plenty of cold water
- Fan brush or gauze, timer, petrolatum, fan, eye pads, gloves

## Procedure step by step
1. Cleanse, degrease and dry the skin. Protect the eyes and apply petrolatum to the alae, commissures and canthi.
2. Start the timer and apply GA quickly with a fan brush, from the forehead to the cheeks, nose, chin and perioral area.
3. First session: 20–35% for 2–3 minutes. Later sessions increase time (by 1 minute) or concentration, one variable at a time.
4. Watch continuously. **Endpoint**: uniform pink erythema, or the planned time, whichever comes first.
5. If grey-white **frosting** appears in any area, neutralise that area immediately. Frost means epidermolysis, which raises the PIH risk in brown skin.
6. Neutralise all over with bicarbonate solution until fizzing stops, then rinse with cool water.
7. Apply moisturiser and sunscreen.

## Post-procedure care
- Mild erythema for a few hours; fine flaking for 2–5 days
- Gentle cleanser, moisturiser, strict SPF 30+; avoid heat, steam and the gym for 24 h
- Restart depigmenting agents after 3–5 days

## Complications & management
- Persistent erythema or crusting: topical steroid for a short course, emollients
- Focal frosting or epidermolysis: neutralise, cool, apply antibiotic ointment, follow up in 48 h
- PIH: depigmenting agents, photoprotection; delay the next peel
- Herpes: treatment-dose antiviral
- Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis: stop, topical steroid

## Sessions & follow-up
- Every 2–3 weeks for 4–6 sessions, then maintenance every 1–2 months as needed
- Keep a log of concentration, time, endpoint and reaction for each session

posts.title: Intralesional steroid injection
posts.summary: Triamcinolone injection for keloids, alopecia areata, cysts and plaques
posts.body:
Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide (TA) puts a high concentration of steroid into the lesion with little systemic effect. Correct concentration, depth and spacing determine success and limit atrophy and hypopigmentation — both very visible in brown skin.

## Indications
- Keloids and hypertrophic scars
- Alopecia areata (patchy, beard, eyebrows)
- Inflamed acne cysts and nodules
- Lichen simplex chronicus, prurigo nodularis, hypertrophic lichen planus
- Discoid lupus, localised psoriasis or nail psoriasis, granuloma annulare, sarcoid, necrobiosis lipoidica

## Contraindications
- Local infection at site (infected cyst — drain first)
- Allergy to triamcinolone or excipients
- Relative: uncontrolled diabetes, bleeding disorder, very large total dose needed
- Avoid repeated injection into atrophic or depigmented areas

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: pain, atrophy (dent), hypopigmentation, telangiectasia, rarely infection; repeated sessions needed
- Explain that a dent is often temporary but can last months
- Photograph and measure lesions
- Topical anaesthetic for children and painful sites
- Check total dose per session

## Equipment
- TA 40 mg/mL (or 10 mg/mL vial)
- Diluent: normal saline or 1–2% lignocaine
- 1 mL insulin or Luer-lock syringe; 27–30G needle (26G for firm keloids)
- Spirit swabs, gauze, gloves

## Procedure step by step
1. Prepare the concentration:
- Face, eyebrows, alopecia areata: 2.5–5 mg/mL
- Acne cysts: 2.5 mg/mL (low to avoid atrophy)
- Body plaques, LSC, hypertrophic LP: 5–10 mg/mL
- Keloids: 10–40 mg/mL depending on thickness
2. Clean the site with spirit.
3. Keep the needle bevel up and inject into the **dermis** (into the keloid substance; mid-dermis for alopecia areata), not into the fat.
4. **Alopecia areata**: about 0.1 mL per site, spaced 1 cm apart.
5. **Keloid**: inject until the lesion blanches; firm keloids need high pressure (use Luer-lock).
6. **Endpoint**: slight blanching of the treated tissue; stop if any site becomes very white with pain or refluxes.
7. Keep total dose under about 20–40 mg per session in adults (lower in children); record the total.
8. Pressure for haemostasis.

## Post-procedure care
- Plaster for a few hours
- Silicone gel or sheeting for keloids after the injection site settles
- Report signs of infection

## Complications & management
- Atrophy: stop at that site; usually recovers over 3–6 months
- Hypopigmentation or depigmentation (along lymphatics): stop at that site; recovers slowly
- Telangiectasia: pulsed dye laser if persistent
- Infection: antibiotics
- Systemic effects (rare): menstrual irregularities, hyperglycaemia; keep doses low

## Sessions & follow-up
- Alopecia areata, plaques: every 4–6 weeks
- Keloids: every 3–4 weeks until flat
- Stop if no response after 3–4 sessions; reassess

posts.title: Milia extraction
posts.summary: Nick-and-express removal of primary and secondary milia
posts.body:
Milia are small keratin cysts in the upper dermis. They do not resolve with topical therapy alone in most cases, and simple extraction is quick and well tolerated. Secondary milia follow blistering diseases, burns, dermabrasion, chronic steroid use or radiation.

## Indications
- Primary milia of the face and eyelids
- Secondary milia after blistering (epidermolysis bullosa, porphyria cutanea tarda, bullous pemphigoid), resurfacing or trauma
- Milia en plaque (extraction plus topical retinoid)
- Cosmetic concern

## Contraindications
- Active infection or dermatitis at site
- Neonatal milia (resolve spontaneously)
- Lesions on the eyelid margin very close to the lashes (refer or take extra care)
- Bleeding disorder (relative)
- Uncertain diagnosis: syringoma, xanthoma, sebaceous hyperplasia, molluscum, colloid milium

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: brief discomfort, pinpoint bleeding, rare scarring, PIH, recurrence
- Explain that new milia may develop
- Topical anaesthetic (EMLA/lidocaine–prilocaine) under occlusion for 30–45 minutes if needed
- Eye shield or careful positioning for periocular lesions

## Equipment
- Sterile 26G hypodermic needle or No. 11 blade
- Comedone extractor (Unna or Schamberg) or two cotton buds
- Spirit swabs, sterile gauze, gloves
- Good light and magnification loupe

## Procedure step by step
1. Clean the area with spirit; let it dry.
2. Stretch the skin with the non-dominant hand.
3. Hold the needle bevel up, nearly parallel to the skin, and make a tiny nick over the dome of the milium.
4. Apply gentle pressure with the comedone extractor loop or two cotton buds at the sides.
5. **Endpoint**: the whole white keratin pearl comes out, leaving an empty pit.
6. If the cyst does not come out, slightly enlarge the nick; do not squeeze hard.
7. Apply pressure with gauze for pinpoint bleeding.
8. Apply antibiotic ointment if many lesions were treated.

## Post-procedure care
- Keep clean; avoid makeup for 24 hours
- Sunscreen on the face to reduce PIH
- Topical retinoid at night (adapalene or tretinoin) for prevention once the skin heals
- Avoid heavy occlusive creams on milia-prone areas

## Complications & management
- Pinpoint bleeding: pressure
- Infection: topical antibiotic
- PIH: sunscreen, azelaic acid
- Small scar from deep or wide nicks: use the smallest nick possible
- Incomplete extraction: repeat at next visit

## Sessions & follow-up
- Usually a single session; review in 4–6 weeks
- Recurrence is common; preventive retinoid helps
- For secondary milia, manage the underlying condition

posts.title: Molluscum contagiosum extraction
posts.summary: Physical removal of molluscum bodies by expression or curettage
posts.body:
Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection that usually resolves on its own over months to a couple of years. Treatment shortens the course, reduces spread and autoinoculation, and helps with itching or cosmetic concern. Physical extraction is quick, cheap and effective in a cooperative patient.

## Indications
- Few to moderate lesions in children or adults
- Genital molluscum in adults (sexually transmitted; screen partner)
- Lesions spreading by scratching, or with molluscum dermatitis
- Patient or parent preference for active treatment

## Contraindications
- Very young or uncooperative child with many lesions (consider topical KOH or cantharidin, or watchful waiting)
- Inflamed lesions (BOTE sign) — these are resolving; leave them
- Lesions on the eyelid margin (refer to ophthalmology)
- Bleeding disorder (relative)

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: brief pain, pinpoint bleeding, small pitted scars, new lesions may still appear
- **Adults with many, large or facial lesions: test for HIV** and consider other immunosuppression
- Topical anaesthetic (lidocaine–prilocaine) under occlusion for 45–60 minutes in children; respect the maximum area for age
- Count and map the lesions

## Equipment
- Comedone extractor, fine curette, or 26G needle
- Fine forceps
- Povidone-iodine or spirit, gauze, gloves
- Antibiotic ointment, small dressings

## Procedure step by step
1. Clean with antiseptic.
2. **Expression**: make a tiny nick in the umbilicated centre with the needle; press the extractor loop around the papule until the white, cheesy molluscum body comes out.
3. **Curettage**: stabilise the skin and remove the papule with one quick scoop of a small curette.
4. **Endpoint**: the whole core is out and only a small, clean, bleeding crater remains.
5. Dab the base with povidone-iodine (some apply 10% KOH or phenol to the base; do so carefully).
6. Press for haemostasis.
7. Treat all visible lesions in one session if tolerated; small ones may be missed, so re-examine carefully.

## Post-procedure care
- Keep clean; apply antibiotic ointment for 2–3 days
- Avoid scratching, shaving or waxing over affected areas
- Do not share towels; avoid shared baths and pools until clear
- Treat molluscum dermatitis with emollients and mild topical steroid

## Complications & management
- Bleeding: pressure
- Secondary infection: topical antibiotic
- Pitted scar or PIH: sunscreen; usually fades
- New lesions: from incubation (up to 6 weeks); treat at review
- Anxiety in children: use distraction; stop if not tolerated

## Sessions & follow-up
- Review every 3–4 weeks and treat new lesions
- Usually 2–3 sessions
- Genital cases: screen for other STIs

posts.title: NB-UVB phototherapy — basics & targeted hand/foot units
posts.summary: 311 nm UVB: indications, dosing logic and palmoplantar targeted units
posts.body:
Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB) emits a peak at 311–313 nm. It is the first-line phototherapy for psoriasis and vitiligo. It is immunomodulatory and, in vitiligo, stimulates melanocytes. This SOP covers the principles and **targeted hand/foot units**; for cabin dosing see the Whole-body phototherapy SOP.

## Indications
- Psoriasis (plaque, guttate; palmoplantar with hand/foot units)
- Vitiligo (non-segmental, generalised or acrofacial)
- Atopic dermatitis, chronic hand eczema, prurigo
- Pruritus (uraemic, cholestatic), lichen planus, pityriasis rosea, PLEVA
- Early mycosis fungoides (patch stage)
- Polymorphic light eruption (prophylactic hardening)

## Contraindications
- Absolute: xeroderma pigmentosum, lupus erythematosus with photosensitivity, photosensitive genodermatoses
- Relative: history of melanoma or multiple NMSC, photosensitising drugs, prior arsenic or ionising radiation, immunosuppression (e.g. ciclosporin), cataract or aphakia, inability to stand or attend regularly, claustrophobia (cabin)
- Pregnancy: NB-UVB is acceptable; check folate status

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: needs 2–3 visits a week for months; erythema, tanning, itching; small long-term skin-cancer concern
- History of photosensitivity, drugs (doxycycline, NSAIDs, hydrochlorothiazide, fluoroquinolones, amiodarone), skin cancer
- Baseline: photographs, BSA/PASI or VASI; ANA if lupus is suspected
- Stop tar and avoid perfumes on treatment days; apply a thin layer of mineral oil on scaly psoriasis to improve penetration

## Equipment
- Calibrated NB-UVB unit with a UV meter; dose log book
- **Hand/foot unit**: a box with TL-01 tubes for palms and soles (and dorsa when the hands are turned)
- UV-protective goggles; cloth covers for uninvolved skin
- MED test template if MED-based dosing is used

## Procedure step by step (hand/foot unit)
1. Confirm the identity, the last dose and any erythema since the last session.
2. Remove rings and watches; cover the forearms and ankles with cloth.
3. Starting dose depends on the machine and the disease. Palms and soles tolerate higher doses because of their thick stratum corneum; start at the unit protocol dose (often about 0.3–0.5 J/cm²).
4. Treat palms, then dorsa (flip the hands); soles can be treated in the same or a separate unit.
5. Increase by 10–20% per session if there is no erythema or pain.
6. **Endpoint**: faint, painless erythema the next day; hold the dose if erythema is visible.
7. Record the dose, cumulative dose and any reaction in the log.

## Post-procedure care
- Emollients after each session; sunscreen on treated areas if going outdoors
- Avoid extra sun exposure on treatment days
- Continue topical steroid or calcipotriol in psoriasis, and topical calcineurin inhibitor in vitiligo, applied after the session

## Complications & management
- Erythema or burning: skip a session and restart at a lower dose
- Blisters: stop until healed, then restart at about 50% of the last dose
- Pruritus and xerosis: emollients
- Perilesional hyperpigmentation in vitiligo: reassure
- Flare of HSV or PLE: treat and adjust

## Sessions & follow-up
- 2–3 times a week on non-consecutive days
- Psoriasis: clearance usually in 20–30 sessions; vitiligo: first repigmentation at 2–3 months and assess at 6 months
- Stop if there is no response at 6 months (vitiligo) or ~30 sessions (psoriasis)
- Annual skin check with long courses

posts.title: Paring of warts and corns
posts.summary: Debulking plantar warts, corns and calluses with a blade before topical therapy
posts.body:
Paring removes hyperkeratosis so that topical agents or cryotherapy work better, and it relieves pain. It is also diagnostic: warts show thrombosed capillaries (black dots) and interrupt skin lines; corns have a central translucent core and skin lines pass around them; calluses are diffuse with no core.

## Indications
- Plantar and palmar warts (before salicylic acid, cryotherapy or other topical treatment)
- Hard corns (heloma durum), soft interdigital corns (heloma molle)
- Calluses over pressure points
- Diagnostic paring when wart and corn cannot be told apart

## Contraindications
- Peripheral vascular disease or poor foot pulses (refer to podiatry or vascular)
- Diabetic or other neuropathic foot: only with extreme care, superficial paring, never to bleeding
- Bleeding disorder or anticoagulants (relative; superficial only)
- Local infection or ulceration

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: mild discomfort, small risk of bleeding and infection; recurrence is common
- Check foot pulses and sensation (monofilament) in diabetics
- Soak the area in warm water for 10–15 minutes to soften keratin
- No anaesthesia is usually needed because the tissue is avascular; stop at sensitivity

## Equipment
- No. 15 or No. 10 scalpel blade on a handle (or disposable scalpel)
- Gauze, povidone-iodine or spirit, gloves
- Foot pumice, hydrocolloid or felt padding
- Salicylic acid 12–40% preparations for after-care

## Procedure step by step
1. Clean the area with antiseptic; wear gloves (warts are infectious).
2. Stretch the skin with the non-dominant hand.
3. Hold the blade almost parallel to the skin and shave thin layers in a controlled, sweeping movement.
4. **Wart endpoint**: pinpoint bleeding points or the black dots appear and the wart surface is level with surrounding skin. Stop at the first pinpoint bleeding.
5. **Corn endpoint**: the translucent central core is exposed; enucleate it with the blade tip, keeping within the core. Stop when the patient feels pressure-tenderness relief or there is any pink tissue.
6. **Callus**: pare until surrounding skin is level; do not go to bleeding.
7. Achieve haemostasis with pressure; apply a dry dressing or the topical agent.
8. For corns, apply a felt ring or silicone pad to offload pressure.

## Post-procedure care
- Warts: salicylic acid nightly after soaking and filing; cover with tape; pare again at each visit
- Corns/calluses: correct footwear, silicone pads, insoles; urea 10–20% cream daily
- Keep the area clean and dry; use own towels and footwear (warts)

## Complications & management
- Bleeding: pressure; it usually stops quickly
- Infection: topical antibiotic; oral antibiotic for cellulitis
- Over-paring causing pain on walking: offload and allow healing
- Neuropathic ulcer in diabetics: stop and refer to diabetic foot clinic

## Sessions & follow-up
- Warts: pare every 2–3 weeks along with topical therapy or cryotherapy; most need 3–6 months
- Corns: recur unless the pressure source is removed; refer to podiatry or orthopaedics for bony deformity

posts.title: Punch biopsy
posts.summary: Full-thickness skin sample with a circular punch for histopathology or DIF
posts.body:
A punch biopsy gives a full-thickness cylinder of epidermis, dermis and upper fat. It is the standard biopsy for inflammatory dermatoses and many tumours. Choosing the right lesion and site, and handling the specimen gently, matters more than the technique itself.

## Indications
- Inflammatory dermatoses where histology helps (lichenoid, psoriasiform, granulomatous, vasculitis)
- Immunobullous disease: lesional biopsy for H&E, perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence (DIF)
- Suspected tumours where an incisional sample is enough (small BCC, CTCL, granulomas)
- Hansen's disease and other infections (with tissue for culture)
- Hair disorders (4 mm scalp biopsies for horizontal and vertical sections)

## Contraindications
- Infection at the site
- Uncontrolled bleeding diathesis (relative; do not stop warfarin or antiplatelets for a punch biopsy, check INR if very high)
- Allergy to local anaesthetic (use alternative agent or saline)
- Lesions where full excision is needed (suspected melanoma: excision biopsy preferred)
- Caution: shins in elderly or diabetic patients, over nerves (lateral neck, ulnar groove, temple)

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: small scar, bleeding, infection, hypertrophic scar or keloid (ask about history), pigment change
- Choose a new, fully developed, untreated lesion; avoid excoriated, crusted or ulcerated areas
- Blister: lesional for H&E at edge of a fresh blister; DIF from perilesional skin within 1 cm
- Label the site on a diagram; photograph
- Request form with history and differential diagnoses

## Equipment
- Sterile punch 3–4 mm (6 mm for panniculitis or alopecia, 2 mm for face)
- Lignocaine 2% (with adrenaline unless contraindicated), 26–30G needle
- Fine-toothed forceps or skin hook, iris scissors, needle holder
- Suture: 4-0 nylon/silk (body), 5-0 or 6-0 (face)
- Formalin 10% (volume 10–20 times the specimen) and Michel's medium or saline for DIF

## Procedure step by step
1. Clean with povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine; drape.
2. Infiltrate local anaesthetic intradermally around and under the site (lignocaine maximum ~4.5 mg/kg plain, ~7 mg/kg with adrenaline).
3. Stretch the skin perpendicular to the relaxed skin tension lines so the wound becomes an ellipse.
4. Hold the punch vertical and rotate with gentle downward pressure until you feel a give at the subcutaneous fat.
5. Lift the core with a needle or forceps holding only the fat; avoid crushing the epidermis.
6. Cut the base at the level of fat with scissors.
7. Place immediately in formalin (or Michel's/saline for DIF). Label clearly.
8. Achieve haemostasis with pressure; close with one or two simple interrupted sutures (3 mm may heal by secondary intention).
9. Apply antibiotic ointment and a dressing.

## Post-procedure care
- Keep dry for 24–48 h; then clean daily with water and apply ointment
- Suture removal: face 5–7 days; trunk and arms 10–14 days; legs and back 14 days
- Report fever, spreading redness or pus

## Complications & management
- Bleeding: firm pressure for 10 minutes; additional suture
- Infection: topical or oral antibiotic
- Hypertrophic scar or keloid: intralesional steroid
- Non-diagnostic sample: discuss with the pathologist; rebiopsy with better site choice

## Sessions & follow-up
- Single procedure; review at suture removal
- Follow up the histopathology report and correlate clinically

posts.title: Radiofrequency vs electrocautery
posts.summary: How RF and cautery differ, modes, pacemaker precautions, steps and plume safety
posts.body:
Both devices remove or coagulate tissue using heat, but they work differently, and choosing the right one matters for safety and cosmesis.

## Principle
- **Radiofrequency (RF)**: high-frequency alternating current (around 4 MHz) passes through the tissue. Cell water heats and vaporises at the electrode tip, giving "cold" cutting with minimal lateral heat damage and less charring.
- **Electrocautery (EC)**: a metal tip is heated by current, and the heat is transferred to tissue by direct contact. No current passes through the patient. It chars more and spreads heat more widely.

## Modes (RF)
- **Cut**: fully filtered current, clean incision with little haemostasis
- **Cut-coag (blend)**: cutting with some haemostasis
- **Coag**: haemostasis, tissue shrinkage
- **Fulguration**: spark gap from the tip held slightly off the skin; superficial destruction

## Indications
- DPN, seborrhoeic keratosis, skin tags, syringoma, small warts
- Shave excision of naevi (benign, for cosmesis) and biopsies
- Haemostasis during minor surgery
- Rhinophyma sculpting, sebaceous hyperplasia, xanthelasma (careful use)

## Contraindications
- Pacemaker or ICD: avoid RF (current can interfere); use EC instead
- Flammable surroundings: alcohol not dried, oxygen in use
- Uncertain diagnosis: biopsy first
- Keloid tendency (relative)

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: scab, pigment changes, scar, recurrence
- Ask about pacemaker, implants and metal near the site
- Topical or local anaesthesia
- Let alcohol dry fully; keep oxygen away

## Equipment
- RF unit or EC unit (check your machine's settings — they vary)
- Electrodes: **loop** (shave excision), **ball** (coagulation), **fine needle** (DPN, syringoma)
- Passive (return) plate when required by the manual
- Smoke evacuator and surgical mask
- Saline gauze, antibiotic ointment, sunscreen

## Procedure step by step
1. Consent and mark lesions.
2. Clean with antiseptic and let alcohol dry fully.
3. Give local anaesthetic.
4. Place the passive plate if the machine requires it, close to the site, on dry, hairless skin.
5. Choose the electrode and mode for the lesion.
6. Start at the lowest power; increase until the tissue responds without drag or sparking.
7. Switch on the smoke evacuator; staff and patient wear masks (plume may contain HPV and other particles).
8. Use quick, light strokes; avoid lingering at one spot.
9. Wipe char with saline gauze, then re-check depth.
10. **Endpoint**: lesion removed or flattened, with surrounding skin intact.

## Post-procedure care
- Antibiotic ointment twice daily until healed
- Sunscreen for 4–6 weeks to limit PIH
- Do not pick the scab

## Complications & management
- Burn at plate site: correct plate placement
- PIH or hypopigmentation: sunscreen; lower power
- Scar: avoid deep or repeated passes
- Infection: topical or oral antibiotics
- Fire: never use with wet alcohol or oxygen

## Sessions & follow-up
- Review at 1–2 weeks for healing
- Touch-up at 4–6 weeks as needed

posts.title: Salicylic acid peel
posts.summary: Lipophilic superficial peel for acne, oily skin and PIH; safe in skin types IV–V
posts.body:
Salicylic acid (SA) is a lipophilic beta-hydroxy acid. It dissolves in sebum, so it works well in the follicle and on oily, acne-prone skin. Clinic strength is usually 20–30% in an ethanol base. It is a superficial peel, comedolytic and mildly anti-inflammatory, and among the safest peels for Indian skin.

## Indications
- Comedonal and mild–moderate inflammatory acne
- Post-acne PIH, oily skin, enlarged pores
- Superficial melasma and facial melanoses (adjunct to topical therapy)
- Rough photo-damaged texture, keratosis pilaris (body)

## Contraindications
- Salicylate (aspirin) allergy
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding
- Active infection at the site: herpes labialis, impetigo, warts, open wounds
- Eczema, dermatitis or recent sunburn at the site
- Unrealistic expectations or poor sun-protection compliance
- Large-area peels in renal or hepatic disease (salicylism risk)

## Pre-procedure
- Written consent: expected stinging, dryness, flaking, and possible PIH
- Counsel that 4–6 sessions are needed and results are gradual
- **Priming 2–4 weeks**: broad-spectrum sunscreen + 2–4% hydroquinone or azelaic acid ± tretinoin 0.025% at night
- Stop retinoids and scrubs 3–5 days before; no waxing or threading for 1 week
- Herpes history: start acyclovir/valacyclovir on the day of the peel
- Test patch behind the ear or on the jawline before the first full peel
- Clinical photographs in standard lighting

## Equipment
- SA 20% and 30% solution, gloves, gauze, cotton-tipped applicators
- Cleanser, alcohol or acetone for degreasing
- Petrolatum for the nasal alae, lip commissures and inner canthi
- Hand-held fan, timer, cool water, ice packs

## Procedure step by step
1. Cleanse the face and degrease with alcohol or acetone; let it dry.
2. Protect the eyes; apply petrolatum to the alar creases, commissures and canthi.
3. Apply the first coat quickly and evenly with gauze: forehead, cheeks, nose, chin, then perioral.
4. Expect burning for 1–2 minutes, then a relative numbness from the anaesthetic effect of SA; use the fan.
5. **Endpoint**: an even white crystalline precipitate (pseudofrost) with mild erythema, usually at 3–5 minutes. This is salicylic acid crystallising, not protein coagulation.
6. A second coat can be applied to oily or acne-prone areas in later sessions.
7. Neutralisation is not required (the peel is self-limiting). Wash off with plain water after 3–5 minutes.
8. Apply a bland moisturiser and sunscreen before the patient leaves.

## Post-procedure care
- Gentle cleanser, plain moisturiser, SPF 30+ reapplied every 3 hours outdoors
- Do not pick or peel the flakes; mild flaking lasts 2–4 days
- Restart priming agents after 3–5 days once the skin is calm

## Complications & management
- Excess erythema or burning: cool compresses, mid-potency topical steroid for 2–3 days
- PIH: hydroquinone or azelaic acid, strict photoprotection; space out sessions
- Acneiform flare: usually settles with continued treatment
- Herpes reactivation: treatment-dose antiviral
- Salicylism (tinnitus, nausea, dizziness) with large areas: stop and wash off; avoid body peels over large surfaces

## Sessions & follow-up
- Every 2–3 weeks for 4–6 sessions; start at 20% and step up to 30% if tolerated
- Review the photographs at each visit; continue maintenance topicals between sessions

posts.title: Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) peel
posts.summary: Non-neutralised peel graded by frost; superficial use and TCA CROSS for scars
posts.body:
Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) coagulates epidermal proteins and produces a visible **frost**. Depth depends on concentration, number of coats, how much is applied and how the skin is prepared. It does not need neutralising, and it is not systemically toxic. Concentrations of 10–25% act superficially. At 35% and above it reaches the papillary dermis (medium depth), and in skin types IV–V scarring and PIH become real risks.

## Indications
- Superficial (10–20%): melasma, PIH, lentigines, fine lines, superficial acne scars
- Medium-depth (35%, usually combined with Jessner's or GA): rarely used in Indian skin; consider only after careful selection
- **TCA CROSS** (70–100%, focal): ice-pick and narrow boxcar acne scars
- Focal: xanthelasma, seborrhoeic keratoses (experienced hands only)

## Contraindications
- Active infection or dermatitis at the site, open wounds
- Keloid or hypertrophic scar tendency
- Isotretinoin in the past 6 months (deeper peels)
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding
- Previous radiotherapy at the site, poor wound healing
- Inability to follow sun protection and aftercare

## Pre-procedure
- Written consent: visible peeling for 5–7 days, PIH, scarring and hypopigmentation
- **Priming 2–4 weeks** with tretinoin and hydroquinone; this is essential in skin types IV–V
- Antiviral prophylaxis for perioral and full-face peels
- Test spot with the planned concentration
- Baseline photographs

## Equipment
- Freshly made TCA in the required w/v concentration, in labelled amber bottles
- Cotton-tipped applicators (moist, not dripping), gauze
- For CROSS: wooden toothpick or fine applicator
- Degreaser, petrolatum, cold compresses, fan

## Procedure step by step
1. Cleanse and degrease thoroughly; uneven degreasing gives patchy frost.
2. Protect the eyes; apply petrolatum to the alae, commissures and canthi.
3. Apply TCA one cosmetic unit at a time, with even strokes.
4. Wait 2–3 minutes after each coat; frost develops slowly. Add a further coat only where the frost is short of the target.
5. **Endpoints by frost level**:
- Level I: erythema with scattered speckles of frost (superficial; the usual goal in skin types IV–V)
- Level II: white frost with pink showing through (upper papillary dermis)
- Level III: solid opaque white frost (deeper; avoid in brown skin except focal CROSS)
6. Apply cool compresses for comfort. No neutralisation is needed.
7. **TCA CROSS**: press the sharpened applicator into the base of each pitted scar for a few seconds, until the scar turns white. Do not treat adjacent normal skin.

## Post-procedure care
- Skin darkens and peels on days 3–7; do not pick
- Bland ointment or moisturiser, gentle cleanser, strict photoprotection
- Restart priming agents only after peeling is complete

## Complications & management
- PIH: common in skin types IV–V; hydroquinone, sunscreen, delay further peels
- Persistent erythema beyond 3 weeks: suspect impending scarring and start a potent topical steroid early
- Hypertrophic scarring: intralesional steroid, silicone gel
- Infection (bacterial, candida, herpes): swab and treat promptly
- Hypopigmentation or demarcation lines: feather the edges at the jawline

## Sessions & follow-up
- Superficial TCA every 3–4 weeks for 3–4 sessions
- TCA CROSS every 4–6 weeks for 3–6 sessions
- Review at day 7 after the first peel

posts.title: Whole-body phototherapy (cabin NB-UVB ± PUVA)
posts.summary: Cabin NB-UVB and PUVA: dosing, protection, missed doses, logs, stopping
posts.body:
Whole-body phototherapy treats patients standing in a cabin lined with UV tubes. NB-UVB (311 nm) is first line; PUVA (oral psoralen plus UVA) is reserved for thick or resistant disease. Safe practice depends on careful dosing and record-keeping.

## Indications
- Psoriasis involving more than ~10% body surface area, or resistant to topicals
- Generalised vitiligo (NB-UVB is first line)
- Atopic dermatitis, generalised pruritus, prurigo
- Mycosis fungoides (patch / thin plaque: NB-UVB; thicker plaque: PUVA)
- PLE prophylaxis, lichen planus, pityriasis lichenoides

## Contraindications
- Absolute: XP, photosensitive lupus, porphyria, history of melanoma; PUVA: pregnancy, breastfeeding, children under 12 (for oral psoralen)
- Relative: multiple NMSC, photosensitising drugs, immunosuppressants, cataract, liver disease (PUVA), claustrophobia, unable to stand for several minutes
- NB-UVB is acceptable in pregnancy (consider folate supplement)

## Pre-procedure
- Consent: long course, 2–3 visits per week; erythema, itching, tanning; skin-cancer and cataract risk with PUVA
- Determine skin type (Fitzpatrick) and, if available, **MED** (NB-UVB) or **MPD** (PUVA)
- Baseline: drug history, ANA if suspicion of lupus, LFT for PUVA, eye check for PUVA
- Photographs, PASI/BSA or VASI

## Equipment
- Calibrated cabin; UV meter; dosimetry software or log book
- UV-blocking goggles for every session
- Genital protection (shields for men), face shield if face not affected
- PUVA: 8-methoxypsoralen tablets; UVA-blocking glasses for after the session

## Procedure step by step
1. **Starting dose (NB-UVB)**: 70% of MED, or by skin type when MED is not done (psoriasis: roughly 0.33 J/cm² for type IV and 0.35 J/cm² for type V). Vitiligo is commonly started at a fixed low dose of about 0.2 J/cm² regardless of type.
2. **Increments**: 10–20% each session if no erythema; hold if mild erythema.
3. **PUVA**: give 8-MOP 0.6 mg/kg orally 1.5–2 hours before exposure with food; start UVA around 1.5–2.5 J/cm² for skin types IV–V (or 70% of MPD); increase by 0.5–1 J/cm² per session; treat twice weekly, not on consecutive days.
4. Patient stands in the centre of the cabin with goggles and genital protection.
5. **Endpoint**: faint, painless erythema the next day (NB-UVB) or at 48–72 h (PUVA, so no dose increase within 72 h of a previous increase).
6. **Missed-dose rules (NB-UVB)**:
- Under 1 week: same dose
- 1–2 weeks: reduce by 25%
- 2–3 weeks: reduce by 50%
- More than 3–4 weeks: restart at the initial dose
7. **Cumulative dose log**: record each session's dose and running total; document the number of treatments.

## Post-procedure care
- PUVA: UVA-blocking glasses for 12–24 hours after psoralen and sun protection on that day
- Emollients; avoid extra sun exposure on treatment days
- Report erythema, blistering or itching

## Complications & management
- Painful erythema: skip until settled; resume at 10–20% lower dose
- Blistering: stop until healed; resume at 50% of the last dose
- Nausea from psoralen: take with food, split dose
- Polymorphic light eruption: reduce dose
- Long-term: photoageing and skin-cancer risk (higher with PUVA, especially beyond about 150–200 treatments)

## Sessions & follow-up
- NB-UVB: 2–3 times weekly; PUVA: twice weekly
- Psoriasis: clearance usually takes 20–30 sessions
- Vitiligo: assess at 3 and 6 months; stop if no repigmentation at 6 months
- Stop at clearance; taper only if relapse risk is high
- Annual skin examination for long courses

posts.title: Wood's lamp examination
posts.summary: 365 nm UVA examination: fluorescence patterns and pigment depth
posts.body:
A Wood's lamp emits long-wave UVA (peak about 365 nm) through a nickel oxide filter. Under it, some organisms and compounds fluoresce, and differences in epidermal pigment become easier to see. It is a quick, painless bedside test.

## Indications
- Vitiligo: diagnosis, extent, and activity in fair or early lesions
- Fungal and bacterial infections: tinea capitis, pityriasis versicolor, erythrasma, Pseudomonas
- Pigmentary disorders: depth of pigment in melasma, ash-leaf macules in tuberous sclerosis, hypopigmented macules
- Porphyria: urine, stool or teeth fluorescence
- Comedones and acne bacteria (orange-red fluorescence)

## Contraindications
- None important
- Do not look directly into the lamp
- Do not use on recently washed or treated skin (topicals and soaps alter or mask fluorescence)

## Pre-procedure
- Explain that the room will be dark and the test is painless
- Ask the patient not to apply topicals or wash the area before the test
- Warm up the lamp for about 1 minute

## Equipment
- Wood's lamp (with magnifier if possible)
- Dark room
- Comparison normal skin

## Procedure step by step
1. Darken the room fully; allow the examiner's eyes to adapt for about 1 minute.
2. Hold the lamp 10–15 cm from the skin.
3. Examine the lesion and compare with normal skin.
4. **Interpret findings**:
- Vitiligo: sharp, bright blue-white (milky) depigmentation
- Hypopigmentation (pityriasis alba, leprosy, post-inflammatory): less contrast, off-white
- Ash-leaf macules: more visible
- Epidermal pigment (e.g. epidermal melasma): accentuated; dermal pigment is not
- Tinea capitis (Microsporum): bright green; T. schoenleinii: dull blue-green; T. tonsurans: none
- Pityriasis versicolor: yellow to coppery-orange
- Erythrasma: coral red
- Pseudomonas: green
- Porphyria: pink-red urine or teeth
5. Record the findings; photograph if possible.

## Post-procedure care
- None needed

## Complications & management
- None significant
- False positives: lint, soap, creams, cosmetics, ink
- False negatives: recent washing, topical antifungals, non-fluorescent species
- In skin types IV–V, epidermal vs dermal melasma differentiation is less reliable; use dermoscopy as well

## Sessions & follow-up
- Repeat at follow-up visits to track vitiligo extent and response
- Recheck tinea capitis fluorescence after treatment
